name: or-block-utilization
description: Reviews operating room block time allocation and recommends releases, additions, or reallocation. Use when a surgeon or service line asks for more block time, when prime-time utilization drops below the committee threshold, when the OR committee is preparing its quarterly block review, or when the schedule is full of late add-on cases while rooms sit empty.
expansions: surgeon wants more block time
or prime time sitting empty
quarterly block release review
orthopedics asking for another room day
block utilization below seventy percent
too many late add-on cases
first case on-time starts slipping
turnover times dragging out the day

atoms.obligation: Calculate block utilization from actual in-room to out-of-room minutes plus one turnover, never from scheduled case length.
atoms.lesson: Committees typically set prime-time block utilization targets at 75 to 80 percent, measured as in-room to out-of-room minutes plus one standard turnover per case, divided by allocated block minutes. Using scheduled minutes instead of actual hides no-shows, early finishes, and chronic overbooking by the same surgeons who complain about access. Exclude blocks released before the automatic release window from both numerator and denominator, since that time already returned to open scheduling.

atoms.obligation: Report block abandonment separately from utilization so time given back too late to fill is not credited as efficiency.
atoms.lesson: Abandonment is the share of allocated minutes returned inside the release window, commonly seven to fourteen days for elective service lines. A surgeon running 85 percent utilization who abandons a third of the block still starves the room, because time released at 72 hours almost never fills. Track release lead time by surgeon, and trigger reallocation only after two consecutive quarters so vacation and case-mix swings do not drive the decision.

atoms.obligation: Convert any proposed block change into staffed room-days and confirm anesthesia and recovery coverage before promising a service line new time.
atoms.lesson: A block grant is a staffing commitment, not calendar space. One eight-hour room-day generally needs a circulator, a scrub tech, an anesthesiologist or CRNA, and post-anesthesia recovery capacity. Evening and weekend blocks trigger premium pay and usually expose a PACU or sterile processing bottleneck rather than an OR bottleneck. Anesthesia group contracts often cap concurrently staffed rooms and attach a subsidy to each additional site of service, so check coverage terms first.

atoms.obligation: Present first-case on-time starts and room turnover as separate measures, because different departments own each one.
atoms.lesson: On-time starts depend on pre-op arrival time, consent and marking, and surgeon arrival; turnover depends on environmental services, instrument tray availability, and how quickly the next patient is ready in pre-op. Blending them into a single efficiency score lets surgeons and nursing blame each other indefinitely. A workable standard is 80 percent of first cases in the room by scheduled time and 30-minute turnover for general cases, with longer targets for total joints and cardiac.

name: clinic-template-redesign
description: Rebuilds outpatient clinic scheduling templates so slot types, lengths, and volumes match real demand and real visit duration. Use when third-next-available keeps climbing, when a newly hired provider needs a template built from scratch, when a clinic wants to add same-day capacity, or when providers say they run an hour behind every session.
expansions: third next available keeps climbing
new provider needs a schedule template
clinic wants same day slots
visits running longer than the slot
follow-ups crowding out new patients
provider says the template is unworkable
adding a half day of procedures
rebuild template for the two-provider pod

atoms.obligation: Measure third-next-available separately for new and established visit types before changing any slot in the template.
atoms.lesson: Third next available is the standard access measure because the first two openings are usually late cancellations and overstate true access. Typical targets are about seven days for new primary care and fourteen for specialty consults. New and established demand behave differently, so a blended average of ten days can conceal a 45-day new-patient wait when follow-ups are allowed to consume unrestricted slots. Sample on the same weekday each week to avoid Monday inflation.

atoms.obligation: Set slot length from the seventy-fifth percentile of observed visit duration for each visit type, not from the historical template.
atoms.lesson: A fifteen-minute follow-up that actually runs twenty-one minutes puts the provider a full hour behind by mid-session, and the clinic pays in overtime, complaints, and late lunch breaks. Pull room-in to provider-out times for at least eight weeks by visit type. Complex visits such as new consults, wound care, Medicare annual wellness visits, and anticoagulation management deserve their own slot type rather than being squeezed into the standard grid.

atoms.obligation: Compare weekly appointment demand against template supply for each provider and address panel size before adding slots.
atoms.lesson: Access failure is usually a demand and supply mismatch rather than a template defect. Estimate demand as appointment requests per week including calls that end without a booking, and supply as slots offered per week times sessions actually worked. A primary care panel of roughly 1,800 to 2,200 patients per full-time physician generates three to four visits per patient-year. When demand persistently exceeds supply, rearranging the grid changes nothing; close the panel or recruit.

atoms.obligation: Protect a fixed share of same-day capacity in every session and write an explicit rule for when unused slots release.
atoms.lesson: Carved-out same-day capacity only works when it is defended. Reserve roughly the observed same-day demand, often 25 to 35 percent of primary care sessions, and release the unused portion at a set hour such as ten in the morning for afternoon slots. Without a release rule the slots sit empty and providers lose confidence in the template. Never allow routine follow-ups to be pre-booked into same-day slots the day before.

name: no-show-reduction-plan
description: Diagnoses missed appointments and builds a reduction plan covering reminders, confirmation, overbooking, and access barriers. Use when a clinic reports a rising no-show rate, when providers ask to overbook, when a specific population or clinic session is missing appointments disproportionately, or when leadership wants to know what empty slots are costing.
expansions: no show rate climbing in behavioral health
providers asking to double book
empty chairs in the afternoon session
what are missed appointments costing us
reminder calls do not seem to work
medicaid patients missing more visits
same day cancellations spiking
first appointment after referral never happens

atoms.obligation: Define no-show, late cancellation, and same-day cancellation distinctly and count each against scheduled visits by clinic session.
atoms.lesson: Mixing categories makes every intervention look ineffective. A no-show is an arrival failure with no notice; a late cancellation typically means notice inside 24 hours, which is still unfillable but signals different patient behavior. Rates vary enormously by specialty: primary care often runs 5 to 12 percent, behavioral health and safety-net dental frequently exceed 25 percent. Report by clinic, session, day of week, and appointment lead time, since bookings made more than 30 days out fail far more often.

atoms.obligation: Segment missed appointments by patient population and lead time before choosing any intervention.
atoms.lesson: No-shows concentrate. Common drivers are long booking lead time, transportation, hourly work schedules, childcare, interpreter needs, and prior negative experience with the clinic. A blanket reminder campaign spends the same effort on patients who never miss visits. Segmenting usually reveals that a small share of appointment types and time slots produce most losses, which directs effort toward transport vouchers, evening sessions, interpreter scheduling, or shorter booking horizons instead of more phone calls.

atoms.obligation: Build a layered reminder sequence with a real confirmation response and a defined path for reaching unconfirmed patients.
atoms.lesson: Reminders reduce missed visits only when they allow the patient to cancel or rebook easily. A workable sequence is a text seven days out, a text or call two days out that accepts a confirm or cancel reply, and same-day outreach to unconfirmed high-risk appointments. Verify contact numbers at every registration, since bad phone data drives much of the failure. Cancellations harvested this way are useful only if the clinic has a waitlist ready to fill them.

atoms.obligation: Base any overbooking on the measured no-show rate for that specific slot type, and review discharge policies for fairness.
atoms.lesson: Overbooking a session with a 20 percent no-show rate means adding roughly one extra patient per five slots, placed where late arrivals do the least harm rather than at the end of the session. Overbooking a low no-show clinic just creates waiting-room delays and provider overtime. Policies that dismiss patients after three missed visits fall hardest on patients with transportation and work barriers and can create access and compliance problems for Medicaid populations, so review them before enforcing.

name: ed-throughput-review
description: Analyzes emergency department flow and identifies where patients are waiting and why. Use when left-without-being-seen climbs, when ambulances are being diverted, when admitted patients are boarding in the department for hours, or when leadership wants an intervention plan for waiting room times and door-to-provider intervals.
expansions: lwbs rate doubled last month
admitted patients boarding all night
ambulance diversion three times this week
door to provider time is awful
waiting room full at shift change
psych patients holding for days
fast track never seems to help
triage backing up on weekends

atoms.obligation: Break total length of stay into arrival to triage, triage to provider, provider to disposition, and disposition to departure.
atoms.lesson: Each interval has a different owner and a different fix. Arrival to triage reflects greeting and intake staffing; triage to provider reflects room availability and provider coverage; provider to disposition reflects imaging and lab turnaround plus consultant response; disposition to departure is boarding, which belongs to inpatient capacity, not the emergency department. Common benchmarks are under thirty minutes door to provider and under sixty minutes from admit decision to inpatient bed.

atoms.obligation: State plainly when boarding, not arrival volume, is the constraint, and route the fix to inpatient capacity rather than the department.
atoms.lesson: Crowding is usually an output problem. When admitted patients occupy treatment spaces for four or more hours after the admit decision, effective bed count falls and every downstream interval degrades regardless of triage effort. Boarding correlates with mortality, ambulance diversion, and left-without-being-seen. Fixes live upstream in the hospital: earlier discharge orders, weekend discharge staffing, ancillary coverage, and inpatient bed assignment rules. Adding emergency department staff to a boarding problem buys almost nothing.

atoms.obligation: Track left-without-being-seen and elopement by hour of day and acuity level, not as a single monthly figure.
atoms.lesson: Left-without-being-seen above about two percent signals unsafe waiting, and it clusters sharply between late afternoon and midnight when arrival volume peaks against fixed staffing. Break it out by triage acuity, since low-acuity walkouts are a revenue and access issue while level three walkouts are a safety issue that belongs in the safety event review. Pair the rate with median wait at the time of walkout so the trigger point becomes visible.

atoms.obligation: Match provider and nurse coverage to the arrival curve by hour rather than to twelve-hour block convenience.
atoms.lesson: Emergency arrivals follow a predictable daily curve, typically rising from mid-morning, peaking between noon and eight in the evening, and falling after midnight, with Monday the heaviest day in most communities. Staffing on uniform twelve-hour blocks guarantees an afternoon deficit and an overnight surplus. Overlapping or staggered shifts, a provider in triage during the peak, and vertical or results-waiting areas for ambulatory patients tend to move door-to-provider time more than any process redesign.

name: bed-capacity-escalation
description: Runs the hospital capacity huddle and defines escalation tiers when beds run short. Use when census is at or above the safe operating threshold, when the house supervisor needs an escalation plan, when elective admissions may need deferral, or when leadership wants a standing structure for daily bed management and surge response.
expansions: census at ninety five percent again
house supervisor needs escalation criteria
should we defer elective admissions
bed huddle is not producing decisions
telemetry beds full but medsurg open
surge plan has not been updated
discharges all happening after five
holding admissions in pacu overnight

atoms.obligation: Run a short structured capacity huddle at fixed times with named accountable roles and decisions recorded on the spot.
atoms.lesson: An effective huddle takes fifteen minutes, runs at least twice daily, and includes the house supervisor, charge nurses, case management, emergency department, environmental services, and the operating room. Each unit reports current census, expected discharges with times, pending admissions, and specific barriers. Without a decision owner named in the room, huddles become status recitals. The output should be a bed plan for the next eight hours, not a list of problems for someone else to solve.

atoms.obligation: Predict discharges by hour rather than by day, and require a named barrier for every patient not leaving before noon.
atoms.lesson: Hospitals fill in the morning and empty in the late afternoon, which is why the emergency department and post-anesthesia care unit absorb the mismatch. Discharge before noon rates commonly sit near 15 percent when hospitals target 30 or more. Useful barriers are concrete: pending ride, awaiting infusion, no skilled nursing bed, physician has not rounded, discharge summary unsigned. Categorized barriers reveal whether the constraint is transport, placement, or physician workflow.

atoms.obligation: Write escalation tiers with numeric triggers and pre-approved actions rather than leaving the response to judgment at the moment.
atoms.lesson: Tiers usually key on occupancy percent, boarded admissions, and unstaffed beds. For example, green under 85 percent occupancy, yellow at 85 to 92 with expanded discharge rounds and staffing calls, red above 92 or with more than six boarders triggering elective deferral review, opening flex space, and administrator on call notification. Naming the actions in advance is what makes escalation happen at three in the morning without a debate.

atoms.obligation: Use peak and midnight census together, and count staffed beds rather than licensed beds when reporting capacity.
atoms.lesson: Midnight census is a billing convention and understates the crowding that actually occurs at four in the afternoon. Licensed beds are a certificate number; staffed beds are what nursing can safely cover today, and the gap can be dozens of beds. Capacity must also be reported by unit type, since a hospital with open medical-surgical beds and no telemetry or negative-pressure beds is functionally full for the patients waiting in the emergency department.

name: avoidable-day-review
description: Reviews long-stay inpatients to find and categorize days of care that no longer required the hospital. Use when observed length of stay is running above the expected benchmark, when case management needs to explain outlier cases to leadership, when patients are stuck awaiting placement, or when denials cite lack of continued medical necessity.
expansions: length of stay above geometric mean
patients stuck waiting for snf beds
case management outlier list review
payer denying the last four days
guardianship case sitting for weeks
why is this patient still here
observation status conversions questioned
weekend discharges basically stopped

atoms.obligation: Compare observed length of stay against the expected value for the same diagnosis group and severity, never against a hospital-wide average.
atoms.lesson: Length of stay is only interpretable against case mix. Use the geometric mean length of stay for the assigned diagnosis-related group, which is also what drives transfer and outlier payment rules, and review the observed over expected ratio by service line. A ratio near 1.0 with wide variance points to a few extreme outliers rather than systemic delay. Arithmetic means are pulled badly by the ten percent of patients waiting on placement.

atoms.obligation: Assign every non-acute day a specific barrier reason code and the department that owns clearing it.
atoms.lesson: Standard categories include awaiting skilled nursing or rehabilitation placement, insurance authorization pending, guardianship or capacity determination, homelessness or no safe discharge destination, family decision delay, physician rounding or order delay, dialysis chair availability, and internal test scheduling. Coding days this way turns anecdote into a ranked work list. Placement and authorization usually dominate volume, while physician order timing dominates the short one-day delays that recur across every unit.

atoms.obligation: Confirm patient status matches the documented level of care before the stay ends, not after billing rejects it.
atoms.lesson: Inpatient versus observation status turns on expected length of stay and documented medical necessity, with the two-midnight expectation as the Medicare benchmark and condition code 44 available only while the patient remains hospitalized and with concurrence from utilization review and the attending. Corrections after discharge require a costly self-denial rebill. Utilization review must touch each case within a day of admission and again at the second midnight, when the decision is still fixable.

atoms.obligation: Track discharge volume by day of week and identify what specifically stops on the weekend.
atoms.lesson: Most hospitals discharge far fewer patients on Saturday and Sunday, which pushes census into Monday and lengthens stays by one to two days for patients who become ready on Friday afternoon. The usual culprits are absent case management, no weekend physical therapy evaluation, closed imaging modalities, and skilled nursing facilities that do not accept weekend admissions. Fixing one link alone does nothing; the chain has to be staffed together to shift the pattern.

name: prior-authorization-workflow
description: Designs and troubleshoots the prior authorization process for procedures, imaging, infusions, and specialty drugs. Use when services are being performed without authorization, when scheduled cases are cancelled at the last minute for missing approval, when payers add new authorization requirements, or when denials trace back to intake rather than clinical care.
expansions: case cancelled morning of for no auth
payer added auth for advanced imaging
infusion started before approval came
auth expired before the procedure date
peer to peer requests piling up
who owns getting the authorization
units approved fewer than administered
referrals sitting unworked for two weeks

atoms.obligation: Maintain a current list of which procedure codes each payer requires authorization for and check it at scheduling, not at check-in.
atoms.lesson: Authorization requirements change quarterly and differ by plan product within the same payer, especially for advanced imaging, sleep studies, spine and joint surgery, infusion biologics, and outpatient behavioral health. Many plans delegate radiology and musculoskeletal review to a vendor with its own portal and clinical criteria. Screening at scheduling gives a week or more of lead time; screening at arrival guarantees either a cancellation or a service delivered at financial risk.

atoms.obligation: Record the authorization number, approved code set, unit or visit count, and validity dates in the account before the service happens.
atoms.lesson: Approvals are narrow. An authorization is tied to specific procedure codes, a date range often thirty to ninety days, a site of service, a rendering provider, and a unit count. Cases fail when the surgeon changes approach, an assistant surgeon is added, the service moves from hospital outpatient to the ambulatory center, or infusion doses exceed approved units. Any of these requires an update request before delivery, since retroactive amendment is rarely granted.

atoms.obligation: Escalate adverse determinations to peer-to-peer review inside the payer window and record the reviewer, time, and outcome.
atoms.lesson: Peer-to-peer windows are short, often 24 to 72 hours from the adverse decision, and once missed the case drops into the slower formal appeal path. The requesting physician needs the payer's clinical criteria in hand, since the reviewer is scoring against a specific rule set such as conservative therapy duration, imaging findings, or failed first-line agents. Logging reviewer names and denial rationale by payer builds the pattern evidence needed at contract renewal.

atoms.obligation: Trace authorization-related denials back to the step that failed and report them to the department that owns that step.
atoms.lesson: Authorization denials are almost never a coding error; they originate in scheduling, referral intake, or clinical documentation. Route each one to its origin: no authorization obtained, wrong code authorized, expired approval, wrong site of service, or notification of admission not given within the required window, which is frequently 24 to 48 hours for urgent inpatient admissions. Without this feedback loop the revenue cycle keeps writing off the same preventable failure every month.

name: claim-denial-appeals
description: Works payer denials into categorized root causes and builds appeals that stand a chance. Use when the denial rate or write-off volume rises, when a payer is systematically denying a service line, when an appeal deadline is approaching, or when someone needs to decide whether a specific denial is worth appealing at all.
expansions: denial rate jumped this quarter
payer denying all observation claims
appeal deadline in four days
is this denial worth appealing
medical necessity denials on cardiac cases
overturn rate on first level appeals
underpayment versus outright denial
downgraded from inpatient to observation

atoms.obligation: Group denials by remittance reason code and by true root cause, and report volume alongside dollars for each group.
atoms.lesson: Remittance reason and remark codes tell you what the payer said, not what went wrong. Cluster them into actionable families: registration and eligibility, authorization, coding and modifier, medical necessity, timely filing, duplicate, and coordination of benefits. Eligibility and authorization families are usually the largest by volume and are almost entirely preventable upstream. Ranking by dollars alone hides high-frequency small-dollar failures that consume the most staff time to rework.

atoms.obligation: Check the payer-specific appeal deadline before any other work, and file within it even if the packet is thin.
atoms.lesson: Appeal windows run from the remittance date and vary widely, commonly 90 to 180 days commercially, with Medicare redetermination at 120 days from the initial determination and a five-level appeal ladder beyond it. Managed care contracts often shorten the window further. A missed deadline converts a winnable claim into a write-off with no recourse, so file a placeholder appeal on time and supplement with records rather than waiting for a complete packet.

atoms.obligation: Write clinical appeals against the specific criteria the payer applied and quote the documentation that satisfies each element.
atoms.lesson: Medical necessity denials are scored against a published rule set such as commercial screening criteria or a local or national coverage determination. A letter arguing that the physician exercised judgment loses; a letter mapping documented vital signs, oxygen requirement, failed outpatient therapy, and comorbid burden to each named criterion wins. Have the treating physician sign clinical appeals, attach only the relevant record sections, and cite the exact criterion number the payer used.

atoms.obligation: Track overturn rate by payer, denial family, and appeal level, and set a dollar threshold below which claims are not appealed.
atoms.lesson: Rework costs real money, commonly twenty-five to fifty dollars of staff time per appealed claim, so appealing everything destroys margin. Measure first-level overturn rates by denial family; medical necessity often overturns at 40 to 60 percent while duplicate and non-covered service denials rarely do. Payers with high denial and high overturn rates are producing administrative waste, and that evidence belongs in contract negotiation as a demand for authorization or edit changes.

name: charge-capture-audit
description: Audits whether documented services are actually being charged, and keeps the charge master current. Use when net revenue drops without a volume change, when a department suspects missing charges, when annual code updates land, or when late charges and credit adjustments are piling up after billing.
expansions: revenue down but volume is flat
infusion charges look under-reported
late charges after bill drop
annual code update just released
supply items never getting charged
observation hours billed incorrectly
charge master has retired codes
clinic visit levels all the same

atoms.obligation: Reconcile documented services against charges posted for a sample of accounts in each department every quarter.
atoms.lesson: Charge capture leakage concentrates in areas where clinical work and charging are separated: infusion and injection time units, respiratory therapy treatments, wound care, implants and high-cost supplies, observation hours, and emergency department facility levels. Pull thirty accounts per department, compare the clinical record against posted charges line by line, and quantify both missing and unsupported charges. Auditing only the revenue side finds shortfalls; auditing both directions also finds compliance exposure.

atoms.obligation: Update the charge description master on the annual code cycle and remove deleted or unbillable line items before they generate rejections.
atoms.lesson: Procedure code changes take effect on the first of January, with quarterly outpatient code and device edits in between. A charge master carrying retired codes produces front-end rejections that never reach the payer, so the loss is invisible in the denial report. Each line item needs a valid code, revenue code, description, and unit definition, and any item with an incorrect unit basis, such as charging per vial where the payer measures per milligram, systematically under- or over-bills.

atoms.obligation: Review modifier use against edit pairs before submission and confirm the record supports every modifier applied.
atoms.lesson: The costly modifiers are those that override edits or add payment: the separate evaluation modifier appended to a visit on a procedure day, the distinct procedural service modifier used to bypass bundling edits, bilateral and repeat procedure modifiers, and the outpatient hospital modifiers for discontinued procedures. Blanket application to clear edits is a recognized audit target. The documentation must show a separately identifiable service or a genuinely different site, session, or lesion.

atoms.obligation: Monitor charge lag in days by department and set a hard cutoff after which charges are treated as exceptions.
atoms.lesson: Charge lag is the interval from date of service to charge posting, and every day added delays cash and increases the chance a charge is dropped after the claim is submitted. Three days is a reasonable target for most departments. Persistent lag usually points at a specific handoff, such as anesthesia records posted weekly or clinic encounters left unclosed. Track unbilled accounts by reason and by physician, since a small number of unclosed encounters usually explains most of it.

name: payer-contract-modeling
description: Evaluates a managed care contract offer using actual utilization and flags the language that matters as much as the rates. Use when a payer sends a renewal or amendment, when preparing to negotiate rates, when a contract is approaching termination, or when someone asks whether a proposed increase actually covers a specific service line.
expansions: payer sent a renewal proposal
is this rate increase actually positive
contract auto renews in sixty days
implant costs exceed the case rate
lesser of language in the amendment
how do our rates compare to medicare
payer wants to add a narrow network product
termination notice period question

atoms.obligation: Model the proposed terms against a full year of actual claims volume and mix, not against list prices or last year's rates.
atoms.lesson: A percentage increase applied to the wrong mix can reduce revenue. Reprice at least twelve months of paid claims under both current and proposed terms, by diagnosis group for inpatient and by procedure code for outpatient, holding volume constant. Watch for shifts in the payment basis, such as moving outpatient surgery from a percent of charges to an ambulatory classification schedule, which changes winners and losers case by case even when the headline number rises.

atoms.obligation: Read and price the non-rate terms, since language on filing, escalators, and payment rules often outweighs the rate change.
atoms.lesson: The terms that quietly cost money are timely filing limits shortened to ninety days, lesser-of language paying the billed charge when it falls below the fee schedule, unilateral policy amendment rights, medical policy incorporated by reference, silent evergreen renewal with no escalator, retroactive recoupment windows beyond twelve months, and termination-without-cause clauses shorter than the notice needed to inform patients. Each should be priced or struck rather than accepted as boilerplate.

atoms.obligation: Negotiate explicit carve-outs for high-cost implants, specialty drugs, and outlier cases rather than folding them into case rates.
atoms.lesson: A case rate that averages implant cost across all joint replacements loses money on every revision and complex construct. Standard protections are invoice-plus carve-outs for devices above a threshold such as ten thousand dollars, separate reimbursement for specialty pharmacy and blood factor products, and stop-loss provisions that convert to a percent of charges once a case exceeds a set threshold. Without them, case-rate contracts silently penalize the highest-acuity referrals the system receives.

atoms.obligation: Express current and proposed rates as a percentage of the government fee schedule for each major service to make comparisons possible.
atoms.lesson: Percent of Medicare is the common currency for comparing payers, service lines, and market position, because it normalizes for wage index, case mix, and code-level differences. Commercial inpatient rates commonly land between 150 and 250 percent of Medicare depending on market leverage, with outpatient and imaging often higher and professional services lower. Knowing where each payer sits, and how it moved since the last renewal, is what turns a rate discussion into a defensible position.

name: financial-assistance-screening
description: Applies the charity care and financial assistance policy to patient accounts and keeps the process compliant. Use when a patient says they cannot pay, when accounts are heading to collections, when the assistance policy is up for review, or when a self-pay patient asks what a service will cost before scheduling.
expansions: patient says they cannot pay the balance
account about to go to collections
uninsured patient wants a price estimate
charity care policy needs annual review
presumptive eligibility for homeless patients
sliding scale for the clinic population
payment plan versus write off
patient qualifies for medicaid instead

atoms.obligation: Screen for public coverage eligibility before applying charity care, since enrollment may cover the current stay retroactively.
atoms.lesson: Many patients presenting as self-pay are eligible for Medicaid, marketplace coverage with a special enrollment period triggered by a life event, or a state catastrophic program. Medicaid can pay retroactively for the months surrounding the service date in many states, which converts a write-off into revenue and gives the patient ongoing coverage. Financial counselors should reach the bedside before discharge, since post-discharge enrollment success drops sharply once the patient is unreachable.

atoms.obligation: Apply a written assistance policy with published income thresholds and a plain-language summary available wherever patients register.
atoms.lesson: Nonprofit hospitals must maintain a financial assistance policy, an emergency care policy, a plain-language summary, and an application, all widely publicized and translated for significant language groups in the service area. Thresholds are commonly full write-off at or below two hundred percent of the federal poverty level with a sliding scale up to four or five hundred percent. Patients approved for assistance may not be charged more than amounts generally billed to insured patients.

atoms.obligation: Make reasonable efforts to determine eligibility before any extraordinary collection action, and document the attempts.
atoms.lesson: Extraordinary collection actions include selling debt, reporting to credit agencies, lawsuits, liens, and wage garnishment. They are barred until reasonable efforts to determine eligibility have been made, and a notification period of at least one hundred twenty days from the first post-discharge bill applies, with a final written notice at least thirty days before action. If an application arrives during the application window, collection must pause. Document each notice date and outreach attempt in the account.

atoms.obligation: Use presumptive eligibility criteria to approve clearly qualifying patients without forcing a full application.
atoms.lesson: Requiring pay stubs and tax returns from a homeless patient or a person already enrolled in nutrition assistance produces denials for paperwork reasons rather than income reasons. Presumptive criteria typically include homelessness, deceased with no estate, enrollment in a means-tested program, eligibility for a state subsidy, or a third-party scoring model. Approving these accounts automatically reduces bad debt reported, improves community benefit reporting accuracy, and cuts collection expense on accounts that were never collectible.

name: provider-credentialing-file
description: Prepares and reviews medical staff credentialing and privileging files for appointment, reappointment, and payer enrollment. Use when a new physician or advanced practice provider is starting, when reappointment is due, when a file has gaps or adverse findings, or when a provider cannot bill because enrollment has not caught up with the start date.
expansions: new surgeon starts in six weeks
reappointment cycle is due
gap in work history needs explanation
provider not enrolled with the payers yet
requesting privileges for a new procedure
malpractice claim disclosed on application
locum needs temporary privileges
credentialing committee packet review

atoms.obligation: Verify every credential from the primary source and record the date and method of each verification in the file.
atoms.lesson: Primary source verification means confirming licensure with the state board, education with the school, training with the residency program, board certification with the certifying board, and current registration for controlled substances directly with the issuing authority. Copies supplied by the applicant do not satisfy this. A national practitioner data bank query is required at appointment and reappointment, and license and sanction checks should be re-run monthly against exclusion lists rather than only at reappointment.

atoms.obligation: Require a written explanation for any gap in professional activity longer than thirty days and verify the account given.
atoms.lesson: Unexplained gaps are one of the strongest signals in a credentialing file and one of the most commonly deferred items at committee. Reasonable explanations include parental leave, illness, immigration processing, or study; the concern is a surrendered privilege or an investigation left unreported. Cross-check the timeline against affiliation letters from every hospital where the applicant held privileges in the last five years, and require a query response rather than a form letter for anything ambiguous.

atoms.obligation: Grant privileges by delineated procedure with volume and training criteria, not by broad specialty label.
atoms.lesson: Privileges must be specific and evidence-based: a general surgeon requesting robotic or endoscopic procedures needs documented training and a minimum recent case volume, often stated as a number of cases in the preceding twenty-four months with proctored cases for new technology. New appointees enter focused professional practice evaluation with a defined case review period, and all practitioners are subject to ongoing evaluation with data reviewed at least every six to nine months.

atoms.obligation: Start payer enrollment in parallel with medical staff appointment and track expected effective dates against the start date.
atoms.lesson: Hospital privileging and payer enrollment are separate processes with separate clocks. Government enrollment commonly takes sixty to ninety days and can allow limited retroactive billing, while commercial enrollment often runs ninety to one hundred twenty days with no retroactivity, so services billed before the effective date are unrecoverable. Delegated credentialing agreements shorten this considerably. Hold claims rather than dropping them, and give the practice manager the projected effective date before the provider's schedule is built.

name: nurse-staffing-plan
description: Builds and defends a unit nurse staffing plan covering hours per patient day, skill mix, and contingency coverage. Use when a unit is running over budget on premium labor, when the staffing committee reviews the annual plan, when a new unit opens, or when agency and overtime use has replaced core hiring.
expansions: agency spend is out of control
unit over budget on overtime
annual staffing plan committee review
opening eight more medsurg beds
charge nurse has a full assignment
hppd looks high but staff feel short
vacancy rate driving premium pay
break relief never happens on nights

atoms.obligation: Set target hours per patient day by unit type and acuity, and state which roles are counted in the number.
atoms.lesson: Hours per patient day is meaningless without its definition. Decide whether it includes only registered nurses and aides at the bedside or also charge nurses, unit secretaries, and educators, then apply it consistently. Typical worked ranges are roughly seven to nine hours for adult medical-surgical units, twelve to sixteen for intensive care, and higher for burn and transplant. Acuity systems adjust within a unit but cannot substitute for a defensible baseline and a stated skill mix.

atoms.obligation: Convert the plan into required full-time equivalents using a replacement factor for benefit time, orientation, and education.
atoms.lesson: Worked hours are not paid hours. A position covering seven days needs roughly 1.4 to 1.6 people per shift line before benefit replacement, and a replacement factor of about fifteen to twenty percent covers vacation, sick, holiday, orientation, and mandatory education. Budgeting only worked full-time equivalents guarantees a structural hole that gets filled with overtime at time and a half or agency at two to three times the loaded staff rate.

atoms.obligation: Treat vacancy rate and turnover as the driver of premium labor and report them alongside the staffing variance.
atoms.lesson: Overtime and agency use are symptoms; the underlying figure is the vacancy rate against the approved position count, plus first-year turnover, which frequently runs above twenty percent for new graduates. Each experienced nurse replacement costs roughly forty to sixty thousand dollars in recruiting, orientation, and lost productivity. A staffing variance presented without vacancy, time to fill, and turnover reads as poor management when the real constraint is a hiring pipeline problem.

atoms.obligation: Write the contingency plan that names who covers unexpected absence and census surge for every shift, including nights and weekends.
atoms.lesson: Plans fail on the shifts nobody planned. Contingency tiers usually run from float pool and voluntary extra shifts, through incentive pay and on-call activation, to closing beds or diverting admissions. Charge nurse assignment rules, break relief coverage, and sitter or observation demand belong in the plan because they consume real hours that never appear in the budgeted ratio. Several states also mandate a staffing committee with nurse majority and public posting of the plan.

name: physician-compensation-review
description: Reviews or designs employed physician compensation using productivity, quality, and market benchmarks while staying inside regulatory limits. Use when negotiating a physician contract, when a specialty's pay looks out of line with production, when building a compensation plan for a new service, or when someone questions whether an arrangement is defensible.
expansions: cardiologist contract renewal terms
comp per rvu above the benchmark
physician wants credit for supervising apps
new plan for the hospitalist group
is this arrangement fair market value
quality bonus never gets paid out
loss per employed physician rising
call pay stipend request from surgeons

atoms.obligation: Benchmark compensation and production against the same survey source and percentile, and check that both sit in a similar range.
atoms.lesson: Compensation percentile and work relative value unit percentile should track each other. A physician paid at the seventy-fifth percentile while producing at the fortieth is the classic red flag, and so is a compensation per work unit rate above the survey ninetieth percentile. Use published specialty surveys, match the specialty and region carefully, and note that surveys lag the market by a year or more, which matters in specialties with acute shortages.

atoms.obligation: Confirm that no element of compensation varies with the volume or value of referrals for designated health services.
atoms.lesson: Physician self-referral and anti-kickback rules permit productivity pay based on the physician's own personally performed services, but not payment that fluctuates with the ancillaries, imaging, laboratory, or hospital admissions the physician generates. Group practice profit-sharing must be distributed on a basis unrelated to referral volume. Arrangements need a written signed agreement, a set term of at least one year, commercially reasonable terms, and compensation set in advance at fair market value.

atoms.obligation: Write explicit crediting rules for shared visits, supervision, procedures, and non-clinical time before the plan starts.
atoms.lesson: Most disputes are about attribution, not rate. Decide in advance how work units are credited for split or shared inpatient visits, advanced practice provider services billed under supervision, surgical assists, telehealth encounters, and interpretation of studies. Also define paid non-clinical time for medical directorship, teaching, and committee work as separate stipends supported by time logs, rather than folding them into the productivity rate where they distort the comparison to survey data.

atoms.obligation: Keep quality and citizenship components large enough to change behavior and tie them to measures the physician can influence.
atoms.lesson: A bonus of two or three percent of total compensation is administrative overhead, not an incentive; ten to twenty percent gets attention. The measures must be attributable to the individual or a small group, refreshed annually, and reported at least quarterly so the physician can see standing. Common workable measures include documentation closure timeliness, patient experience scores with adequate sample size, preventive care gap closure, and access metrics such as third next available.

name: documentation-query-review
description: Reviews clinical documentation improvement queries for compliance and effectiveness before they reach physicians. Use when a query looks leading, when the coded severity does not match how sick the patient clearly was, when physician response rates are falling, or when a payer challenges a diagnosis-related group assignment.
expansions: query looks like it leads the physician
sepsis documented but not coded
physicians not answering queries
drg downgraded on payer review
severity of illness looks too low
cdi program needs a compliance check
malnutrition documentation challenged
query volume way up this month

atoms.obligation: Write queries that present clinical indicators and offer multiple reasonable options, including an option to state no additional diagnosis.
atoms.lesson: A compliant query is non-leading: it cites the clinical indicators found in the record, asks the provider to clarify, and offers choices including other, clinically undetermined, and none of the above. Naming a single desirable diagnosis, mentioning payment impact, or attaching the query to a financial target makes it leading and creates audit exposure. Multiple-choice format is acceptable; the options simply must be clinically plausible and drawn from the record.

atoms.obligation: Query only when documentation is conflicting, ambiguous, incomplete, or clinically unsupported, and record which condition triggered it.
atoms.lesson: The legitimate triggers are conflicting documentation between providers, a treated condition never named, a diagnosis stated without supporting clinical criteria, or an unspecified term where specificity changes the clinical picture. Classic examples are pneumonia treated with broad-spectrum coverage where the organism is documented only in cultures, acute blood loss anemia after transfusion, malnutrition assessed by dietitian but not physician-documented, and heart failure without acuity or type stated.

atoms.obligation: Track physician response rate and agreement rate by individual and escalate unanswered queries through the medical staff structure.
atoms.lesson: Response rates below about eighty percent indicate a workflow problem rather than physician resistance: queries arriving after discharge, buried in the inbox, or sent to the wrong provider of record. Track time to response, agreement rate, and query volume per physician, then feed outliers to the department chair and the medical staff bylaws process, which usually ties chart completion to privileges. Post-discharge queries should be rare and must never be used to change a signed record improperly.

atoms.obligation: Report query impact as severity and risk of mortality capture, not only as payment change.
atoms.lesson: Documentation specificity drives complication and comorbidity capture, which sets the diagnosis-related group weight, but it also drives severity of illness and risk of mortality scoring used in public quality ratings and observed-to-expected mortality comparisons. A program judged solely on revenue invites the accusation of upcoding. Presenting case mix index alongside severity capture and denial overturn rates shows the program is improving accuracy of the record rather than chasing weight.

name: survey-readiness-tracer
description: Prepares units for accreditation and licensure survey using tracer methodology and mock survey findings. Use when a survey window is open, when a prior deficiency needs evidence of correction, when a unit wants a mock tracer, or when leadership wants to know where practice has drifted away from written policy.
expansions: survey window opens next month
mock tracer on the surgical unit
evidence of standards compliance due
life safety deficiency from last survey
medication storage found unlocked
staff cannot answer emergency codes
policy says one thing practice does another
validation survey after complaint visit

atoms.obligation: Trace a real patient forward through the record, the unit, and the staff who cared for them rather than auditing policies in a room.
atoms.lesson: Tracer methodology follows one patient across the care continuum: admission assessment timing, reassessment intervals, pain management, restraint orders and monitoring, medication reconciliation at each transition, consent, and discharge instructions. Surveyors then branch to the systems the case touches, such as sterile processing or pharmacy storage. Reviewing binders finds policy problems; tracing finds practice problems, and practice is what gets cited.

atoms.obligation: Concentrate mock survey effort on the standards most frequently cited nationally rather than spreading attention evenly.
atoms.lesson: Citations cluster year after year in the physical environment and life safety chapter, infection prevention, medication management, and provision of care. Recurring specifics include blocked exits and improper storage in corridors, penetrations in fire barriers, ceiling tile gaps, expired or unsecured medications, single-dose vials used for multiple patients, high-level disinfection technique, eyewash station access, and refrigerator temperature logs with gaps. Walk these first; they are visible within minutes of a surveyor entering a unit.

atoms.obligation: Interview frontline staff with open questions and treat any answer they cannot give as a training gap to close before survey.
atoms.lesson: Surveyors ask staff directly, and the answers are scored. Staff should be able to describe how they identify a patient using two identifiers, where to find safety data sheets, how to report a safety event, what the emergency codes are, how to escalate a deteriorating patient, when hand hygiene is required, and what their role is in a fire response. Scripted memorization fails; staff need to demonstrate the actual workflow at their own workstation.

atoms.obligation: Close each prior finding with dated evidence of sustained compliance rather than a corrective policy alone.
atoms.lesson: Post-survey corrective plans require evidence that the fix held, typically several months of monitoring data with a defined sample, a threshold, and named accountability, and findings scored as higher risk require faster action and leadership attention. A revised policy with a signature page is not evidence. Keep the monitoring active until performance is stable at target, then move the measure into routine quality reporting so it survives the next leadership change.

name: infection-surveillance-report
description: Compiles and validates healthcare-associated infection surveillance before it is reported or presented. Use when quarterly infection reporting is due, when a unit's central line or catheter infection count rises, when a surgical site infection cluster appears, or when reported rates disagree with what clinicians believe they are seeing.
expansions: three clabsi on the icu this quarter
quarterly surveillance submission due
cauti numbers do not match our chart review
surgical site infections after colon cases
c diff rate above the national ratio
device utilization ratio climbing
infection committee needs the report
hand hygiene compliance data questioned

atoms.obligation: Apply the surveillance definitions exactly as written, even when they disagree with the treating clinician's diagnosis.
atoms.lesson: Surveillance definitions are deliberately mechanical: a bloodstream infection attributed to a central line depends on device presence for more than two consecutive calendar days, the collection date window, and the organism list, not on whether the physician believes the line was the source. Urinary infection criteria require specific symptoms plus a colony count threshold within a defined device window. Applying clinical judgment instead of the definition makes rates incomparable and invites a validation finding.

atoms.obligation: Report the standardized infection ratio with its predicted count, never a raw count or a bare percentage.
atoms.lesson: The standardized infection ratio divides observed infections by a predicted number derived from a national baseline adjusted for unit type, hospital characteristics, and case mix, so a ratio of 1.0 means performance equal to the baseline. Small units generate unstable ratios, and a predicted count below one makes the ratio uninterpretable, which is why counts are reported alongside. A single infection on a low-volume unit can look catastrophic in ratio form.

atoms.obligation: Report device utilization alongside infection rates, since reducing device days changes both numerator and denominator.
atoms.lesson: Device utilization ratio is device days divided by patient days, and it is the most actionable lever available. Many infections are prevented by removing the line or catheter rather than by better maintenance, so a falling utilization ratio with a stable infection rate is real progress. Utilization also explains cross-unit differences: an intensive care unit at 0.6 catheter utilization is not comparable to one at 0.3, and daily necessity review is the intervention that moves it.

atoms.obligation: Validate numerators and denominators against the source records before any submission or public presentation.
atoms.lesson: Validation means re-reviewing a sample of positive cultures and denominator day counts against the record, because under-reporting is the most common finding when regulators audit and it carries payment and credibility consequences. Denominator errors from manual day counting are frequent. Reconcile laboratory-identified organism reports against reported events, confirm present-on-admission determinations, and lock the data before quarterly deadlines, since resubmission after public reporting windows close is generally not possible.

name: safety-event-rca
description: Runs the review of a patient safety event from severity classification through corrective actions. Use when a serious harm event or near miss is reported, when a sentinel event triggers a mandated review, when the safety committee needs an analysis with actions, or when the same type of event keeps recurring despite prior education.
expansions: wrong site block on a patient
retained sponge after surgery
patient fall with hip fracture
insulin overdose reached the patient
same medication error happened again
near miss caught by pharmacy
root cause meeting next week
actions from last review never implemented

atoms.obligation: Classify the event by actual harm and by potential for harm, and use both to decide the depth of review.
atoms.lesson: A harm scale runs from circumstance or near miss through no-harm reaching the patient, temporary harm, permanent harm, and death. Review intensity should follow potential as well as actual harm, because a near miss with catastrophic potential deserves full analysis. Sentinel events, including unanticipated death, permanent harm, wrong-site surgery, retained foreign objects, and infant abduction, require comprehensive review with corrective action, conventionally completed within about forty-five days.

atoms.obligation: Build the timeline from records and interviews before proposing causes, and keep the analysis focused on systems rather than individuals.
atoms.lesson: Start with a factual chronology to the minute, assembled from the record, device logs, staffing assignments, and interviews conducted individually and soon after the event while memory is fresh. Then work through the contributing factor categories: staffing and workload, communication and handoff, equipment and technology, physical environment, policies and training, and supervision. Hindsight bias makes the outcome look predictable; ask what the clinician knew and saw at each step, not what they should have known.

atoms.obligation: Choose corrective actions from the stronger end of the intervention hierarchy and reject education as a standalone action.
atoms.lesson: Actions rank by reliability: forcing functions and physical constraints such as removing concentrated electrolytes from the floor stock, then substitution and automation, then standardization, protocols, and checklists, then double checks and warnings, and weakest of all education, reminders, and new policy. Most reviews default to reeducation, which is why the same event recurs. Every action needs a named owner, a date, and a follow-up measure verifying the change actually took hold.

atoms.obligation: Protect the reporting culture by separating accountability decisions from the learning review and telling reporters what changed.
atoms.lesson: Event reporting volume is a measure of psychological safety, not of danger, and near-miss reports are the cheapest data a hospital gets. A just culture framework distinguishes human error, at-risk behavior, and reckless conduct, and only the last is a discipline matter. If staff see colleagues punished for reported errors, reporting collapses within weeks. Closing the loop, by telling the reporting unit what changed as a result, is what sustains volume over time.

name: grievance-resolution-workflow
description: Handles patient and family complaints and formal grievances through to a compliant written resolution. Use when a patient or family escalates a concern, when a complaint arrives about care quality or staff conduct, when a written response deadline is approaching, or when someone needs to know whether an issue counts as a grievance at all.
expansions: family demanding to speak to an administrator
is this a complaint or a grievance
written response deadline approaching
patient alleges rude treatment by nursing
billing complaint mixed with care concern
same unit generating repeat complaints
patient wants to file with the state
discharge dispute escalated to the board

atoms.obligation: Determine at intake whether the concern is a complaint resolvable on the spot or a grievance requiring formal written response.
atoms.lesson: A concern raised and resolved promptly by staff present, such as cold food or a missing blanket, is a complaint. It becomes a grievance when it is written, when it is made after discharge, when it alleges abuse, neglect, or a violation of patient rights, when it concerns premature discharge, or when it cannot be resolved by the staff present at the time. Billing complaints alone are not grievances unless they include a quality-of-care allegation.

atoms.obligation: Acknowledge the grievance quickly and send a written response naming the contact person, the steps taken, the results, and the completion date.
atoms.lesson: Regulations require a written response containing the name of a hospital contact, the steps taken to investigate, the results of the process, and the date of completion. Seven days is the widely used standard for the response, with an interim letter and a realistic completion estimate when the investigation runs longer. The letter should not include clinical findings that breach another patient's privacy or peer review protections, and it should never read as a denial of the experience.

atoms.obligation: Investigate through the department involved and use quality review channels for any allegation about clinical care.
atoms.lesson: Care-quality allegations belong in peer review or the quality committee, where protections apply, while conduct and service allegations are handled through management and human resources. Interview the staff involved, review the record, and separate what happened from how it was communicated, since most grievances are as much about communication as about care. Preserve the record, since grievances alleging harm frequently precede a claim and the file becomes discoverable evidence of the response.

atoms.obligation: Trend grievances by unit, theme, and staff involved, and report the pattern to the governing body that has delegated oversight.
atoms.lesson: The governing body is ultimately responsible for the grievance process and typically delegates it to a committee, so it needs periodic reporting on volume, categories, resolution timeliness, and actions taken. Trending exposes what a case-by-case view hides: one nursing unit generating half the conduct complaints, a discharge process producing repeated premature-discharge allegations, or an access barrier surfacing as complaints about phone response. That analysis is what connects grievances to service recovery and experience improvement.

name: privacy-incident-assessment
description: Assesses a suspected privacy incident, decides whether it is a reportable breach, and drives the notification and mitigation steps. Use when records are disclosed to the wrong person, when an employee accesses a chart without a treatment relationship, when a device or paper record goes missing, or when a vendor reports an exposure involving patient data.
expansions: discharge papers given to wrong patient
employee looked up a celebrity chart
laptop with patient list went missing
fax of results sent to wrong number
vendor reported an exposure of our data
do we have to notify these patients
staff member accessed a relative record
records left in a public area

atoms.obligation: Presume the incident is reportable and document a four-factor risk assessment if you conclude notification is not required.
atoms.lesson: An impermissible use or disclosure of protected health information is presumed to be a breach unless a documented assessment shows low probability of compromise, weighing the nature and extent of the information including identifiers and likelihood of re-identification, who the unauthorized recipient was, whether the information was actually acquired or viewed, and the extent to which risk has been mitigated. Encryption meeting the recognized standard is a safe harbor; password protection alone is not.

atoms.obligation: Notify affected individuals without unreasonable delay and no later than sixty days from discovery, and meet the separate large-incident requirements.
atoms.lesson: Individual notice is due within sixty calendar days of discovery, which is the day the incident became known or reasonably should have. Incidents involving five hundred or more residents of a state or jurisdiction additionally require prominent media notice and immediate federal reporting; smaller incidents may be logged and reported annually within sixty days of year end. Notices must describe what happened, the information involved, steps individuals should take, what the organization is doing, and contact details.

atoms.obligation: Determine the access path and check whether the same actor or workflow produced other unreported exposures.
atoms.lesson: A single incident is rarely isolated. Audit the employee's access history across the relevant period, since inappropriate chart access typically shows a pattern involving relatives, neighbors, coworkers, or high-profile patients rather than one lookup. For misdirected communications, check whether a stored wrong number or a template error produced repeated disclosures over months. Sampling only the reported instance understates the affected population and produces a second, worse notification later.

atoms.obligation: Complete mitigation, workforce sanctions, and the minimum necessary review, and confirm vendor agreement obligations were followed.
atoms.lesson: Mitigation includes retrieving or confirming destruction of the information, notifying the recipient of their obligation, and correcting the workflow. Sanctions must be applied consistently against a written scale, since inconsistency is itself a finding. Where a vendor caused the incident, the business associate agreement governs discovery notification timelines and cooperation duties, and the covered entity remains accountable for individual notice regardless of who lost the data.

name: value-analysis-request
description: Evaluates a request to add, switch, or standardize a clinical supply, device, or product. Use when a physician asks for a new implant or instrument, when a committee is reviewing conversion to a single vendor, when supply cost per case rises, or when a vendor claims savings that need independent checking.
expansions: surgeon wants a new implant vendor
convert to a single glove supplier
supply cost per case increasing
vendor claims fifteen percent savings
new wound dressing trial request
three brands of the same catheter on shelf
off contract purchases climbing
is this device worth the price premium

atoms.obligation: Require clinical evidence of benefit and the total cost of ownership before considering any product change.
atoms.lesson: Total cost of ownership includes unit price, reprocessing or disposable consumables, instrument trays and their sterilization, service contracts, training, storage space, waste disposal, and the cost of maintaining a second inventory during transition. Evidence should be peer-reviewed and specific to the population, not a vendor-supplied case series. Where evidence shows equivalence, the decision is properly a price decision, which is exactly the argument standardization committees need documented in advance.

atoms.obligation: Benchmark the quoted price against group purchasing tiers and comparable facility pricing before accepting a vendor figure.
atoms.lesson: Group purchasing agreements price by tier based on committed volume and compliance percentage, so a quote is meaningless without knowing the current tier and whether the change breaks a commitment that raises prices on other lines. Physician preference items such as orthopedic implants, cardiac rhythm devices, and trauma constructs carry the widest price variation and are usually where the savings sit. Local pricing comparisons and construct-level pricing beat list discount percentages every time.

atoms.obligation: Write a conversion plan naming who trials the product, for how long, and what result decides adoption.
atoms.lesson: A trial without a decision rule becomes a permanent second product on the shelf. Define participating units and physicians, duration long enough to cover normal case variation, the clinical and operational measures that count, and who makes the final call. Plan the transition explicitly: sequence the old stock down, retrain staff, update preference cards and order catalogs, and set a cutover date, because parallel inventory is where projected savings quietly disappear.

atoms.obligation: Verify realized savings against actual purchase history several months after implementation and report the variance.
atoms.lesson: Projected savings and realized savings diverge for predictable reasons: volume assumptions missed, off-contract purchasing continued, the case mix shifted toward premium constructs, or a rebate condition was not met. Pull actual spend by item and by physician for the period after conversion and compare it against the projection at the same case volume. Committees that never audit results lose credibility with both finance and the medical staff within about a year.

name: capital-request-review
description: Reviews and ranks capital equipment and facility requests for the budget cycle. Use when a department submits an equipment request, when aging equipment is failing and needs replacement priority, when the capital pool is oversubscribed, or when a request needs a defensible justification before it goes to the finance committee.
expansions: imaging wants a replacement scanner
capital pool is oversubscribed again
aging equipment keeps going down
justify the request to finance committee
lease versus purchase for the analyzer
request came in mid year off cycle
what is the payback on this equipment
construction cost was left out

atoms.obligation: Apply the capitalization threshold and useful life rules first, and separate routine replacement from strategic growth requests.
atoms.lesson: Capital is generally an item above a dollar threshold, often five thousand dollars, with a useful life beyond one year; below that it is an operating expense and does not belong in the capital cycle. Splitting the pool into routine replacement, regulatory and safety, information systems, and strategic growth stops a replacement sterilizer from competing head to head with a new service line. Each pool needs its own criteria, because payback analysis cannot rank a fire alarm upgrade.

atoms.obligation: Include every cost required to put the asset into service, not just the purchase price.
atoms.lesson: The purchase price is often half the true number. Add installation, room renovation and structural or shielding work, electrical and mechanical upgrades, network connections, interface work, staff training, the service contract after the warranty year, disposables, and any temporary capacity lost during construction. Ask when the vendor discount expires and whether the quoted price assumes a multi-year service commitment, which converts a capital decision into a long operating obligation.

atoms.obligation: Test the volume and reimbursement assumptions behind any request justified by new revenue, and require incremental rather than total volume.
atoms.lesson: Requests justified by growth usually count total projected studies rather than the increment above what current equipment already handles, which double-counts existing revenue. Check whether the assumed payer mix matches the department's actual mix, whether the procedure is separately reimbursed or packaged into the visit payment, and whether the referring physician base exists today. A payback period beyond seven years on equipment with a five-year technology life is not an investment case.

atoms.obligation: Rank replacement requests using equipment age, failure history, downtime impact, and parts availability rather than department seniority.
atoms.lesson: Clinical engineering holds the data that should drive replacement: age against expected useful life, work order and repair cost history, unplanned downtime hours, and whether the manufacturer has ended support or parts supply. Equipment past end of support is both a safety and an operational risk regardless of how well it currently runs. Presenting this ranking objectively converts the capital committee from a lobbying contest into a risk-based decision the medical staff can accept.

name: service-line-proforma
description: Builds or stress-tests the financial and operational case for a new or expanded clinical service. Use when leadership is considering a new service line, when a physician group proposes a program, when an existing service needs a viability review, or when a proposal's projections look optimistic and need challenging.
expansions: proposal for a new cardiac program
should we open a second urgent care
is the sleep lab still viable
projections in this plan look optimistic
recruiting two specialists for the service
contribution margin on bariatrics
community need for infusion center
what happens if volume comes in low

atoms.obligation: Build the volume projection from service area population and realistic market share, not from physician enthusiasm.
atoms.lesson: Start with the service area defined by actual patient origin, apply age-and-sex-adjusted use rates for the procedures involved, and subtract volume already captured by competitors and by your own facilities. Then state the market share assumption explicitly and defend it against who the referring physicians are today. A plan assuming a jump from eight to twenty-five percent share within two years needs a named mechanism, usually a specific recruit or a payer contract, or it is a wish.

atoms.obligation: Project net revenue per case using the actual payer mix rather than charges or a blended average rate.
atoms.lesson: Gross charges are meaningless for planning. Model expected payment by payer for the specific codes involved, weighted by the payer mix the service will actually attract, which often differs from the hospital average: joint replacement skews Medicare, bariatrics and behavioral health skew commercial and self-pay, and obstetrics skews Medicaid in many markets. Site of service matters too, since the same procedure pays differently in a hospital outpatient department, an ambulatory surgery center, and an office.

atoms.obligation: Report contribution margin using incremental costs and show the ramp period before steady state.
atoms.lesson: Separate direct variable costs such as supplies, implants, drugs, and worked labor from fixed overhead allocations, since allocated overhead does not disappear if the service is declined. A service with positive contribution margin can still lose money after allocation and remain worth doing. Model a ramp of twelve to twenty-four months, because staff and equipment cost from day one while volume builds, and the cumulative cash trough is usually the number that decides feasibility.

atoms.obligation: List the dependencies and regulatory prerequisites with lead times, then rerun the case at a materially lower volume.
atoms.lesson: The common blockers are physician recruitment timelines of nine to eighteen months including credentialing and enrollment, space and renovation approvals, licensure or certificate of need review where the state requires it, accreditation for programs such as stroke or bariatric surgery, payer contracting for a new site, and specialized staff who are simply unavailable locally. Then run a downside case at roughly seventy percent of projected volume and state at what point the service would be discontinued.

name: job-description-drafting
description: Turns a hiring manager's rough ask into a job description that survives legal review and actually attracts the right applicants. Use when a requisition is being opened, when a posting has been copied from an old role and no longer matches the work, or when recruiters report a weak or badly mismatched applicant pool. Also use when a role needs levelling against the existing job architecture before it can go live.
expansions: manager wants a req opened tomorrow
old job ad reused for a new role
applicant pool is all wrong seniority
need essential functions written properly
rewrite this posting before it goes live
role has no level or band yet
job ad reads like a wish list
posting needs a pay range added

atoms.obligation: Separate essential functions from marginal duties and state each one as an observable task rather than a personal trait.
atoms.lesson: Essential functions are the anchor for every later accommodation and capability decision, so they must describe what gets done and how often: handles roughly forty inbound tickets a day, drives between three depots weekly, lifts twenty kilos unaided. Traits like reliable, passionate or detail-oriented cannot be adjusted, evidenced at interview or tested at probation, and a duty listed but performed twice a year is marginal, not essential.

atoms.obligation: Level the role against the existing job architecture and confirm the band before writing a single line of the posting.
atoms.lesson: Scope, decision rights and span determine the level; the title follows. Writing the advert first invites title inflation, a senior label attached to a mid-level scope, and an offer that lands above band and compresses the incumbents. Check what a person at that level already owns in the same family, confirm the band midpoint the recruiter can work to, and confirm the headcount is approved against that band, not against the manager's preferred number.

atoms.obligation: Strip requirements that are not genuinely necessary and check the wording for terms that deter or exclude protected groups.
atoms.lesson: Degree requirements on roles where nobody currently in post used the degree shrink the pool and carry disparate impact exposure. Digital native and recent graduate read as age proxies; demands for ten years of a technology that has existed for five are unmeetable and signal carelessness. Split must-have from nice-to-have, because women and under-represented applicants disproportionately self-select out when they miss a stated requirement.

atoms.obligation: Include the pay range and its basis wherever the posting reaches a jurisdiction that requires disclosure.
atoms.lesson: Pay transparency rules bite on where the candidate could work, not where the employer sits, so a remote posting reachable from Colorado, California, New York or Washington needs a good-faith range. The EU Pay Transparency Directive extends this across member states from mid-2026 and bars asking applicants for pay history. Publish the range you will actually pay to, plus the variable and equity components, because a range nobody is hired into invites a complaint.

name: interview-scorecard-design
description: Designs a structured interview loop: which competencies get assessed, who assesses each one, the questions that evidence them and the rating anchors interviewers score against. Use when a new loop is being stood up, when debriefs keep dissolving into disagreement or gut feel, or when scorecards come back one line long. Also use when a hiring manager asks for a vague culture-fit round.
expansions: panel keeps asking the same questions
interviewers disagree after every debrief
need a rubric for this loop
hiring manager wants a culture fit round
scorecards come back one word long
design questions for a senior manager loop
candidates all rated four out of five
debrief turns into a popularity contest

atoms.obligation: Assign each competency to exactly one interviewer and give that interviewer the questions that evidence it.
atoms.lesson: Without a coverage matrix, three people spend forty-five minutes each on conflict stories and nobody probes the technical depth the role actually needs. Two competencies per interviewer is the practical ceiling for a forty-five minute slot once introductions and candidate questions are removed. Publish the matrix before the loop, name who covers what, and make sure at least one interviewer is outside the hiring manager's reporting line.

atoms.obligation: Write behavioural anchors that describe what a weak, adequate and strong answer sounds like at each rating point.
atoms.lesson: Unanchored scales drift: leniency pushes everyone to four, and a five-point scale lets undecided interviewers park on the midpoint. A four-point scale with written anchors forces a side.
