Capture bay width, shelf count, notch pitch, depth and fixed obstacles per cluster, and take item dimensions from measured samples rather than supplier specification sheets, which are frequently wrong on packaging height.

atoms.obligation: Give stores an explicit reset sequence including what to do with delisted stock and with gaps.
atoms.lesson: Reset execution is where the theory leaks. The brief needs a running order, empty the bay, adjust shelf heights, then place left to right from the flow anchor, a named action for delisted items such as return to depot, clearance bay or sell through in place, and a rule for undelivered new lines, which is never to leave a hole but to widen the neighbour. Include a photograph of the finished bay, because audited compliance without one typically runs only sixty to eighty percent.

name: feature-space-planning
description: Plans what occupies high-traffic feature space, meaning endcaps, gondola ends, dump bins, front-of-store tables and their online equivalents, and holds each slot to a productivity standard. Trigger it when someone asks what should be on the endcap in a given week, when a supplier wants to buy a gondola end, or when promotional space is not earning. It covers uplift measurement, calendar sequencing, slot pricing and execution requirements.
expansions: what goes on the endcap in week 34
supplier wants to buy a gondola end
promo space is not earning its keep
front of store table for the season
dump bin for the holiday line
features cannibalising each other
feature calendar for the quarter
which sku earns the aisle end

atoms.obligation: Judge every feature slot on incremental sales lift against control stores, not on the units rung up in the display.
atoms.lesson: An endcap always sells; the question is whether it sold anything the shelf would not have sold anyway. Measure against matched control stores without the feature and net off the item's own base-shelf sales during the same period. Typical grocery uplifts run three to eight times rate of sale on a well-executed end, far less for an item already on deal. A feature showing six times uplift that simply pulls forward the next two weeks of demand nets out at close to nothing.

atoms.obligation: Sequence the feature calendar so competing categories and offers are not on display at the same time.
atoms.lesson: Features cannibalise each other. Two soft drink ends in one store in one week roughly halve each other's uplift, and a feature for an item that is simultaneously in the leaflet at a deeper price simply confuses the offer. Build the calendar as a grid of slots by week and by zone, assign one category per zone per week, and enforce a minimum gap, commonly four weeks, before a category is allowed back into the same zone.

atoms.obligation: Price space sold to a supplier from what the slot would otherwise have earned rather than from a flat rate card.
atoms.lesson: Supplier-funded features only pay if the fee beats the margin the slot would have generated anyway. Take the slot's baseline cash margin per week from its own history, add the retailer margin on the incremental units the supplier's promotion should deliver, and set the fee above the gap. Selling a peak-week front-of-store table at the same rate as a third-week-of-January end destroys value, so slots need tiering by traffic week and by store footfall.

atoms.obligation: Specify stock quantity, signage and duration as conditions of the booking rather than leaving execution to the store.
atoms.lesson: Features fail on availability far more often than on choice, because an empty end is worse than no end at all. Set a minimum fill quantity derived from the uplifted rate of sale, confirm the stock is physically in the store before the display date, define the signage kit, and set start and end days that follow the traffic pattern. Displays generally go live ahead of the weekend peak rather than on a Monday morning when nobody is shopping.

name: item-data-onboarding
description: Gets a new product correctly created in the merchandising systems: identifiers, hierarchy placement, dimensions, tax, compliance flags and the attributes the site needs to make it findable. Use it when a new line is live but has no size filter, when forty new lines arrive from a supplier, or when an item will not allocate because dimensions are missing. It covers mandatory fields, verification against samples, hierarchy choice and go-live timing.
expansions: new line live but no size filter
set up forty skus from a supplier
item will not allocate missing dimensions
wrong category hierarchy on new products
barcode clashing with an existing item
supplier sent an incomplete item form
attributes missing so filters break
tax code wrong on food items

atoms.obligation: Require the complete attribute set before an item is allowed to go live rather than fixing it afterwards.
atoms.lesson: An item missing colour, size, material or dimension attributes cannot be filtered, cannot be recommended and often cannot be allocated or shipped correctly, and the launch-then-fix pattern never actually gets fixed because the merchant moves on. Define a mandatory field list per category covering hierarchy node, barcode, supplier code, case configuration, unit and shipping dimensions and weight, tax code, country of origin, hazard flags and the category's own facets, then block activation on any missing field.

atoms.obligation: Verify identifiers and packaging hierarchy against physical samples instead of trusting the supplier's form.
atoms.lesson: Supplier item forms carry errors at meaningful rates: transposed barcodes, case quantities changed at the last minute, dimensions quoted for the inner rather than the outer, weights in the wrong unit. A wrong case quantity breaks every ordering calculation downstream and a wrong outer dimension breaks pallet fill, vehicle fill and the planogram. Scan the actual barcodes on unit, inner and outer, measure and weigh a real sample, and check the barcode is not already live on another item.

atoms.obligation: Place the item in the hierarchy where shoppers will look for it rather than where the supplier's catalogue puts it.
atoms.lesson: Suppliers classify by their own brand architecture while shoppers navigate by need. A protein bar sits in sports nutrition for the supplier and in snacking for the shopper, and the placement decides which category's reporting, planogram and site navigation it lands in. Decide from onsite search terms and from how the physical category is organised, and record the reasoning, because a later reclassification breaks year-on-year comparison for both the category losing it and the one gaining it.

atoms.obligation: Set the go-live date to follow first receipt so an item is never sellable with no stock behind it.
atoms.lesson: An item live before stock lands generates orders you cannot fill, cancellations and a damaged search ranking that persists well after stock arrives, since most ranking models penalise availability gaps. Tie activation to a confirmed goods-in event, or use a pre-order flag that states a dispatch date explicitly so the shopper's expectation is set. For store items, align activation with the delivery schedule so the shelf label does not appear days before the product does.

name: product-copy-standards
description: Writes and reviews product detail page copy: titles, bullets, descriptions and specification blocks, so items are findable, comparable and legally defensible. Trigger it when someone asks to rewrite titles across a category, says the pages read like a supplier brochure, or traces returns back to a vague description. It covers title structure, the questions bullets must answer, variant differentiation and claim substantiation.
expansions: rewrite titles for this category
copy reads like a supplier brochure
returns because the description is vague
bullets not answering buying questions
same copy pasted across every variant
title too long and truncating
specs missing the key measurements
copy for a new own brand launch

atoms.obligation: Structure the title so the most identifying words come first and it still reads when truncated.
atoms.lesson: Titles get truncated almost everywhere, in search results, category tiles, basket lines, order emails and paid listings, often somewhere around sixty to seventy characters. Lead with brand, then the product noun, then the one or two differentiating attributes such as size, colour or pack count, and leave decoration at the end. Front-loading also matches how relevance models weight terms. Never repeat keywords for weight, since it reads as spam to shoppers and is penalised by most ranking systems.

atoms.obligation: Write bullets that answer the questions which actually stop a purchase instead of restating features.
atoms.lesson: The questions that block conversion are consistent within a category: will it fit, what is in the box, how do I care for it, is it compatible with what I already own, how long will it last. Read your own returns reason codes and customer service contact drivers to find them, then answer each one explicitly. In apparel the highest-value line is a fit note against a reference, such as model height and size worn or runs small take a size up, because it removes buy-two-return-one behaviour.

atoms.obligation: Differentiate copy across variants and near-identical lines rather than duplicating one block of text.
atoms.lesson: Duplicated descriptions leave onsite and external search unable to tell variants apart and leave the shopper unable to see why one costs more than another. Write the shared story once at parent level and push the genuine differences, capacity, coverage, power, material weight, into variant-level structured specification fields rather than prose. Structured specifications also feed comparison tables and faceted filters, which duplicated marketing prose cannot do at all.

atoms.obligation: Keep every factual claim in the copy traceable to evidence the business can defend.
atoms.lesson: Product copy carries real legal exposure, since claims about sustainability, health, origin, performance and price comparison are regulated in most markets and vague environmental claims are an active enforcement area. Require a substantiation reference for each claim, a test report, certification number or supplier warranty, held against the item record. Avoid absolutes such as eco-friendly or unbreakable and never lift claims straight from supplier marketing, because the retailer is usually liable as the seller.

name: product-imagery-standards
description: Sets and enforces the image requirements for product pages: shot lists, technical standards for the first image, colour accuracy, video and asset rights, and audits a category against them. Use it when imagery across a range looks inconsistent, when a season's shoot needs briefing, or when listings are missing a scale shot. It covers what to shoot, how the grid should read, colour management and licence expiry.
expansions: images inconsistent across the range
brief the shoot for next season
listings missing a scale shot
supplier images have watermarks
cutouts on white but shadows differ
swatch not matching the real colour
how many angles per product
video for high consideration items

atoms.obligation: Define a mandatory shot list per category and audit live listings against it rather than accepting whatever arrives.
atoms.lesson: Shot lists differ by category according to what a shopper cannot judge remotely. Furniture needs a scale reference and a room context, apparel needs front, back, detail and on-body with stated model measurements, food needs pack front, a legible ingredient panel and the food out of the pack, electronics need ports and what is in the box. Five to seven images is a typical minimum for conversion, with the incremental benefit flattening out beyond roughly eight.

atoms.obligation: Hold the first image to a strict technical standard so the category grid reads as one coherent range.
atoms.lesson: The grid is where a range gets judged, and inconsistent crop, fill ratio, shadow and background make an assortment look cheap regardless of the products in it. Specify a single defined background, a fixed product fill of around eighty to eighty-five percent of the frame, consistent lighting direction and shadow treatment, a square aspect for grid use, and enough resolution to support zoom, typically sixteen hundred pixels on the short side. Reject supplier images carrying logos, burst badges or overlay text.

atoms.obligation: Colour-manage imagery against physical samples because colour mismatch drives avoidable returns.
atoms.lesson: Colour is one of the largest return reasons in apparel and home. Shoot with a colour reference chart in frame, retouch against the physical sample rather than a screen preview, and check the result on both a calibrated display and an ordinary uncalibrated phone. Where a shade is genuinely hard to reproduce, say so in the copy and add a close-up swatch image, because a shopper warned about variation returns far less often than one surprised by it on unboxing.

atoms.obligation: Record usage rights and expiry against every asset so licensed imagery is retired on time.
atoms.lesson: Licensed imagery, model shoots, third-party lifestyle photography and brand assets supplied under a campaign agreement, carries usage windows, territory limits and channel limits. Assets outliving their licence create liability, and with model releases a genuine legal problem. Store the licence end date, permitted channels and permitted territories against each asset and set an expiry review, so a lifestyle shot from a campaign two years dead is not still sitting on a live product page.

name: category-page-merchandising
description: Curates onsite category and landing pages: default sort, pinned positions, filters, editorial rows and how deep the result set runs, so the page sells rather than just lists. Trigger it when a category page opens on out-of-stock items, when a new arrivals page needs merchandising, or when best sellers are buried on page four. It covers sort logic, pin discipline, facet design and breaking up long result sets.
expansions: category page opens with out of stock items
merchandise the new arrivals page
best sellers sitting on page four
default sort is not converting
pin the campaign items to the top
filters not useful for this category
seasonal landing page for the promo
too many results and no structure

atoms.obligation: Define the default sort as a blend of demand, margin and availability rather than a single field.
atoms.lesson: Sorting on popularity alone ossifies a range because new items never surface, while sorting on newest buries proven sellers. A workable default weights recent conversion rate, units, margin contribution and stock cover, with a hard demotion for anything out of stock or below a size-availability floor. Give new items a temporary boost window, usually two to four weeks, so they accumulate enough traffic to earn a genuine ranking signal rather than dying from lack of exposure.

atoms.obligation: Pin only a small number of positions by hand and attach an expiry date to every pin.
atoms.lesson: Manual pinning is how category pages rot, because each pin overrides a ranking model that is usually right and pins outlive the campaign that justified them since nobody owns removal. Cap pins at the first row or two, require an end date at the moment of pinning, and audit the pin list weekly for items now out of stock, marked down or attached to a finished campaign. Record who pinned and why so the next merchant can judge whether it still holds.

atoms.obligation: Design the filter set from the attributes shoppers in this category actually use to narrow down.
atoms.lesson: Facets should be category-specific and evidenced. Watch which facets get clicked and which within-category searches imply a missing one, since repeated queries for waterproof or under five hundred mean the facet does not exist or is not populated. Keep values shallow and mutually exclusive, suppress values matching only a handful of items, and never expose a facet the item data populates badly, because an empty result set is worse for trust than having no filter at all.

atoms.obligation: Break long result sets with structured entry points instead of relying on endless scrolling.
atoms.lesson: Pages with hundreds of results convert poorly because the shopper cannot form a shortlist. Insert sub-navigation tiles for the main need states or sub-categories near the top, and consider an editorial row such as top picks, new in or price tiers after the first screen. Depth matters, since the large majority of clicks land within the first two screens, so anything the merchant genuinely wants sold must sit there or be one filter click away.

name: onsite-search-tuning
description: Diagnoses and fixes onsite search: zero-result queries, wrong results, synonyms, misspellings and query-level merchandising. Use it when shoppers search for something and get nothing, when the no-results report keeps growing, or when a top query returns an accessory rather than the product. It covers classifying query failures, building synonym lists from real language, curating head terms and measuring changes on revenue rather than opinion.
expansions: shoppers search and get zero results
no result queries in the weekly report
top query returns an accessory
brand name misspelled by customers
category term returns random items
synonyms for regional words missing
promo term not matching anything
search converting worse than browse

atoms.obligation: Work the zero-result and low-conversion query report weekly and classify the cause before applying any fix.
atoms.lesson: Zero results have four distinct causes with four different fixes: you do not sell the thing, which is a range gap to report to the buyer; you sell it under different words, which is a synonym; the query is misspelled, which needs fuzzy matching or a correction rule; or the item data lacks the term, which is an attribute or copy fix. Fixing all four with synonyms creates a tangle. Sort by search volume, because fixing the top fifty terms usually moves the metric.

atoms.obligation: Maintain a synonym list built from real shopper language including regional and colloquial terms.
atoms.lesson: Shoppers do not use the retailer's vocabulary. They search jumper for sweater, hoover for vacuum, trainers for sneakers, sofa for couch, and brand names as category terms. Build the list from query logs, customer service transcripts and competitor navigation, and keep mappings one-directional where the terms are not truly equivalent, so cot returns crib but a narrow branded term does not expand into a whole category. Review the list after every range change, since deletions create new dead ends.

atoms.obligation: Treat the highest-volume queries as merchandisable surfaces with deliberately curated top results.
atoms.lesson: The head of the query distribution carries a large share of search traffic and converts far better than browsing when handled properly. For each top term check the first row: is the intended product first, is it in stock, is the price right, is the breadth of the result set sensible. Curate the first few positions for seasonal and campaign terms such as gifts for him or back to school, and set them to expire, or the Christmas curation is still showing in March.

atoms.obligation: Judge search changes on conversion and revenue per search rather than on relevance opinion.
atoms.lesson: Relevance gets argued about endlessly, so measure it instead. Track searches per session, click-through position, add-to-basket rate per query and revenue per search, split between head and tail terms. A change that lifts click-through but drops add-to-basket has surfaced attractive but wrong items. Where volume allows, test on a slice of traffic; where it does not, compare the same query across matched weeks and watch carefully for seasonality confounding the read.

name: cross-sell-bundle-build
description: Designs bundles, multibuys and cross-sell placements that raise basket value without discounting things shoppers were going to buy anyway. Trigger it when someone wants a bundle built around a new hero product, says a multibuy is losing margin, or asks what should be recommended on a product page. It covers affinity evidence, bundle pricing arithmetic, where in the journey to place the offer and the stock rules that keep it fulfillable.
expansions: build a bundle around the new console
multibuy is losing us margin
what to recommend on this product page
attach rate on accessories is low
three for two on the wrong items
kit a starter set for beginners
basket value flat despite traffic
bundle pricing for the gifting season

atoms.obligation: Build bundles from observed basket affinity rather than from what feels logically related.
atoms.lesson: Affinity analysis on transaction data finds pairs that genuinely co-occur above chance, and the answers are often unintuitive. Use lift rather than raw co-occurrence or you will simply bundle the two best sellers, which need no help at all. Then apply a merchant filter: the pair must make sense to a shopper, both items must be reliably in stock, and the secondary item should carry higher margin than the anchor so the bundle improves mix instead of diluting it.

atoms.obligation: Take the discount on the attachment item and hold the anchor at price so blended margin stays above the floor.
atoms.lesson: The arithmetic that kills bundles is discounting the anchor product. Discount the attachment instead, which usually carries higher margin and often would not have been bought at all, so a bundle showing a fifteen to twenty percent saving on the accessory can still blend above the anchor's standalone margin. Model the cannibalisation rate, meaning the share of bundle buyers who would have bought both items anyway, because that share is pure margin handed over for nothing.

atoms.obligation: Place the cross-sell at the point the shopper has already committed rather than while they are still choosing.
atoms.lesson: Recommendations shown beside the product under consideration create comparison and hesitation, while recommendations after add-to-basket or on the basket page capture attachment without disturbing the decision. Each placement needs different logic: the product page should show alternatives and variants, the basket should show complements and consumables, and the order confirmation should show replenishables and warranty-type add-ons. Running one recommendation model across all three underperforms all three.

atoms.obligation: Set stock and operational rules so a bundle does not break when one component runs out.
atoms.lesson: Virtual bundles assembled at pick time fail when the cheapest component sells out, leaving a live offer that cannot be fulfilled. Decide up front whether the bundle is a real stocked item with its own barcode and inventory or a virtual link that must be suppressed when any component falls below a threshold. Physically kitted bundles solve availability but strand inventory that cannot be sold as singles, so only kit quantities that will clear inside the promotional window.

name: price-ladder-architecture
description: Sets the price structure inside a category: opening price point, mainstream and premium tiers, pack-size gradients and the gaps between them, so shoppers can trade up. Use it when good-better-best is muddled, when there is no entry price in a range, or when a multipack costs more per unit than the single. It covers building the price-per-unit grid, sizing tier gaps, defending the opening price point and indexing own brand.
expansions: good better best is muddled
no entry price point in the range
two pack worse value than the single
price gaps too close to matter
where to set the premium tier
own brand priced too near the brand
price architecture for a new category
the trade up path is missing

atoms.obligation: Lay every item in the category onto a price-per-comparable-unit grid and look for gaps and inversions.
atoms.lesson: The grid exposes the two common faults. Crowding is four items sitting within a few percent of each other with no distinct role between them, which wastes shelf space on choices that are not really choices. Inversion is a larger pack or a bundle costing more per unit than the single, which destroys trust because shoppers do check. Normalise to a comparable unit, per hundred grams, per wash, per metre, exactly the way the shelf-edge label already does it.

atoms.obligation: Set the gap between tiers wide enough that trading up is a real decision for the shopper.
atoms.lesson: The working rule across most categories is that a step under roughly fifteen percent is invisible while a step over about forty percent breaks the ladder and pushes the shopper back down instead of up. Space tiers enough to signal genuine difference while keeping the cash gap small at the bottom of the ladder where shoppers are most price-sensitive. Each tier also needs a defensible reason to exist, a real difference in ingredient, material, capacity or service, or the premium simply will not sell.

atoms.obligation: Defend the opening price point as a deliberate position instead of letting it drift upward.
atoms.lesson: The opening price point does most of the work in shopper price perception and is the line most exposed to discounters. It drifts up because it is the lowest-margin item in the range and every cost increase invites a proposal to delete it. Decide the opening price point explicitly per category, hold it against a named competitor benchmark, and where cost becomes untenable, re-engineer the pack size or specification to hold the price point rather than abandoning the position.

atoms.obligation: Set own-brand prices against the branded benchmark at an index the shopper can perceive as fair value.
atoms.lesson: Own label works on a stable relative index rather than an absolute price. Standard-tier own brand usually sits twenty to thirty-five percent below the branded benchmark, a value tier sits far lower and is positioned against discounters rather than the brand, and premium own brand can price at or above the brand where quality is visibly better. The index has to be maintained when the brand promotes, otherwise the own-label proposition disappears every time the brand runs a deal.

name: competitive-price-monitoring
description: Tracks competitor pricing on the lines that shape price perception and decides where to match, hold or ignore. Trigger it when someone says the business is being undercut on key value items, asks whether to match a rival's promotion, or wants monitoring set up for a category. It covers choosing the monitored basket, like-for-like comparison, pre-agreed response rules with margin floors, and reporting position as an index.
expansions: being undercut on key value items
set up monitoring for this category
should we match their promotion
competitor cut price on our hero line
price index slipping in the north
which lines do shoppers actually check
matching everything is killing margin
delisted item still in the comparison basket

atoms.obligation: Define a small basket of price-sensitive lines to monitor closely instead of tracking the whole range.
atoms.lesson: Shoppers build price perception from a limited set of known-value items, the lines they buy often and remember the price of, typically fifty to a hundred and fifty per category covering staples, opening price points and heavily advertised brands. Match those tightly and monitor them daily. Across the long tail shoppers hold no reference price, so competitive matching there costs margin and buys nothing. Rebuild the basket at least annually, since which lines are price-sensitive shifts with inflation and advertising.

atoms.obligation: Compare like for like on pack size, specification and total delivered cost before concluding you are beaten.
atoms.lesson: Naive comparisons mislead, because competitors deliberately use non-standard pack sizes and exclusive model numbers so no direct comparison exists. Normalise to unit price, confirm the specification is genuinely equivalent, and online include delivery charges, delivery speed and any membership requirement, since an item ten percent cheaper behind a paid delivery threshold is not cheaper for that basket. Check also whether the rival price is a short promotion or a base price, because matching a two-day deal with a base cut is expensive.

atoms.obligation: Agree a response rule and a margin floor for each monitored line before the situation actually arises.
atoms.lesson: Pricing decisions taken under pressure over-match. Assign each line a role in advance: match immediately, match within a tolerance band, hold and monitor, or ignore entirely. Attach a margin floor to every rule so no automated or manual match can breach it without sign-off. Bear in mind too that visibly reacting to every competitor move can start a price war neither side wins, and that in many markets coordinated or signalled pricing behaviour carries genuine legal risk.

atoms.obligation: Report price position as a volume-weighted index over time rather than as a list of individual comparisons.
atoms.lesson: The useful management view is a weighted index: your basket at your prices against the same basket at competitor prices, weighted by your own sales volume. Tracked weekly it reveals drift that item-by-item comparisons hide completely. Segment it by region where competitors price locally, and separate base price from promotional price, because a business can look competitive on the index while being badly beaten at the shelf edge during every promotional week.

name: promotional-calendar-build
description: Builds and governs the trading calendar: which offers run in which weeks, at what depth, funded by whom, across every channel. Use it when the quarter's promo calendar needs locking, when two categories have clashing offers in the same week, or when a line has been on deal so often its base price has eroded. It covers building around trading events, capping promotional weeks, recording funding and evaluating incremental margin afterwards.
expansions: lock the promo calendar for q4
two clashing offers in week twelve
the same deal has run too often
supplier funding for the autumn plan
how many weeks on deal per year
promo depth for the peak event
calendar before the leaflet deadline
offers overlapping between channels

atoms.obligation: Build the calendar from the trading events and shopper occasions of the year, then fit supplier offers into it.
atoms.lesson: Calendars built bottom-up out of supplier proposals produce an incoherent year with gaps in the weeks that matter most. Start from the fixed shape of demand, seasonal peaks, paydays, school terms, weather-driven categories and the big retail events, and define each week's theme and role first. Negotiate supplier participation into those slots afterwards. Lead times force this discipline anyway, since printed and broadcast media typically lock eight to twelve weeks ahead and volume commitments need longer still.

atoms.obligation: Cap how many weeks a line spends on promotion so the deal price does not become the expected price.
atoms.lesson: A line on promotion more than roughly a third of the year loses its base price in the shopper's mind, full-price sales collapse and every uplift is then measured against an eroded baseline. Set a maximum number of promotional weeks per line per year and a minimum recovery gap between deals, commonly four to six weeks, so the base price re-establishes itself. Watch the full-price baseline trend after each event, since a declining baseline is the early warning of a line being promoted to death.

atoms.obligation: Record the mechanic, depth, funding split, agreed volume and claim process for every offer before it is committed.
atoms.lesson: Promotional disputes with suppliers are almost always about what was actually agreed. Each slot needs its mechanic, straight price cut, multibuy or gift with purchase, its depth, the funding split, the agreed volume, the claim mechanism and the deadline for the supplier to confirm stock. Deep offers need supply confirmed early, because a promotion selling out on day two damages shopper trust and in several markets breaches advertising rules on reasonable availability of advertised goods.

atoms.obligation: Evaluate each promotion after it runs on incremental margin rather than on headline uplift.
atoms.lesson: Post-event analysis has to separate four effects: genuinely incremental volume, cannibalisation of other lines in the category, pull-forward from the following weeks, and pantry loading that suppresses demand for a month. Build the baseline from pre- and post-period trend rather than last year's same week, which was probably also on deal. Many promotions with impressive uplift turn out margin-negative once funding is netted and cannibalisation counted, so feed the result into next year's calendar.

name: vendor-trade-terms-negotiation
description: Prepares and runs the annual or ad hoc commercial negotiation with a supplier: cost price, rebates, promotional funding, payment terms, returns allowances and listing commitments. Trigger it when a supplier asks for a cost increase, when a terms review is coming up, or when rebate tiers are not being hit. It covers assembling the full commercial picture, testing cost claims against inputs, converting the deal into cash, and documenting what was agreed.
expansions: supplier wants a six percent cost increase
annual terms review next week
build a negotiation pack for this vendor
rebate tiers not being hit
justify a cost price rise
settlement terms and payment days
funding for the autumn promo plan
supplier threatening to withdraw a line

atoms.obligation: Assemble the whole commercial picture for the supplier before the meeting rather than only the cost sheet.
atoms.lesson: Cost price is one line of a much wider deal. Build a single view covering annual volume and trend, gross and net margin after all income, rebate tiers and how close you are to each, promotional funding received against committed, payment terms, returns and damages allowances, marketing contributions and any listing or space fees. Suppliers walk in holding this view already, so a buyer arriving with only a cost sheet concedes on the parts they cannot see.

atoms.obligation: Test a claimed cost increase against the movement of the underlying inputs rather than accepting a blanket percentage.
atoms.lesson: Cost increase requests usually arrive as a single number covering many inputs. Ask for the build-up: raw material, packaging, labour, energy, freight and currency, each as a share of cost with its own movement. A six percent ask on a product where raw material is thirty percent of cost and has risen ten percent justifies around three. Check whether inputs that rose have since fallen and whether earlier increases were ever reversed, and have alternatives ready before the meeting.

atoms.obligation: Convert every element of the deal into annual cash so unlike options can be compared on one basis.
atoms.lesson: Negotiations trade unlike things, a point of cost price against extra promotional funding, longer payment terms against a rebate. Value each in annual cash on your own volume forecast, so a point of cost on four million pounds of purchases is forty thousand, and thirty extra days of payment terms is a one-off working capital gain worth the cost of capital on a month of purchases. Fixed lump sums are worth less than percentage rebates when volume grows and more when it falls.

atoms.obligation: Write down what was agreed, including conditions and the claim process, before either side starts acting on it.
atoms.lesson: Undocumented trade income is the single largest source of year-end disputes and audit findings and has caused repeated profit restatements in grocery retail. Record the amount, the basis, the period it relates to, the volume conditions, who raises the claim and when, and whether it is deducted from invoices or invoiced separately. Recognise the income in the period it is genuinely earned against actual volume rather than when the deal is signed, or the accounts will overstate margin.

name: private-label-development
description: Takes an own-brand product from identified category gap to launch: benchmark, specification, supplier selection and audit, comparative testing and packaging. Use it when someone says a line should be own-branded, when samples do not match the benchmark, or when quality complaints appear on an existing own-brand item. It covers writing a measurable specification, qualifying factories on compliance as well as price, blind testing before and after launch, and designing packaging that is not a copycat.
expansions: we should own brand this line
samples do not match the benchmark
brief the factory for our own version
which supplier for the private label
packaging that is not a brand copycat
quality complaints on the own brand
tier the own label range
launch pricing against the brand

atoms.obligation: Choose the branded benchmark first and write the specification measurably against it.
atoms.lesson: Own brand fails when the target is vague. Pick the named branded product the shopper will actually compare against, buy it, and specify against it in measurable terms: ingredient or material composition, weight, dimensions, performance test results, sensory panel scores. As good as the brand is not a specification any factory can hit. Where you deliberately differ in order to reach a price, record the difference and its expected consumer impact so the gap is a decision rather than a launch-day surprise.

atoms.obligation: Qualify the supplier on capability and compliance, not only on the quoted price.
atoms.lesson: With own brand the retailer becomes the manufacturer of record for most practical purposes and carries product safety, labelling and recall liability. Audit the site before committing: category certification, capacity against your forecast including peak, traceability of inputs, ethical and labour audit status, and their record with other retailers. A second qualified source for a high-volume line is worth its overhead, because a single-sourced own-brand best seller that loses its factory can take six months to replace.

atoms.obligation: Run blind comparative testing against the benchmark before sign-off and again on a cycle after launch.
atoms.lesson: Blind paired testing with a representative consumer panel is the standard gate, and the own-brand product should reach parity or preference against the benchmark at its specified tier. Test the production sample from the real line rather than a hand-made golden sample, since the two frequently differ. Keep testing after launch, because factories drift through substituted inputs, reduced fill weights and changed processes, and that drift surfaces as review scores and complaints long before anyone re-tests.

atoms.obligation: Design the packaging to carry your own brand assets rather than to imitate the market leader.
atoms.lesson: Copycat packaging invites passing-off and trade mark claims and, more practically, tells the shopper the product is a substitute rather than a choice. Take the category's functional cues, the colour that signals mild, the shape that signals the format, while keeping distinctive brand assets of your own. Make sure the pack carries everything the category legally requires: ingredients and allergens, nutrition, origin, weight, safety warnings, disposal and recycling marks and the responsible business address.

name: replenishment-parameter-tuning
description: Sets and reviews the settings that drive automatic ordering: safety stock, review cycle, minimum display quantity, promotional and seasonal forecast overrides. Trigger it when there is stock in the warehouse but gaps on shelf, when the system keeps over-ordering a line, or when new items need parameters. It covers sizing safety stock from variability, syncing minimums to the planogram, loading overrides in time and working by exception.
expansions: stock in the warehouse but gaps on shelf
system keeps over ordering this line
set parameters for the new items
safety stock too high across the category
promo forecast not loaded before the deal
case size forcing overstock in small stores
availability dips every weekend
seasonal profile missing from the forecast

atoms.obligation: Size safety stock from demand variability and lead time instead of applying one figure across the category.
atoms.lesson: Safety stock should scale with the variability of demand over the replenishment lead time and the service level being targeted, so a steady staple needs far less cover than a weather-driven or promoted line selling at the same rate. A flat percentage across a category overstocks the predictable lines and still fails the volatile ones. Recompute whenever lead time changes, since switching from a domestic to an imported source alters the required buffer more than any forecasting refinement will.

atoms.obligation: Match the minimum display quantity to the planogram capacity so the shelf never orders below a full face.
atoms.lesson: Shelf gaps often come from a mismatch between the ordering minimum and the physical shelf. If a planogram gives an item three facings four deep, the store needs twelve units to look full, and a system minimum of four keeps the bay looking empty while availability reports show it in stock. Sync minimum display quantity to planogram capacity at every reset and check that case size divides sensibly into it, because a case of twenty-four into a shelf holding twelve guarantees back-stock.

atoms.obligation: Load promotional and seasonal forecast overrides before the last ordering cycle that can serve the event.
atoms.lesson: Automatic replenishment reacts to sales after they happen, which is always too late for a promotion. The uplifted forecast must be in place before the final ordering cycle that can deliver for the start date, counted back through supplier lead time plus the internal warehouse cycle. The ramp down matters just as much: leaving the uplift in place after the offer ends produces a fortnight of over-ordering and the post-promotion overstock that then gets blamed on the promotion itself.

atoms.obligation: Work exception reports for the lines the system is handling badly rather than auditing every parameter.
atoms.lesson: Parameter tuning at scale only works by exception. Useful triggers are items with cover above a threshold and falling sales, items with repeated shelf gaps despite depot stock, items whose forecast error has been one-sided for several consecutive weeks, and items where manual orders keep overriding the system. Each pattern points at a different fault, wrong safety stock, wrong minimum display, a missing seasonal profile or a store execution problem, and each needs a different fix.

name: marketplace-listing-compliance
description: Prepares and maintains listings on third-party marketplaces where the platform's own rules govern content, category, variation structure and pricing. Use it when a listing gets suppressed, when the buy box disappears overnight, or when the catalogue needs mapping onto a marketplace taxonomy. It covers required attributes per browse node, monitoring account health, building variation families properly and modelling channel-specific economics without breaching parity rules.
expansions: listing suppressed by the marketplace
lost the buy box overnight
map our catalogue to their taxonomy
restricted category needs approval
duplicate listing competing with ours
account health metrics slipping
variation family set up wrong
prohibited claim flagged in our copy

atoms.obligation: Map the catalogue onto the marketplace's own taxonomy and required attributes rather than exporting your internal structure.
atoms.lesson: Every marketplace runs its own category tree with mandatory attributes per node, and an item in the wrong node loses filters, browse placement and sometimes eligibility altogether. The required fields go well beyond a normal catalogue and include browse node, item type keyword, variation theme, condition and category compliance fields such as battery type, hazardous material class, age grading or textile fibre composition. Missing values often do not error, they silently drop the listing out of filtered results.

atoms.obligation: Monitor listing status and account health daily and treat a suppression as an urgent trading incident.
atoms.lesson: Suppression is silent revenue loss. Common causes are an image failing the platform's standards, a missing compliance attribute, a pricing rule triggered by a price above the platform's fair-price threshold, a policy-violating claim in copy, or an unresolved safety complaint. Most platforms publish a reason code and a reinstatement path, and the clock matters because ranking decays while the listing is down and does not simply snap back to where it was on reinstatement.

atoms.obligation: Structure variations as a proper parent family so shoppers land on one page carrying every size and colour.
atoms.lesson: Split variations fragment reviews, ranking signals and traffic across several pages, and the child with fewest reviews converts worst. Build the parent with a correct variation theme and children differing only on that theme, and never group genuinely different products under one parent to inherit its reviews, which platforms treat as a policy violation. When merging existing listings expect a temporary ranking dip while the platform reconsolidates the sales and review history.

atoms.obligation: Model marketplace economics separately while keeping list prices consistent with the platform's parity rules.
atoms.lesson: Marketplace economics differ from your own site: referral fees typically run eight to fifteen percent by category, fulfilment and storage fees apply, and returns are usually settled in the shopper's favour, so a price that works on your own site can be loss-making there. At the same time most platforms police price parity and will suppress or deprioritise a listing priced materially above the same item elsewhere, so the answer is a channel-specific margin model rather than a channel-specific price.

name: return-rate-reduction
description: Diagnoses why a product or category is being returned and fixes the causes in range, sizing, copy, imagery, packaging or supplier specification. Trigger it when returns on a style pass an unacceptable rate, when reason codes cluster on not as described, or when refunds are eating category margin. It covers splitting avoidable from structural returns, item-level fit guidance, feeding faults back to suppliers and grading returned units on receipt.
expansions: returns on this style over forty percent
reason codes mostly not as described
which lines to pull for quality
customers buying three sizes at once
damage in transit on fragile items
colour looks different in real life
return rate spiked after a copy change
refunds eating the category margin

atoms.obligation: Analyse returns by reason code at item level and separate avoidable causes from the structural cost of the channel.
atoms.lesson: Reason codes group into distinct fixes: fit and size points at sizing guidance, size curve and garment specification; not as described points at copy and imagery; quality or fault points at the supplier and specification; damaged in transit points at packaging and carrier; changed mind and ordered multiples is behavioural and partly the cost of selling online; wrong item sent is fulfilment. Only the first four belong to merchandising. Rank by return cost rather than rate, since twelve percent on a high-value item beats forty on a cheap one.

atoms.obligation: Publish fit and size guidance specific to the item instead of one generic chart for the whole site.
atoms.lesson: Apparel returns concentrate on fit, and generic size charts do not help because garments vary by block and by fabric. Give measured garment dimensions per size, state model height and the size worn, and add a directional note where a style runs small or large. Cumulative review data, the share of buyers reporting it ran small, is the most reliable input. Reducing buy-multiple-sizes behaviour is worth more than any single reason code, because those orders return two thirds of their units by design.

atoms.obligation: Feed persistent quality and transit damage returns back into supplier and packaging decisions with the cost attached.
atoms.lesson: A return rate that stays high on the same fault after copy and imagery are corrected is a product or packaging problem. Quantify it, units returned, reason, and refund plus handling plus disposal cost, and take it into the supplier review where it becomes a chargeback and specification conversation rather than a customer service one. For transit damage, drop-test the actual pack, since many items are packed for palletised warehouse handling and never for single-parcel drops and compression.

atoms.obligation: Decide the grading and routing of returned units before the volume arrives rather than after it stacks up.
atoms.lesson: Returns processing decides how much value is recovered. Grade on receipt into resellable as new, resellable as open-box, refurbishable or scrap, and fix the routing and price for each grade in advance. Speed matters most in seasonal and fast-fashion goods, where a unit sitting three weeks in the returns area misses its selling window entirely and becomes clearance. Track recovery rate as a category metric alongside markdown, because it is exactly the same margin being lost.

name: retail-media-placement
description: Plans and sells onsite advertising placements, meaning sponsored products, banners, category takeovers and email slots, while protecting the shopper experience and the retailer's own priorities. Use it when a supplier wants to sponsor a category, when sponsored results are pushing own brand down the page, or when a homepage banner needs pricing. It covers ad density limits, availability-gated eligibility, defensible campaign reporting and keeping ad money out of range decisions.
expansions: supplier wants to sponsor the category
sponsored results push own brand down
price the homepage banner for the season
how many ad slots per page
brand asking for a category takeover
measure what the campaign actually delivered
ads running on out of stock products
email slot for the launch

atoms.obligation: Cap the density of paid placements on a page and keep the top organic positions unsold.
atoms.lesson: Onsite advertising trades short-term fee income against conversion and trust. Past a few sponsored slots on a results page, click-through and add-to-basket for the whole page decline because shoppers stop trusting the ranking. A workable structure is one or two clearly labelled sponsored positions in the first row with a limited number below and the top organic result protected. Model the fee against the conversion loss across the entire page rather than against the revenue of the slot in isolation.

atoms.obligation: Block advertising from running on items that cannot currently be bought.
atoms.lesson: Paying for a click that lands on an out-of-stock, region-unavailable or delisted item wastes the advertiser's budget and the shopper's trip, and it is the quickest way to lose an advertiser's trust. Wire availability and lifecycle status into ad eligibility so a campaign pauses automatically when stock cover falls below a floor, and check regional and channel availability rather than national stock alone. Show advertisers their paused placements instead of quietly spending the budget elsewhere.

atoms.obligation: Report campaign results on measures the advertiser can act on and the retailer can defend.
atoms.lesson: Suppliers want to know what the spend produced in their category, not impressions. Report attributed sales with the attribution window and method stated, incremental sales against a control group where one can be constructed, new-to-brand share, and the category-level effect so it is clear whether the campaign grew the category or moved share inside it. Be explicit about method, because inflated attribution wins a single campaign and loses the relationship at the annual review.

atoms.obligation: Keep advertising decisions separate from range, ranking and space decisions with different owners.
atoms.lesson: If a supplier's advertising spend starts to influence which lines get listed, how organic search ranks or who wins feature space, the retailer's merchandising judgement is compromised and the shopper's results get worse, which eventually destroys the value of the advertising itself. Hold the commercial advertising conversation and the range review as separate decisions with separate owners, label paid placements clearly, and never let a paid slot present itself as an editorial recommendation.

name: oee-loss-analysis
description: Breaks a line's Overall Equipment Effectiveness into availability, performance and quality losses and points at the largest recoverable bucket. Use when a shift's downtime log needs turning into an explanation of why output missed plan, when a line 'runs fine' but the counter is short, or when preparing the weekly loss review for the plant manager.
expansions: oee dropped from 78 to 61
downtime log from last night's shift
line runs but we miss the count
why is performance loss so high
which loss bucket to attack first
micro stops on the capper
weekly loss review for the plant manager
ideal cycle time versus actual output

atoms.obligation: Separate planned from unplanned stoppage before computing availability, and log every stop longer than the agreed recording threshold.
atoms.lesson: Most plants set a five-minute threshold: anything longer is a logged downtime event hitting availability, anything shorter disappears into performance loss as a micro-stop. Planned events such as scheduled changeover, sanitation and PM windows sit outside loaded time. If breaks and meal reliefs are counted as downtime on one line and excluded on another, availability numbers between lines cannot be compared and the loss ranking is meaningless.

atoms.obligation: Compute performance loss against a validated ideal cycle time rather than the standard rate held in the planning master data.
atoms.lesson: Standard rates drift: they were set at commissioning, negotiated with planning, or inflated to make the schedule fit. The ideal cycle time is the fastest sustained rate the machine has demonstrated on that product with good parts, usually the nameplate rate. Using an understated standard hides speed loss entirely, so a line running at 70 percent of nameplate can report 100 percent performance and the reduced-speed loss never appears.

atoms.obligation: Attribute each stop to the machine that caused it rather than the machine that reported it before ranking the losses.
atoms.lesson: On a connected line a filler that is blocked by a jammed case packer logs the downtime, so the filler looks like the problem asset. Blocked and starved states must be coded to the upstream or downstream cause. Two codes — blocked and starved — plus a cause machine field on the stop record are enough. Without this, maintenance spends its week on the healthiest machine on the line.

atoms.obligation: Rank losses by recoverable minutes on the constraint operation and discount improvements on equipment that is not the bottleneck.
atoms.lesson: Minutes saved on a non-constraint machine convert into more idle time, not more product, because the constraint still gates output. Identify the constraint from sustained rate and buffer behaviour: it is the machine that is rarely starved and rarely blocked. Then convert each loss bucket into recoverable constraint minutes times units per minute, so the loss review argues in cases or units rather than percentages.

name: changeover-time-reduction
description: Runs a SMED-style teardown of a changeover so setup minutes move from internal to external work. Use when a product changeover eats an hour of a shift, when smaller batches are blocked by setup cost, or when someone has filmed a die or mould change and wants it turned into an action list.
expansions: changeover takes ninety minutes
video of the die change
too much time hunting for tools
we cannot run smaller batches
first good part after setup
build a setup cart for the press
reduce mould change on the moulding line
operator waiting for the crane

atoms.obligation: Film the whole changeover from last good part to first good part and timestamp every operator movement and wait.
atoms.lesson: The clock starts at the last saleable part of the outgoing product and stops at the first saleable part of the incoming one, which captures run-down, dial-in and startup scrap that setup sheets ignore. Two angles help: one on the machine, one wide enough to show walking to the tool crib. Expect walking, searching and waiting for a crane or a forklift to be a third of the elapsed time.

atoms.obligation: Classify every step as internal or external work, then move everything that can be done while the machine still runs.
atoms.lesson: Internal work requires the machine stopped; external work does not. Preheating a mould, staging the next die on a cart at machine height, kitting fasteners and inserts, pre-setting tool height blocks and printing the new labels are all external. Simply externalising what is already possible typically removes thirty to fifty percent of the stopped time before a single piece of hardware is changed.

atoms.obligation: Replace threaded fasteners and trial-and-error adjustment with quick clamps, hard stops and recorded numeric settings.
atoms.lesson: A bolt only clamps on the last turn, so pear-shaped slots, U-washers and one-turn cams do the same job in seconds. Dial-in is the other half: replace shimming with die-height blocks, locating pins and a written setting sheet giving pressures, temperatures and stop positions per product. Adjustment is not setup, it is a defect in the fixture design, and it also generates most of the startup scrap.

atoms.obligation: Set a target changeover time per product pair and post the actual time at the machine after every setup.
atoms.lesson: A run chart taped to the press turns setup into a measured event rather than a craft. Track by from-product to-product pair, because a colour change on the same tooling and a full die swap are different jobs. The pair matrix also drives sequencing: schedule products so that the expensive transitions happen once a week instead of twice a shift, which cuts total setup hours without touching the method.

name: line-balance-takt-time
description: Balances station work content against customer takt so a line stops building queues in front of one operator. Trigger when one station is always the pile, when a variant is added to a mixed-model line, or when headcount changes and the standard work must be re-cut.
expansions: station four is always backed up
wip piles between two operators
takt time changed with new demand
adding a variant to the line
draw the operator balance chart
one person idle half the cycle
yamazumi for the assembly cell
cycle time exceeds takt on final test

atoms.obligation: Calculate takt from available production time divided by customer demand, after removing breaks and planned maintenance.
atoms.lesson: Available time is net: subtract breaks, meetings, planned PM and the changeover window, not just the shift length. If two shifts run 450 net minutes each and demand is 900 units a day, takt is sixty seconds. Takt is a demand rate, not a target for a machine, and it must be recalculated whenever demand or manning changes rather than carried over from the last quarter's plan.

atoms.obligation: Time each element of station work separately so content can be moved between stations without re-timing the whole line.
atoms.lesson: Break the station into elements with clear start and stop points — pick fastener, place bracket, run down four screws, scan label — and time ten cycles per element on the fastest reliable operator. Element-level data is what makes rebalancing possible: whole-station times only tell you which station is long. Separate manual time, walk time and machine-automatic time, because only manual and walk time can be moved.

atoms.obligation: Load stations to roughly eighty-five percent of takt and keep the remainder as buffer against variation and recovery.
atoms.lesson: A station loaded to ninety-eight percent of takt will miss whenever a fastener cross-threads or a part arrives out of orientation, and the miss propagates downstream. Eighty to eighty-five percent leaves recovery room. Draw the balance chart as stacked bars per station against the takt line: the target shape is level bars just under takt, not a sawtooth with one bar poking through and two half-empty.

atoms.obligation: Move work content between stations before adding headcount, and gather leftover fractions into a single flex position.
atoms.lesson: Spreading the slack evenly across every station hides it and guarantees no one can be released. Load stations to takt in sequence and let the leftover accumulate at the end of the line, where it becomes a visible fraction of a person who can be redeployed or given the water-spider and quality-check role. Adding an operator to the longest station without re-cutting elements usually just moves the queue one station downstream.

name: preventive-maintenance-plan
description: Builds or prunes a preventive maintenance schedule from failure history, criticality and manufacturer intervals. Use when PM compliance is slipping, when the same component fails twice a quarter, when the planned downtime window is too short for the task list, or when someone asks whether a monthly PM can be stretched.
expansions: pm compliance is under sixty percent
the same bearing failed again
can we stretch this pm to quarterly
which pms are actually useless
planned downtime window is too short
lubrication route for the packing hall
criticality ranking for the asset list
spares for the scheduled shutdown

atoms.obligation: Rank assets by criticality using downtime cost, redundancy, safety exposure and spare availability before assigning any interval.
atoms.lesson: A pump with an installed standby and a two-day lead time on spares does not deserve the same attention as an unbuffered constraint machine whose gearbox is a twelve-week order. Score each asset on production impact, safety and environmental consequence, detectability and spare lead time. The output is a short A list that gets condition monitoring and a long C list that runs to failure deliberately, which is what frees the technician hours.

atoms.obligation: Set intervals from observed failure patterns and drop calendar tasks for components whose failures are random.
atoms.lesson: Only wear-out failures — belts, filters, seals, chain stretch — respond to time-based replacement. Electronics, bearings after infant mortality and hydraulic valves fail randomly, so a calendar replacement introduces fresh infant mortality rather than preventing anything. For those, switch to condition monitoring: vibration route, thermography on panels, oil analysis, or a simple measured check. Look at the work order history before defending an interval that came from a commissioning manual.

atoms.obligation: Write each task as a measurable check with a stated pass limit rather than an instruction to inspect or check condition.
atoms.lesson: 'Inspect drive chain' produces a tick from every technician regardless of condition. 'Measure chain elongation, replace above three percent' produces a number and a decision. Give the tool, the value, the limit and the action on failure, and require the reading to be written on the work order. Recorded values also build the history needed later to argue an interval change with a customer or auditor.

atoms.obligation: Reserve and kit the parts for a PM before it is scheduled so the shutdown window is not spent waiting on the stores.
atoms.lesson: The commonest cause of PM overrun is a technician discovering mid-job that the seal kit is not on the shelf. Kit the job the week before: parts picked into a labelled tote with the work order, special tools reserved, lifting gear booked and the LOTO sheet attached. Kitting also exposes bill-of-material errors on the asset before they cost a shutdown, and it turns a four-hour window into a genuinely four-hour job.

name: eight-d-corrective-action
description: Drives a customer complaint through the 8D discipline from containment to verified, closed corrective action. Trigger with a customer reject notice, a returned batch, a demand for a formal response within 48 hours, or an internal defect that keeps coming back after a quick fix.
expansions: customer rejected the shipment
8d due to the oem in 48 hours
containment for parts in transit
need root cause not a band-aid
why did we not detect it
returned batch of housings
customer wants d3 today
escape point analysis for the defect

atoms.obligation: Contain suspect stock at the customer, in transit, in your warehouse and on the line before investigating the cause.
atoms.lesson: The customer judges the response on containment speed, not analysis quality, and most escalations come from a second bad delivery arriving while the team debated causes. Sweep four locations: customer plant and their line-side stock, goods in transit, your finished goods and WIP, and the supplier pipeline. Mark sorted stock with a distinctive certified label or green dot so the customer can see at their dock which pallets have been screened.

atoms.obligation: State the problem with part number, defect, quantity, dates, batch codes and the process step where it was created.
atoms.lesson: 'Bad surface finish' is not a problem statement. 'Part 41822, revision C, 340 pieces from lot 25-0714, scratches 8 to 15 millimetres on face B, produced on press 4 nights, found at customer incoming' is. Add the is/is-not comparison: which cavities, shifts, machines and date codes are clean. Half of manufacturing root causes fall out of the is/is-not grid before any test is run, because it points straight at the one changed variable.

atoms.obligation: Prove root cause by switching the defect on and off deliberately rather than by agreement in a review meeting.
atoms.lesson: The verification step means reproducing the defect with the suspected cause present and eliminating it with the cause removed, ideally on the same machine with the same tooling. If a worn locating pin is blamed, run parts with the worn pin and with a new one and show the difference in the measurement. Causes that cannot be turned on and off are hypotheses, and customer quality engineers at automotive OEMs routinely reject 8Ds that skip this.

atoms.obligation: Identify the escape point separately from the occurrence cause and correct the detection control as well as the process.
atoms.lesson: Every defect has two failures: it was made, and it got out. The escape point is the last control that should have caught it — a gauge, a vision check, a final audit — and it needs its own why-chain. Typical escapes are a vision system with the wrong region of interest, an inspection frequency of one per hour on a defect that comes in bursts, or a check that only runs at startup. Update the control plan and FMEA detection ranking with both fixes.

name: control-chart-interpretation
description: Reads SPC charts from the floor and says whether the process genuinely shifted or the operator is chasing noise. Use when a chart trips a rule, when someone adjusts a machine after every reading, when limits look wrong after a process change, or when specification limits have been drawn on a control chart.
expansions: chart tripped a run of seven
operator adjusts after every reading
control limits look far too tight
points hug the centre line
when do i recalculate the limits
xbar and r chart on the grinder
is this special cause or normal variation
spec limits drawn on the control chart

atoms.obligation: Judge stability against control limits calculated from the process data and never against the drawing tolerance.
atoms.lesson: Control limits come from within-subgroup variation, typically three sigma estimated through the average range and the d2 constant. Specification limits come from the designer. Putting the spec on the chart teaches operators to adjust whenever a point approaches tolerance, which is textbook overadjustment and inflates variation. Keep them on separate charts, or on a capability histogram where comparing the voice of the process to the voice of the customer is the whole point.

atoms.obligation: Act only on recognised out-of-control signals and leave the process alone while it shows common-cause variation only.
atoms.lesson: Use a fixed rule set and post it at the chart: one point beyond three sigma, nine on one side of centre, six steadily rising or falling, fourteen alternating, two of three beyond two sigma. Each signal has a different meaning — a single spike suggests a one-off such as a bad blank, a run suggests tool wear or a temperature drift, alternation usually means two spindles, two cavities or two operators mixed into one chart.

atoms.obligation: Check how subgroups were formed first when points hug the centre line or the limits look implausibly wide.
atoms.lesson: Rational subgrouping means the pieces in a subgroup were made under conditions as alike as possible: five consecutive parts from one spindle, not one part from each of five cavities. Mixing cavities inflates within-subgroup range, widens the limits and makes everything look in control while the cavities differ badly. The reverse — points glued to the centre line — usually means the subgroup spans a long period and captures between-shift variation.

atoms.obligation: Recalculate control limits only after a deliberate documented process change, and annotate the change on the chart.
atoms.lesson: Limits recalculated every month drift along behind a deteriorating process until nothing ever signals. Freeze limits after an initial study of twenty to twenty-five subgroups from a stable period and hold them. Recalculate when something real changed: a new tool design, a machine rebuild, a different material supplier. Draw a vertical line on the chart at the change with a note, so anyone reading history knows why the centre line moved.

name: gage-rr-study
description: Plans and interprets measurement system analysis so gauge noise is not mistaken for process variation. Trigger when two inspectors disagree on the same part, when a new fixture or measurement program is introduced, when a study comes back failing, or when a customer submission requires an MSA.
expansions: two inspectors get different readings
new gauge before we release it
grr came back at twenty-eight percent
how many parts and trials do we need
attribute gauge for the visual check
the ppap asks for an msa
caliper and cmm disagree on the bore
measurement noise is eating our tolerance

atoms.obligation: Select study parts that span the real process spread instead of parts pulled from a single good batch.
atoms.lesson: The standard crossed study is ten parts, three operators, three trials, but the ten parts must be chosen deliberately across the range the process actually produces, including some near each tolerance limit. Ten near-identical parts make part variation small, so the gauge repeatability share of total variation explodes and a perfectly adequate gauge fails. If parts cannot be spread, report percent of tolerance rather than percent of study variation.

atoms.obligation: Randomise measurement order and keep operators blind to previous readings so the repeat trials stay independent.
atoms.lesson: If an inspector measures part three and remembers 12.04 from the last round, repeatability is fake. Number the parts on a hidden face, have a third person hand them over in a shuffled order each trial, and record on a sheet the operator cannot see. Also fix the measurement location: a bore diameter measured at a different depth or clocking angle each time turns real part form error into apparent gauge noise.

atoms.obligation: Report the result as both percent of tolerance and percent of total variation, and state which one drove the decision.
atoms.lesson: Percent of tolerance answers whether the gauge can sort good from bad; percent of study variation answers whether it can be used for process improvement and SPC. The usual thresholds are under ten percent acceptable, ten to thirty conditionally acceptable depending on cost and criticality, over thirty unacceptable. Also report the number of distinct categories: fewer than five means the system cannot resolve the process distribution well enough for control charting.

atoms.obligation: Fix reproducibility problems with fixturing and method definition before buying a more accurate instrument.
atoms.lesson: Repeatability is the equipment; reproducibility is the operators. High reproducibility with low repeatability means people are doing the job differently — different seating of the part, different pressure on a snap gauge, different interpretation of where the feature starts. The remedy is a fixture that constrains the part, a defined measurement point on the work instruction, and a short hands-on requalification, all of which cost far less than a new coordinate measuring machine.

name: first-article-inspection
description: Prepares or checks a first article and production part approval package for a new or changed part. Use when a tool has been moved to another press, when a drawing revision lands, when a new supplier's first shipment arrives, or when a customer asks for a full dimensional report on first parts.
expansions: fai for the new drawing revision
tool moved to another press
balloon the drawing for the report
ppap level three submission
first parts off the new mould
which characteristics are critical here
customer wants a dimensional report
supplier first shipment needs approval

atoms.obligation: Balloon every drawing characteristic and report a measured value for each, including notes, finishes and material callouts.
atoms.lesson: A first article is a completeness exercise, not a sample of the interesting dimensions. Number every dimension, tolerance, general note, surface finish, plating spec and material requirement on a ballooned print, then give each an actual result and a pass or fail. Notes carry real requirements — burr-free edges, no flash on face A, heat treat to a hardness range — and they are the ones most often missed and most often found at customer audits.

atoms.obligation: Trigger a new first article whenever tooling, process, location or drawing revision changes, not only for brand new parts.
atoms.lesson: The standard triggers are a design change affecting form, fit or function, a change of manufacturing process or method, a tool or die repair or replacement, a move of production to another machine or plant, a new sub-tier supplier, and a lapse in production of usually two years. Partial first articles cover only the affected characteristics, but the delta must be documented against the original full report rather than replacing it.

atoms.obligation: Measure the required consecutive parts made under normal production conditions rather than hand-finished samples.
atoms.lesson: Approval parts must come from production tooling, the production process, the production rate and the intended operators, usually a run of at least three hundred pieces for a full submission. Parts polished by the toolmaker prove nothing about the process that will run on nights. Record the run rate, the machine and the operator on the report, because a customer investigating a later escape will compare the approval conditions with the conditions in the field.

atoms.obligation: Identify special and critical characteristics explicitly and attach their capability study and control plan entries.
atoms.lesson: Safety and regulatory characteristics carry customer-specific symbols and demand a documented capability of typically Ppk 1.67 initially and Cpk 1.33 ongoing, plus a defined reaction plan and often error-proofing. Confirm the customer's symbol set before submission, because an inverted delta on one OEM's print means something different from a diamond on another's. The control plan must show the control method, sample size and frequency for each of those characteristics.

name: nonconforming-material-disposition
description: Moves quarantined material through review to a defensible disposition and closes the paperwork behind it. Trigger with a hold tag on a pallet, a batch that failed final test, a use-as-is request from production, an overflowing quarantine cage, or a question about whether rework needs customer approval.
expansions: pallet on hold since tuesday
can we use this as is
rework or scrap the failed lot
mrb meeting for the suspect batch
deviation request to the customer
quarantine cage is overflowing
who signs off on a concession
sort the suspect batch tonight

atoms.obligation: Physically segregate and tag nonconforming stock with defect, quantity, batch and hold owner before any disposition is discussed.
atoms.lesson: A red tag with no owner and no date is how a pallet sits for six weeks and eventually gets shipped by a night-shift picker. Move suspect material to a locked or clearly bounded quarantine area, block the lot in the system so it cannot be picked, and put the defect description, quantity, batch, discovery date and named owner on the tag. Auditors check that quarantine stock reconciles with the system hold list.

atoms.obligation: Bound the suspect population back to the last known good check and forward to the last verified shipment.
atoms.lesson: The suspect window runs from the last confirmed good inspection result to the point where the process was corrected, and it must include finished goods, WIP, material at the customer and stock in transit. Traceability comes from lot and date codes, machine and cavity marks, and the production record. If the process check frequency is hourly, the exposure is an hour of production plus everything that shipped since, not just the pallet where the defect was noticed.

atoms.obligation: Obtain written customer concession before any use-as-is or repair disposition on a customer-specified characteristic.
atoms.lesson: Scrap and rework to print are internal decisions. Use-as-is and repair change what the customer receives, so they need a deviation request stating the characteristic, the actual values, the quantity, the duration or lot limit and the containment. Automotive and aerospace customers treat unauthorised shipment of known nonconforming product as a controlled shipping trigger. Record the concession number on the shipping paperwork and stop when the approved quantity or date runs out.

atoms.obligation: Re-inspect reworked parts against the same plan as new parts and record rework as a separate traceable operation.
atoms.lesson: Rework routinely introduces new defects — heat marks from regrinding, damaged threads from re-tapping, coating loss where a burr was removed — so the reworked lot needs the full inspection plan and often extra checks on what the rework touched. Book rework as its own operation with its own labour and yield so the true cost of quality is visible; hiding it inside the original work order makes scrap look cheaper than it is.
