customer wants a narrow delivery window
stops per hour is dropping
add a second run in the afternoon
failed deliveries keep repeating
balance routes across drivers
service time longer than planned

atoms.obligation: Build routes from measured service time at each stop, not from driving time plus a flat allowance.
atoms.lesson: Time at the stop commonly accounts for a third to a half of the working day and varies enormously: a kerbside drop at a house, a city centre delivery needing a parking search and a walk, a delivery to a floor with a goods lift, a signature and returns processing, or a supermarket back door with a booking desk. Measure it per stop type from telematics or driver debriefs and hold the figures in the plan; a single average is why the last two routes always run over.

atoms.obligation: Treat legal driving limits, shift length and depot loading cut-offs as hard constraints in the plan.
atoms.lesson: A route that only works if the driver skips a break is a route that fails. Build in the statutory break pattern and daily driving limit, the loading and vehicle check time before departure, and the return and debrief afterwards. Vehicle-specific restrictions bind too: weight limits on bridges and in low emission zones, height restrictions, delivery curfews in residential streets and permitted loading hours in city centres. Check the constraint before the optimiser proposes an elegant illegal plan.

atoms.obligation: Cluster stops by geography and window compatibility before sequencing anything within a route.
atoms.lesson: Route quality is decided by which stops share a vehicle, not by the order they are visited. Narrow time windows fragment density: three morning-only customers scattered across a region can each pull a different vehicle out of its cluster and cost more than the rest of the round. Group by window band first, then by geography, and quantify what a promised window costs so the commercial conversation about premium charges or wider bands can happen with a number attached.

atoms.obligation: Compare planned against actual on every route and feed the deviation back into the next plan.
atoms.lesson: Plans decay. Track planned versus actual departure, arrival at each stop, service duration, route finish time and failure reasons, and look at the pattern by driver, by day of week and by area. Persistent overruns on the same round mean the service time assumptions are stale, not that the driver is slow. Failed deliveries clustered on one estate usually indicate an access or window problem fixable with a pre-advice message rather than a second attempt.

name: shipment-exception-triage
description: Diagnoses a stuck, late, missing or damaged shipment and decides the recovery action. Trigger it when a container is on hold, when a customer escalates an order that has not arrived, when a vehicle breaks down under load, when cargo is rolled from a vessel, or when delivery is disputed.
expansions: container on hold at the port
customer escalated a missing order
truck broke down with our freight
rolled from the vessel again
shipment stuck in customs clearance
proof of delivery signed but nothing received
expedite options for a late load
damaged pallet reported at delivery

atoms.obligation: Establish the physical location and the legal status of the goods before promising anything to the customer.
atoms.lesson: Location and status are different questions. A container can be discharged and sitting on the terminal while customs has not released it, cleared but with no trucking appointment, or released and detained by the carrier for unpaid charges. Pull the last carrier event, the terminal availability status, the customs status and the delivery order status separately, and note the timestamp of each. A tracking page showing arrived is not evidence the goods can move today.

atoms.obligation: Identify which type of hold is in force, because the party able to release it differs by type.
atoms.lesson: A customs documentary query is answered by the broker with paperwork, usually within a day. A non-intrusive scan runs on the authority's queue and cannot be expedited. An intensive examination means devanning at a bonded facility and typically costs days plus handling charges. A partner agency hold needs the relevant agency, not customs. A carrier freight hold clears on payment, and a terminal hold on storage settlement. Naming the hold type correctly is what turns an open-ended delay into an estimate.

atoms.obligation: Compare recovery options on landed cost against the cost of missing the requirement, then choose deliberately.
atoms.lesson: Options are usually air upgrade for part of the quantity, expedited road, a partial shipment now with the balance to follow, substitution from another site, or accepting the delay. Price each including the surcharge, the extra handling and any duty difference, then set it against the actual consequence - a production stoppage, a contractual late penalty, a lost promotional window or an unhappy but tolerant customer. Expediting the whole quantity when a fifth would hold the line is the routine over-reaction.

atoms.obligation: Communicate a revised commitment with a time for the next update, and protect claim rights while recovering.
atoms.lesson: Customers tolerate delay far better than silence, so give a new date, the reason in plain terms, and when you will next speak even if nothing has changed. In parallel preserve the claim: note visible damage or shortage on the delivery receipt before signing, photograph the load and the seal, keep the packaging, and send the carrier written notice inside the mode's notice period. Recovering the shipment and waiving the claim by signing clean is the expensive mistake.

name: cargo-claim-filing
description: Prepares and pursues loss, damage and shortage claims against carriers and cargo insurers. Trigger it when goods arrive crushed, wet, short or missing, when a carrier denies liability, when a container is lost overboard, or when a claim notice deadline is approaching.
expansions: pallets arrived crushed
carrier denied our damage claim
short delivered two cartons
container lost overboard
claim deadline is approaching
notation on the delivery receipt
salvage value on damaged goods
insurance versus carrier liability

atoms.obligation: Note the exception at delivery and preserve the goods and packaging as evidence before anything is moved or scrapped.
atoms.lesson: A clean signed receipt is prima facie evidence the goods arrived in good order, and overturning it later is hard. Write the specific damage or shortage on the receipt, photograph the load in the trailer or container before unloading, capture the seal number and its condition, and keep the damaged packaging until the claim closes. Where damage is only found after opening, most contracts allow a concealed damage notice within a short window, commonly five to fifteen days, and the survey should be requested inside it.

atoms.obligation: File within the notice and suit deadlines that apply to that mode and contract, not to a general assumption.
atoms.lesson: The clocks are short and they differ. Sea carriage under the common convention regime usually requires notice at delivery or within three days for non-apparent damage, and suit within one year. Air carriage requires written complaint within roughly fourteen days for damage and twenty-one days for delay, with two years to sue. Domestic road carriage in the United States typically allows nine months to file the claim and two years plus a day to sue. Diarise both dates when the exception is first recorded.

atoms.obligation: Quantify the claim on the recoverable measure with evidence, rather than on retail or replacement price.
atoms.lesson: Carrier liability is generally the value of the goods at destination, evidenced by the commercial invoice, plus prepaid freight and duty where they are wasted. Lost margin, downstream penalties and lost sales are usually excluded. You must also mitigate: attempt repair, remark or discounted sale, and credit the salvage proceeds against the claim. Assemble the invoice, packing list, transport document, delivery receipt with the exception, photographs, survey report and the repair or salvage evidence into one file.

atoms.obligation: Check the liability limits first, and decide whether cargo insurance rather than the carrier is the real recovery route.
atoms.lesson: Carrier liability is capped by weight or by package under every mode, and for dense low-value freight the cap can be a fraction of the loss - the sea regime limits per package or per kilo, whichever is higher, and road carriers offer released value rates below actual worth. Declaring a higher value costs a premium per shipment. An all-risk marine cargo policy usually recovers faster, on invoice value plus a mark-up, and the insurer then pursues the carrier by subrogation.

name: cold-chain-excursion-review
description: Investigates temperature and humidity excursions on temperature-controlled freight and supports the disposition decision. Trigger it when a data logger shows time out of range, when a reefer alarms in transit, when a pharmaceutical or food shipment arrives warm, or when the same lane keeps producing excursions.
expansions: logger shows two hours above range
reefer alarmed during the ocean leg
pharma pallet arrived warm
can we release this product
set point wrong on the container
vaccines held at the airport
qualify a new temperature lane
repeat excursions on one route

atoms.obligation: Reconstruct the excursion from logger data against the transport timeline before proposing any disposition.
atoms.lesson: Download the full logger file rather than the summary alarm, and note the sampling interval, because a five-minute interval can miss a short spike and a thirty-minute interval understates duration. Align each out-of-range period with the timeline: tarmac dwell, terminal transfer, customs hold, a gate-out with the unit off, or a door opening. Check where the sensor sat - a probe against a container wall reads differently from one in the pallet core - and confirm the calibration certificate is current.

atoms.obligation: Apply the product's own stability data and the quality authority's rules to the release decision rather than deciding alone.
atoms.lesson: Products carry a defined stability budget: an approved cumulative allowance of time outside the labelled range, sometimes split between above and below. Frozen product that thawed is treated very differently from refrigerated product that warmed within its excursion allowance, and a single freeze event can destroy a vaccine that tolerates hours of warmth. Mean kinetic temperature summarises thermal history but does not by itself authorise release. The quality function makes the disposition; logistics supplies the reconstructed evidence.

atoms.obligation: Separate equipment failure from packaging, loading and handling failure when assigning root cause.
atoms.lesson: Look at the unit first: set point wrong or in the wrong scale, fresh air vent open on a chilled load, unit switched off for a road leg or a gate move, failed compressor, or a generator set that ran out of fuel. Then look at the load: no pre-cooling, product loaded warm, stacking above the red line blocking airflow, blocked return air, or a passive shipper packed with coolant that was never conditioned to specification. The paperwork usually names the wrong one of these.

atoms.obligation: Requalify the lane or the pack-out when the same route produces the excursion more than once.
atoms.lesson: A repeat excursion is a design failure, not an incident. Run a summer and a winter profile on the lane, comparing ambient exposure at each handover against the shipper's tested performance, and check the actual dwell times at the airport, the transfer terminal and customs rather than the planned ones. Then change something structural: a longer-duration passive shipper, more or better conditioned coolant, an active container, a different routing with fewer handovers, or a bonded cold store at the hold point.

name: freight-invoice-audit
description: Audits carrier and forwarder invoices against contracted rates and accessorial terms before payment, and recovers overcharges after it. Trigger it when a freight bill does not match the quote, when accessorial charges creep upward, when duplicate invoices appear, at monthly accrual, or before a payment run.
expansions: invoice does not match the quoted rate
accessorial charges keep growing
duplicate invoice for the same load
reweigh and reclass charge on a bill
fuel surcharge calculation looks off
monthly freight accrual review
recover overcharges from last quarter
audit invoices before the payment run

atoms.obligation: Match every invoice to its booking, its contracted rate record and its proof of delivery before approving payment.
atoms.lesson: The three-way match is what catches the bulk of errors: an invoice with no matching booking, a rate that does not exist in the contract, or a delivery never evidenced. Duplicates hide behind a changed reference, so deduplicate on the transport document number and the shipment date rather than on the invoice number alone. Charges for shipments cancelled before pickup and shipments billed to both shipper and consignee are common and only visible when the booking record is the anchor.

atoms.obligation: Recalculate the rate basis from the shipment's actual measured characteristics, not from the figures the carrier asserts.
atoms.lesson: Air and parcel bill on the greater of actual and volumetric weight, so a wrong dimension inflates the charge silently. Less-than-truckload freight is rated by class or by density, and carriers reweigh and reclass in the terminal, generating a supplementary bill that is right about as often as it is wrong. Check the fuel surcharge against the published index for the correct week and the contractual base, and check that any minimum charge or deficit weight rating was applied correctly.

atoms.obligation: Challenge accessorials that lack a contractual basis or documentary evidence, and do it inside the dispute window.
atoms.lesson: Detention, layover, redelivery, reconsignment, tail lift, inside delivery, residential surcharge, congestion and storage all need both a contractual rate and evidence that the event occurred and was not caused by the carrier. Ask for the gate timestamps or the driver log, and compare with your yard record. Disputes generally must be raised within the carrier's stated window, often thirty to one hundred and eighty days, and overcharge recovery against common carriers has its own statutory limit, so age the queue and work oldest first.

atoms.obligation: Code the audited cost to the right lane, order and account so cost per unit reporting can be trusted.
atoms.lesson: An audit that only protects cash still leaves the analytics broken. Allocate each charge to the shipment, the lane, the business unit and the accessorial category, and split linehaul from fuel from accessorials, because a blended figure hides where the money leaks. Accrue unbilled freight from booked but uninvoiced shipments at contract rates each month so the period is complete. The accessorial categories that recur are the ones worth designing out of the operation.

name: shift-schedule-build
description: Builds a weekly labor schedule from a forecast of covers and a labor cost target, station by station. Use it when writing next week's server, cook and dish schedule, when labor percentage ran over budget, when a holiday or a large reservation night needs extra coverage, or when call-outs force a reshuffle. It also checks overtime exposure, minor work rules and advance-posting requirements before the schedule goes up.
expansions: labor cost ran thirty four percent
need next week's server schedule
three call outs saturday night
mothers day staffing plan
cutting shifts to hit labor budget
overtime creeping up on line cooks
who closes on friday
new cook needs training shifts

atoms.obligation: Build the schedule from a forecast of covers by daypart before assigning any names to shifts.
atoms.lesson: Forecast from the same weekday over the last three to four weeks, then adjust for weather, local events and holidays. Convert covers to sales, then sales to labor hours at your productivity standard: roughly one server per twenty to twenty-five covers a shift, one line cook per thirty-five entrees an hour, one host per hundred covers. Kitchen prep hours are largely fixed; line hours are the variable you actually flex.

atoms.obligation: Schedule against a labor percentage target split between fixed salaried hours and variable hourly hours.
atoms.lesson: Full-service total labor typically lands at thirty to thirty-five percent of sales, split roughly twelve to sixteen points front of house and thirteen to sixteen back of house, with management salary fixed on top. Quick service runs lower. Because salary and minimum coverage do not flex, a slow week blows the percentage even with perfect scheduling, so judge the schedule on variable hours per cover, not on the headline percentage alone.

atoms.obligation: Stagger start and cut times across the shift instead of scheduling everyone a full open-to-close block.
atoms.lesson: Mid-shifts absorb the peak without paying for the shoulders: a five-hour four-to-nine server on a Friday costs half a double. Write the cut order on the schedule so the closing manager is not negotiating it at nine o'clock, and rotate it so the same person is not always cut first. Where predictive scheduling laws apply, posting must run fourteen days ahead and late changes carry premium pay.

atoms.obligation: Check overtime, minor work restrictions and required breaks against the draft before posting the schedule.
atoms.lesson: Federal overtime starts above forty hours in a week; California adds daily overtime past eight and double time past twelve. Fourteen and fifteen year olds are limited in hours and hours of day, and no one under eighteen may operate slicers, mixers or fryers. Watch clopening gaps, state meal and rest break rules, and the dual jobs rule limiting untipped side work when a tip credit is taken.

name: shift-briefing-lineup
description: Runs the pre-shift lineup for the floor team: what is 86'd, what is new, who is in the building and what the one focus of the shift is. Use it before doors open, when a special needs a tasting note the servers can actually repeat, when VIPs or large parties are on the book, or when the last service went sideways and the team needs a single correction. Keeps the meeting under ten minutes and ends with section and station assignments.
expansions: what do i cover in preshift
eighty six list for tonight
new special needs tasting notes
vip four top at seven
servers keep forgetting the special
big party in the private room tonight
quick lineup before doors
sunday brunch preshift notes

atoms.obligation: Open the lineup with the eighty-six list, the substitutions and anything running low before any other topic.
atoms.lesson: An eighty-six discovered at the table costs a re-fire, a comp and a guest apology; discovered at lineup it costs nothing. Read the list from the kitchen board, not memory, and include partial counts, since twelve portions of halibut is information a server can sell around. Confirm the board is updated in the point of sale and on the host stand so the kitchen is not printing tickets for a dish that no longer exists.

atoms.obligation: Have the team taste the special and give them one sentence they can actually say to a guest.
atoms.lesson: Servers sell what they have tasted. Plate one portion, taste it together, and hand them a single line covering the protein, the cooking method, the two supporting components and one adjective that is not delicious. Add the price, the allergens and the count available. A special described as chef's preparation of fish sells at a fraction of the rate of one described as olive oil poached halibut with fennel and blood orange.

atoms.obligation: Read out the reservations that need special handling, naming the party, the time and what is required.
atoms.lesson: Flag anniversaries and birthdays with what is arranged, regulars with their known preferences, allergies already declared at booking, guests with mobility needs and their table, press or ownership visits, and any party over six with a preset menu. Say which server owns each and what the timing constraint is, for example a theatre party that must be out by seven fifteen. Vague notes such as VIP at eight produce no action.

atoms.obligation: Assign sections, stations and support roles out loud, then close with one measurable focus for the shift.
atoms.lesson: Name who has which section, who is on expo, who runs food, who is on the door, and who is cutting first. Then pick a single behavior to work on tonight, chosen from last shift's actual failure: greet within ninety seconds, sell one dessert per table, pre-bus before coffee. One focus lands; five become noise. Check that focus at the shift-end huddle so the team sees it was real.

name: menu-engineering-review
description: Analyses the menu mix to find which items carry the profit and which are freeloading, then decides what to keep, reprice, reposition or cut. Use it before a seasonal menu change, when someone asks whether a popular dish is actually making money, when the menu has grown past what the line can execute, or when a price increase is on the table. Works from item sales counts and costed plate margins, not intuition.
expansions: which dishes actually make money
menu mix report for last quarter
should we cut the salmon
burger sells but the margin is thin
too many items on the menu
menu item ranking by profit
reprice or remove the short rib
menu redesign before spring

atoms.obligation: Classify every item by contribution margin in dollars and by share of category sales, not by food cost percentage.
atoms.lesson: Contribution margin is menu price minus plate cost, and it is what pays rent. A thirty percent cost on a twelve dollar pasta returns eight forty; a forty percent cost on a thirty-four dollar steak returns twenty forty. Chasing percentage pushes teams to feature the cheap plate. Set the popularity threshold at seventy percent of an equal share within the category, so with ten entrees anything above seven percent of entree sales counts as popular.

atoms.obligation: Give each quadrant a different action rather than treating low performers as one group to delete.
atoms.lesson: High popularity with high margin is a star: protect the recipe, put it where the eye lands, never discount it. High popularity with low margin is a plowhorse: raise price modestly, reengineer the plate cost, or shrink the garnish rather than cutting a guest favorite. Low popularity with high margin is a puzzle: reposition, rename, train the servers to describe it. Low on both is a dog: cut it unless it is holding a dietary need.

atoms.obligation: Use at least four full weeks of item counts and strip out promotions, events and comped covers first.
atoms.lesson: A single busy weekend or a two-week feature distorts mix badly. Four to six weeks smooths the noise and captures both weekday and weekend behavior. Remove banquet and preset menu covers, staff meal, comps and any item that spent part of the period eighty-sixed, since an item unavailable for nine days looks unpopular when it was simply absent. Compare like periods year over year for seasonal items.

atoms.obligation: Verify the plate cost from a current costed recipe before repricing or cutting any item.
atoms.lesson: Most menu decisions go wrong on stale costs. Pull the recipe card, confirm the yields and portion weights are what the line actually does, and reprice ingredients from the last thirty days of invoices, not from last year. Then check cross-utilization before deleting: a dish that carries the only use for a whole tenderloin trim or a house pickle takes those economics down with it, and the station load may shift onto an already-buried cook.

name: recipe-costing-cards
description: Builds standardized recipe cards with yields, portion specs and true plate costs so the same dish costs and tastes the same every time. Use it when a new dish or special is going on the menu, when portions are drifting on the line, when someone asks what a plate actually costs, or when a whole fish or primal needs a yield test before it can be priced. Also used to re-cost cards when invoice prices move.
expansions: cost out the new short rib dish
what does this plate actually cost
yield test on whole salmon
portion sizes drifting on the line
price the special before it goes on
spec sheet for the sauce
as purchased versus edible portion
recipe card for the prep team

atoms.obligation: Run a yield test and record edible portion cost before costing any dish built on a whole fish or primal.
atoms.lesson: Yield percentage is edible weight divided by purchased weight, and edible portion cost is purchase price divided by that yield. Whole salmon returns roughly fifty-five to sixty percent after scaling and pin-boning; a whole tenderloin around sixty-five to seventy percent trimmed. Nine dollar a pound salmon at fifty-five percent is sixteen thirty-six a pound on the plate, so a six ounce portion costs six fourteen, not three thirty-eight. Credit usable trim to stock or staff meal.

atoms.obligation: State every component with quantity, purchase unit, conversion and cost, including the sub-recipes it draws on.
atoms.lesson: Cost sauces, stocks, pickles and doughs as their own cards with a batch yield, then draw the plated portion from that batch. A demi that costs forty-two dollars for two point five liters is roughly one seventy per fifty millilitre ladle. Record the conversion explicitly, because the most common costing error is mixing purchase units with recipe units, for example costing a case price against a per-pound quantity and understating the plate by a factor of ten.

atoms.obligation: Include the full plate in the cost: garnish, finishing oil, sauce, bread service, condiments and disposables.
atoms.lesson: Operators call the untracked remainder the Q factor and it commonly runs three to eight percent of plate cost. Bread and butter, olive oil, ramekins and sauce cups, lemon wedges, herb garnish, takeaway packaging and even the fryer oil consumed per basket belong somewhere. Assign them to the items that use them where you can and spread the rest as a fixed per-cover adder, or your theoretical cost will always run below actual by several points.

atoms.obligation: Photograph and weight-spec each finished plate, then re-cost the card when key ingredient prices move materially.
atoms.lesson: The card is a control only if the line can reproduce it: state portion weights in grams or ounces, name the pan and the plate, and post a photo at the station. Weigh ten portions off the line during service to confirm the spec is real. Set a re-costing trigger, commonly a five percent move on any ingredient over ten percent of the plate, and re-cost the whole menu at least quarterly.

name: food-cost-variance
description: Closes the period on food cost and explains the gap between theoretical and actual usage. Use it when food cost jumps several points, when the monthly inventory does not reconcile, when protein usage does not match what was sold, or when it is time to close the period and produce a number someone will be asked to defend. Separates price movement from operational waste, over-portioning and shrink.
expansions: food cost jumped four points
theoretical versus actual gap
monthly inventory count is off
protein usage does not match sales
where is the shrink coming from
close the period food cost
invoice prices went up mid month
comps and waste are killing us

atoms.obligation: Calculate actual cost as opening inventory plus purchases minus closing inventory, with transfers and staff meal removed.
atoms.lesson: Cost of goods equals opening plus purchases plus transfers in minus transfers out minus closing. Pull out bar-to-kitchen transfers such as citrus, cream and wine, plus staff meal, research plates and comps, or you will charge the kitchen for the bar's cost. Count at the same hour of the same day each period, in the same units, valued at the most recent invoice price. Counting the day after a large delivery instead of the day before can swing the number two or three points on its own.

atoms.obligation: Compare theoretical usage against actual at the item and category level, never at the total only.
atoms.lesson: Theoretical usage is items sold multiplied by the costed recipe. A single blended variance tells you nothing; splitting it does. Protein overage points at portioning, so weigh ten portions off the line unannounced. Produce overage points at spoilage and over-prep, so check the walk-in and the prep pars. Dairy and oil point at waste or unlogged staff meal. On a hundred and twenty thousand dollar food month, one and a half points is eighteen hundred dollars.

atoms.obligation: Split the variance into a price component and a usage component and report them separately.
atoms.lesson: Price variance is the change in unit cost multiplied by the quantity actually used; usage variance is the extra quantity multiplied by the old cost. If chicken moved from two eighty-nine to three sixty-five a pound and you used four hundred pounds, three hundred and four dollars of the miss is market movement with no operational fault. Track a basket of your top twenty spend items weekly so a supplier increase is visible before the period closes, not after.

atoms.obligation: Audit voids, comps, discounts and waste logs before concluding that product is being stolen.
atoms.lesson: Most unexplained variance is process, not theft. Review voids after the item fired, comps by server and reason code, employee discounts, and any promotion that was not costed. Then check the waste log for entries that stopped appearing, which usually means logging stopped rather than waste stopping. Only after receiving, portioning, waste and comps are clean does a persistent, item-specific gap on high-value product justify tightening access and reviewing deliveries against invoices.

name: pour-cost-inventory
description: Counts the bar and calculates pour cost by category so overpouring, unrung drinks and giveaway show up as numbers. Use it for the weekly or monthly liquor count, when pour cost drifts above target, when the well seems to disappear faster than it sells, or when a cocktail spec is being written and someone needs the cost per drink. Covers spirits, draft, bottled beer and wine separately.
expansions: pour cost is twenty six percent
weekly liquor count
well vodka disappearing
counting bottles by tenths
draft beer yield looks low
cocktail spec versus free pour
bar variance report
count the wine cellar

atoms.obligation: Count open bottles consistently by tenths and weigh anything whose level cannot be judged by eye.
atoms.lesson: The house standard is tenths of a bottle judged against the label, always by the same two people, always in the same order around the bar. Opaque bottles, thick liqueurs and cordials need a scale: gross weight minus the known empty weight, divided by density. Kegs are weighed too, since a full half barrel runs about a hundred and sixty pounds with a thirty pound shell, so a hundred and thirty pounds of beer is roughly fifteen and a half gallons.

atoms.obligation: Calculate and target pour cost separately for spirits, draft beer, bottled beer and wine.
atoms.lesson: The targets are genuinely different: spirits eighteen to twenty-two percent, draft twenty to twenty-four, bottled and canned beer twenty-four to twenty-eight, wine thirty to thirty-eight and higher on a serious bottle list. Blending them into one bar number lets a strong wine month hide a bleeding well. Report each category against its own target and against last period, and note the mix shift, since a busy wine week raises blended cost with nothing wrong at all.

atoms.obligation: Compare ounces depleted from the count against ounces sold from the sales mix at the product level.
atoms.lesson: Multiply each drink sold by its spec to get ounces that should have left the bottle, then compare with what actually did. A one and a quarter ounce spec free-poured at one and a half is a twenty percent overpour; across sixty bottles of well vodka a month at eighteen dollars a bottle that is two hundred and sixteen dollars. Jiggers, measured pourers and an occasional audited shift fix it far faster than accusing anyone.

atoms.obligation: Log spills, breakage, comped drinks, tastings and promotional pours at the time they happen, with a name attached.
atoms.lesson: Unlogged giveaway is the single biggest source of phantom bar variance. Keep a spill and comp sheet at the well, require a manager approval for comped rounds, and record staff tastings of a new cocktail as a batch rather than as invisible ounces. Recipe development, wine training pours and samples to a supplier rep all leave the building as inventory and must return as an entry, or the variance will read as theft.

name: daily-prep-par-list
description: Sets prep pars and writes the daily prep list by station so the kitchen neither runs out mid-service nor throws product away at close. Use it when writing tomorrow's prep, when a component ran out during dinner, when too much prep is going in the bin, or when a big forecast night needs the pars raised. Includes labeling, dating and rotation so what is prepped is actually usable.
expansions: prep list for tomorrow
we ran out of demi at eight
pars for the saute station
too much prep going in the bin
sunday prep for three hundred covers
who preps what station
shelf life on the aioli
prep sheet for the morning cook

atoms.obligation: Set each par from forecast covers multiplied by measured usage per cover, not from a number someone remembers.
atoms.lesson: Derive usage per cover from the sales mix: if the braise sells on eighteen percent of covers and takes a hundred and eighty grams, a two hundred and forty cover Saturday needs about eight kilos plus a safety margin. Carry pars as a par for a slow day and a par for a busy day rather than one figure. Re-derive them after any menu change, because a new dish sharing the same sauce silently doubles that par.

atoms.obligation: Write the prep list by station with quantity, container size, and a named cook against every task.
atoms.lesson: A list that reads reduce demi is unactionable; four litres of demi, two third pans, Marco, by two o'clock is. Order the list so long-lead items start first, stocks and braises before dressings and garnishes, and mark what must be finished before the previous shift leaves. Include the carryover from last night on the same sheet so the cook is prepping the gap, not the full par on top of six litres already in the walk-in.

atoms.obligation: Label every prepped item with contents, production date and use-by, and rotate strictly oldest first.
atoms.lesson: Ready-to-eat food that needs time and temperature control gets a maximum of seven days held at forty-one degrees Fahrenheit or below, counting the day of prep as day one, and the clock does not reset when it is transferred to a new container. Date labels are among the first things an inspector reads. Position the new batch behind the old on the shelf, and make the closing cook responsible for pulling anything dated for tomorrow to the front.

atoms.obligation: Reconcile leftover pars at close and carry both the shortfall and the surplus into the next day's list.
atoms.lesson: Walk the line and the walk-in at close with the prep sheet in hand and write the actual remaining quantity beside each par. Persistent surplus means the par is too high or the item is not selling; persistent zero at nine o'clock means the par is too low and guests were told no. Feed the recurring gaps back into the pars weekly rather than adjusting nightly, and record any item that was eighty-sixed and why.

name: line-check-protocol
description: Runs the pre-service line check across every station: taste, temperature, quantity and mise, with the holding logs signed. Use it before doors open, when a cold well or walk-in is reading warm, when something on the line tastes off, or when service problems keep tracing back to product that was never checked. Ends with a decision on what gets discarded, what gets replaced and what is eighty-sixed for the shift.
expansions: line check before doors
walk in reading forty six degrees
sauce tastes off on the line
hot line holding temps
cold well not holding
who signs the temperature log
check the line before dinner
expo station missing mise

atoms.obligation: Taste, temperature-check and eyeball every item on every station before the doors open, in a fixed order.
atoms.lesson: Work the line the way tickets flow: garde manger, saute, grill, fry, expo, then walk-in and reach-ins. Taste with a clean spoon each time, never the cooking spoon. A check that only reads temperatures misses the real failures, which are a broken emulsion, an over-reduced sauce, a dressing that split overnight and a protein that was portioned yesterday and looks grey. The chef or sous does it, not the cook who prepped the item.

atoms.obligation: Record hot and cold holding temperatures on a signed log with the time and the reading, not a tick.
atoms.lesson: Hot holding stays at one hundred thirty-five degrees Fahrenheit or above, cold at forty-one or below. The code requires checks at least every four hours, but most operators check every two so a drifting item can still be saved rather than discarded. Probe the thickest part, sanitize the probe between items, and calibrate weekly in an ice bath to thirty-two degrees. A log filled in from memory at close is worthless in an inspection and in an illness investigation.

atoms.obligation: Discard anything out of temperature or past its date rather than reworking, reheating or blending it away.
atoms.lesson: Food in the danger zone between forty-one and one hundred thirty-five degrees for under two hours can be rapidly cooled or reheated to one hundred sixty-five; between two and four hours it must be used immediately or discarded; past four hours it is trash however it looks and smells. Reheating for hot holding must reach one hundred sixty-five within two hours. Stirring a warm sauce into a fresh batch contaminates the fresh batch instead of saving the old one.

atoms.obligation: Close the check with the replacement work assigned and the eighty-six list communicated before service begins.
atoms.lesson: A line check that produces a list and no owner repeats itself tomorrow. Name who is remaking the aioli, who is dropping fresh fryer oil, who is moving product out of the failing low-boy, and by when. Anything that cannot be replaced before doors goes on the eighty-six board, into the point of sale and to the host stand so tickets stop coming. Log the equipment fault at the same moment, because a well that failed once fails again on Saturday.

name: allergen-service-protocol
description: Handles a declared food allergy from the moment a guest mentions it to the moment the plate is hand-delivered. Use it when a guest declares a severe allergy or celiac disease, when a server is unsure whether a dish contains a hidden allergen, when someone asks whether the fryer is shared, or when a reaction has occurred and the incident needs handling. Covers verification, cross contact prevention and honest limits.
expansions: guest says severe shellfish allergy
gluten free table of six
does the fryer share oil
allergy ticket at the pass
server unsure about the dressing
celiac guest asking about the bun
sesame in the brioche buns
guest had a reaction last night

atoms.obligation: Route every declared allergy through one named person who verifies ingredients with the kitchen before the order fires.
atoms.lesson: The nine major allergens in the United States are milk, egg, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soy and sesame, sesame having been added by the FASTER Act. The traps are hidden sources: anchovy in Worcestershire and Caesar dressing, fish sauce in curry paste and some kimchi, wheat in soy sauce, sesame on bun tops and in tahini, milk in a butter-basted steak, and nut oils in a finishing drizzle. Read the actual product label, not the recipe memory.

atoms.obligation: Prevent cross contact with fresh gloves, clean boards, dedicated utensils and a clean pan rather than rinsing.
atoms.lesson: Protein transfers by contact, so rinsing a pan or wiping a board does not clear it. The three commonest failures are a shared fryer, a shared grill surface and shared tongs; shared pasta water is a fourth. Any gluten-free claim is void if the item comes out of oil that has fried breaded product. Change gloves and wash hands first, because gloves carry allergen just as skin does, and build the plate on a cleared section of the pass.

atoms.obligation: Tell the guest plainly what you cannot guarantee instead of promising a plate is completely safe.
atoms.lesson: A busy kitchen with flour in the air and shared equipment cannot promise zero traces, and saying so is both honest and protective. Use specific language: we can cook this without butter on a clean pan, but our bread is baked in a kitchen that handles wheat and we cannot call it celiac safe. Offer the dishes you are confident in rather than modifying one you are not. Let the guest decide with real information; most severe-allergy guests respect it and return.

atoms.obligation: Deliver the allergen plate separately by hand, and if a reaction occurs call emergency services first, then document.
atoms.lesson: Mark the plate so it never gets caught in a run of identical dishes, and have the person who took the order carry it and name the allergy at the table. If a guest reacts, call emergency services immediately rather than waiting for the guest to insist they are fine, since anaphylaxis can rebound. Afterwards record the time, the items ordered, what was said at the table, who cooked it, and preserve any remaining food and the ticket for the insurer.

name: health-inspection-prep
description: Prepares the operation for a health inspection by self-auditing against the categories that actually get scored and closing the critical findings first. Use it when an inspection is due, after a poor result that needs corrective action, when a walkthrough finds chemicals stored over prep or a hand sink blocked, or when cooling and reheating logs have gaps. Produces dated corrective actions with owners rather than a list of observations.
expansions: inspector due this quarter
we lost points last inspection
self audit walkthrough today
chemicals stored above the prep table
no soap at the hand sink
food manager certificate expired
cooling log has gaps
critical violation write up

atoms.obligation: Self-audit against the priority risk factors an inspector scores and close the critical items before anything cosmetic.
atoms.lesson: Priority violations are the ones that make people ill: holding temperatures, cooling and reheating, hand washing and blocked hand sinks, bare hand contact with ready-to-eat food, cross contamination and raw over ready-to-eat storage, chemical storage and labeling, employee illness reporting, and a certified food protection manager on site. Non-critical findings such as a cracked floor tile or an unlabeled squeeze bottle cost points but never close a store. Fix criticals the same day.

atoms.obligation: Verify cooling on cooked items with a two-stage time and temperature check and record the intermediate reading.
atoms.lesson: The Food Code requires cooling from one hundred thirty-five to seventy degrees Fahrenheit within two hours, then down to forty-one within four more, six hours in total. A full Cambro of chili or stock will never make it, so use two-inch shallow pans, ice paddles and ice baths, keep containers uncovered until cold, and never stack them. The missing seventy degree reading at two hours is scored as a failure even if the final temperature is fine.

atoms.obligation: Keep required certifications, permits, illness policies and logs current, complete and available where they are asked for.
atoms.lesson: Have the current permit posted, the certified food protection manager certificate on file and a certified person on every shift, food handler cards for staff, the employee health policy signed with the reportable illnesses listed, the pest control service reports, the hood cleaning certificate and the grease trap service record. Logs filled retrospectively in identical handwriting read as fabricated and invite a harder inspection, so keep them at the station and sign them in real time.

atoms.obligation: Write a dated corrective action with a named owner for every finding, then re-check that it held.
atoms.lesson: Inspectors and insurers both look for a closed loop: the finding, the immediate correction, the root cause, the systemic fix and the verification date. Chemicals over prep is corrected by moving them, but fixed by a labeled chemical shelf below and away from food and a line on the closing checklist. Re-walk the same points two weeks later, because ninety percent of repeat violations are the ones marked corrected on site and never structurally addressed.

name: equipment-maintenance-schedule
description: Builds and runs the preventive maintenance program for kitchen and facility equipment so failures happen on a schedule instead of on a Saturday night. Use it when a walk-in is icing up, a fryer will not hold temperature, hood cleaning is overdue, the dish machine is not sanitizing, or when deciding whether to repair or replace an aging unit. Covers asset records, service intervals, daily verification and vendor response.
expansions: walk in compressor icing up
fryer not holding temperature
hood cleaning is overdue
ice machine making cloudy ice
dish machine not sanitizing
grease trap smells
preventive maintenance schedule for the kitchen
repair or replace the combi oven

atoms.obligation: Maintain an asset register with model, serial, install date, warranty end and service vendor for every powered unit.
atoms.lesson: Half of a breakdown call is spent finding the model and serial on a plate behind a hot line. Photograph the data plate at install, store it against the asset, and record the warranty end and the parts distributor. Add the location and the circuit or gas line it sits on. Without the register nobody knows the compressor is four months inside warranty, and the same unit gets a paid service call for a fault the manufacturer would have covered.

atoms.obligation: Schedule cleaning and service by duty cycle, with hood and grease systems on the interval the fire code requires.
atoms.lesson: Hood and duct cleaning frequency follows cooking volume: monthly for solid fuel, quarterly for high-volume or wok and charbroil operations, semiannually for moderate volume, annually for low volume. Grease interceptors are pumped once solids and grease reach about a quarter of the depth. Fryers get daily filtration and a weekly boil-out, which roughly doubles oil life. Refrigeration condensers cleaned quarterly prevent most compressor failures and the icing that follows a starved coil.

atoms.obligation: Verify dish machine sanitation daily at the plate, using a thermometer or test strip rather than the gauge.
atoms.lesson: High temperature machines need a final rinse reaching one hundred eighty degrees Fahrenheit at the manifold and one hundred sixty at the plate surface, checked with a plate thermometer or a thermolabel, because the dial reads what the boiler thinks, not what the dishes get. Low temperature chemical machines need fifty to one hundred parts per million of chlorine at the plate, tested each shift with a strip. Deliming monthly in hard water keeps both from drifting.

atoms.obligation: Log every failure, downtime and repair cost against the asset and use the history to decide repair versus replacement.
atoms.lesson: Track the date, the fault, the vendor, the cost and the hours the unit was down. The common rule is to replace once annual repair spend passes roughly half of replacement cost, or once the same fault recurs three times, but the decision should include lost sales from downtime and the energy difference on refrigeration and dish machines. A record of three compressor calls in a year turns an argued capital request into an obvious one.

name: supplier-price-negotiation
description: Prepares and runs a supplier bid or price negotiation for food, beverage and disposables. Use it when a distributor raises prices again, when the produce or protein list needs bidding out, when deciding whether to sign a prime vendor agreement, or when comparing two quotes that are not structured the same way. Covers the market basket, the pricing mechanism, the service terms and how much of the list to leave with a second supplier.
expansions: distributor raised prices again
bid out the produce list
prime vendor agreement worth signing
cost plus versus market price
chicken contract for six months
minimum drop size penalty
compare two distributor quotes
supplier keeps shorting deliveries

atoms.obligation: Bid a market basket of your actual highest-spend items, in your real pack sizes and real weekly volumes.
atoms.lesson: Distributors win bids by pricing twenty visible line items sharply and recovering it across three hundred others, so bid the items that make up the top eighty percent of your spend by dollar rather than a convenient sample. Specify grade, brand tier, pack and format exactly, since four-ounce individually frozen chicken breast and random weight fresh are not the same product. Re-bid volatile categories quarterly and dry goods, paper and chemicals annually.

atoms.obligation: Understand how each quoted price is constructed before treating two supplier numbers as comparable.
atoms.lesson: Cost-plus agreements quote the distributor's landed cost plus a fixed markup per case or a percentage, so establish whether cost means the invoice from the manufacturer, and whether freight, fuel surcharge and any rebate sit inside or outside it. Fixed price sheets hide the timing of increases. Market categories such as produce, seafood and beef move weekly and cannot be locked the way chicken, cheese and frying oil can, which are commonly contracted three to six months against a published index.

atoms.obligation: Put drop sizes, delivery windows, substitution rules, shorting credits and price change notice into the written agreement.
atoms.lesson: Most of the money lost with a supplier is lost after the price is agreed. Fix the minimum drop and the fee below it, the delivery days and window, who may sign, the return and credit process for shorts and damage, whether substitutions are allowed without a call, and the notice period before a price change takes effect. Require the weekly price sheet in advance so the kitchen can react on the menu rather than discovering the increase on the invoice.

atoms.obligation: Keep a secondary supplier active on core items even where the primary is a few points cheaper.
atoms.lesson: A prime vendor agreement buys better pricing and one truck, but it also removes leverage and exposes you to a single point of failure during shortages, weather closures and supplier labor disputes. Keep five to fifteen percent of spend, particularly core proteins and one produce line, running through a second vendor with live account terms and recent orders, so the alternative can scale within a day and so the primary knows its pricing is being benchmarked every week.

name: guest-complaint-recovery
description: Handles a guest complaint at the table: the approach, the fix, when to discount and how to record it. Use it when a table has waited too long, when a dish comes back wrong twice, when a guest asks for the manager, when someone finds a foreign object, or when a server is unsure whether to comp a course or the whole check. Also covers the follow-up after the guest leaves and the nightly review of comps.
expansions: table waited forty minutes for entrees
guest found a hair in the food
steak came back well done twice
angry table asking for the manager
should i comp the whole check
birthday dessert never came out
loud complaint in the dining room
guest left unhappy last night

atoms.obligation: Go to the table yourself, listen without interrupting and name the specific failure before offering anything at all.
atoms.lesson: Guests escalate when they feel unheard, not when they feel unpaid. Approach from the side, at eye level, and let them finish; then repeat the specific problem back, your entrees took forty minutes while the table next to you was served, rather than a generic sorry about that. Never explain the kitchen's difficulties or blame a station, a shortage or another department. Ask what would make the rest of the meal right before you propose a remedy.

atoms.obligation: Repair the food and the timing first, and discount only after the experience itself has been put right.
atoms.lesson: Service recovery research consistently finds speed and acknowledgement matter more than money. A remade entree fired on the fly with a check-back beats twenty percent off a cold plate every time. The comp ladder most operators use is a drink or dessert for a minor slip, the item comped for a wrong or badly delayed dish, and the check comped when an occasion was genuinely ruined. Reflexive full comps teach staff to buy their way out of every problem.

atoms.obligation: Record every comp and void with a reason code, the item, the server and the approving manager's name.
atoms.lesson: Comps and voids after an item has fired are the largest single channel for internal theft in restaurants, so require manager approval on each one and a reason code such as kitchen error, service timing, guest dissatisfaction or promotion. Review them nightly by server and by reason. A server whose comp rate is three times the house average is a coaching conversation and a pattern to watch, not an accusation, and the same report reveals which station is actually generating the errors.

atoms.obligation: Follow up after the visit through a named person with a specific invitation back, not a generic apology.
atoms.lesson: The recovery paradox only works if the guest returns, so make the return easy and personal. Send a short note within twenty-four to forty-eight hours from a real name and direct email or phone, referencing what happened and what changed, and invite them back with a held reservation rather than a voucher they must remember to use. Flag the profile so whoever is on the door the next visit knows, and tell the guest that has been done.

name: online-review-response
description: Writes and manages responses to public guest reviews across rating platforms. Use it when a one star review lands, when a reviewer names an employee, when the average rating slips, when a review alleges illness or a foreign object, or when someone asks whether to respond at all. Sets tone, timing and what must never appear in a public reply, and routes safety allegations off the public thread.
expansions: one star review about the wait
should we respond to this review
reviewer named a server
rating dropped below four stars
fake review from a competitor
guest posted photos of a dirty table
reply to a glowing review
review mentions food poisoning

atoms.obligation: Respond within a day or two in a consistent owner voice, acknowledging the specific issue without disputing the facts.
atoms.lesson: Most prospective guests read the three most recent reviews and the replies underneath them, so the response is written for them rather than for the reviewer. Use a fixed structure: thank, restate the specific problem in the guest's own terms, say what has actually changed, offer a direct name and email, and close warmly. Never write that you have no record of the visit, never argue the timeline, and never copy and paste the same reply beneath every review.

atoms.obligation: Never name, defend against or discipline an employee in a public reply, whatever the review says about them.
atoms.lesson: A reply that identifies a named server, even to praise, exposes that person to strangers and turns an operational issue into a personal one; a reply that distances the business from an employee destroys trust with the whole team. Say the team, or that member of our team, and take the failure institutionally. Handle the actual performance conversation privately, with the ticket times and the shift record, and tell the employee the review exists before they find it themselves.

atoms.obligation: Move any allegation of illness, injury or a foreign object off the public thread after a single brief reply.
atoms.lesson: A public claim of foodborne illness is both a liability exposure and a public health matter. Post one short reply with a direct contact and nothing else, then internally record the meal date and time, party size, every item ordered, who cooked and served, and preserve prep and holding logs, the invoice for the lot and any remaining product. Notify the insurer and check whether other reports cluster on the same date or item. Never admit fault or offer a settlement in writing on a public page.

atoms.obligation: Report reviews that breach platform guidelines through the platform process instead of fighting them in the thread.
atoms.lesson: Platforms will remove reviews that are demonstrably not from a guest, that contain a competitor's promotion, that include personal attacks or protected-class abuse, or that are duplicated across accounts. Gather the evidence first, such as no reservation or ticket matching the claimed date and party, then file the report and wait; removal rates are modest and slow. In the meantime the strongest defense is volume, so ask satisfied guests at the table to review and keep the recent set fresh.

name: reservation-pacing-plan
description: Sets the booking grid so covers arrive at a rate the kitchen and floor can absorb, and handles turn times, walk-ins and no-shows. Use it when the kitchen gets slammed at a single seating time, when quoted wait times keep missing, when large parties block the room, or when no-shows on prime nights need a deposit policy. Also used to decide how much of the room to hold back for same-day demand.
expansions: kitchen got slammed at seven thirty
too many covers booked at once
no show rate on saturdays
how long is a two top turn
hold tables for walk ins
deposit policy for large parties
waitlist quoting wrong times
private room blocks the whole night

atoms.obligation: Pace bookings by covers per fifteen minute slot against what the kitchen can genuinely fire in that window.
atoms.lesson: Kitchen capacity is measured in entrees per hour per station, not in covers per night. A four-station line comfortably firing sixty to seventy entrees an hour collapses if forty covers are seated in one fifteen minute slot, because the first seating orders appetizers and entrees simultaneously. A hundred seat room typically caps at eight to twelve covers per fifteen minutes, tighter at the start of service and looser once the room is staggered and tables are turning.

atoms.obligation: Set turn times by party size, quote them at booking, and measure what the turns actually are.
atoms.lesson: Measured turns run roughly seventy-five to ninety minutes for a two-top, a hundred and five to a hundred and twenty for a four-top, and over two hours for six or more; wine-led and tasting menu rooms run considerably longer. Turn time ends at check drop plus seven to ten minutes to bus and reset, so a grid built on seated-to-seated understates it. If second seatings depend on the turn, say so at booking and again at the table.

atoms.obligation: Hold a defined share of the room and of prime times for walk-ins and same-day demand.
atoms.lesson: Most rooms keep roughly ten to twenty percent of covers unbooked, weighted to the bar, the counter and two-tops, because walk-ins spend comparably, fill the gaps a grid cannot, and are the only inventory left when a party of six cancels at six o'clock. Release held tables progressively rather than all at once, and never hold so much that the book looks empty online, since visible availability drives further bookings.

atoms.obligation: Reduce no-shows with confirmation contact, card holds on larger parties and a written cancellation policy applied consistently.
atoms.lesson: No-show rates commonly run five to twenty percent and spike on holidays and prime weekend slots. A text confirmation twenty-four to forty-eight hours ahead with a one-tap cancel, plus a card hold and a stated per-person fee for parties of six or more and for peak dates, typically drops it below five percent. State the policy at booking and in the confirmation, and either charge it consistently or do not have it, because selective enforcement is what generates public complaints.

name: banquet-event-order
description: Writes the banquet event order that turns a signed contract into an executable plan for kitchen, bar, service and facilities. Use it when an event is booked and the details need capturing, when a client changes the guest count, when the final guarantee is due, or when a room set, bar package and timeline must be distributed to every department. Covers guarantees and oversets, minute-by-minute timing, and every charge that will appear on the invoice.
expansions: write the beo for saturday's wedding
client changed the guest count
final guarantee is due friday
plated versus buffet for a hundred twenty
bar package for the rehearsal dinner
room set for a forty person seminar
distribute the beo to kitchen and bar
avoid surprises on event day

atoms.obligation: Capture the guaranteed guest count, the deadline it is due, and the overset the kitchen will actually prepare.
atoms.lesson: The industry standard is a final guarantee seventy-two business hours before the event, billed on the guarantee or the actual served count, whichever is higher. Houses prepare three to five percent over on plated events, usually capping the overset at ten to twenty-five covers on large parties. Write the guarantee date on the contract, chase it the morning it falls due, and state the surcharge for late increases, because the kitchen is ordering protein against that number.

atoms.obligation: Write one document that states timing, room set, menu, service style, bar and staffing minute by minute.
atoms.lesson: The order is read by people who were never in the sales conversation, so it must be self-contained: load-in and vendor access times, room set with diagram and count per round, ceremony or presentation timings, cocktail hour start and passed item counts per person, the exact moment each course fires, dietary and allergy plates by seat, bar open and last call, and the staffing plan with call times. Anything agreed by phone and not written on it will not happen.

atoms.obligation: Itemize every charge on the order, distinguishing the mandatory service charge from any gratuity paid to staff.
atoms.lesson: A mandatory service charge is house revenue, is taxable in most states, and any share paid to staff is a wage that raises overtime pay; a gratuity belongs to the employees. Labeling one as the other on a client invoice is a wage-and-hour problem, not a formatting choice. Itemize room fee, food and beverage minimum, cake cutting, corkage, linen and chair rental, bartender fees, audiovisual and the overtime rate after a stated hour, so the final bill matches the signed order exactly.

atoms.obligation: Distribute the final order to every department with changes highlighted and a single named owner for revisions.
atoms.lesson: Kitchen, bar, service, stewarding, facilities and the front desk each execute a different part, and each needs the same version. Number the revisions, date and time stamp them, and highlight what changed since the last issue rather than reissuing a clean copy that nobody rereads. Route every client change through one coordinator, hold a short pre-event meeting with the leads the day before, and cut off changes at a stated hour so the kitchen is not re-planning during load-in.

name: delivery-channel-ops
description: Runs the takeout and third-party delivery channel so food travels well and the margin survives the commission. Use it when delivery orders arrive cold or wrong, when the order tablet backs up during the rush, when drivers wait too long, when commission is eating the profit, or when deciding which items should not be available for delivery at all. Covers channel pricing, sequencing, packaging and pausing.
expansions: delivery orders coming out cold
tablet backlog during dinner rush
driver waiting twenty minutes
delivery pricing versus dine in
wrong items in the bag
commission eating the margin
pause the channel when slammed
packaging for fried food

atoms.obligation: Price the delivery menu to absorb commission rather than publishing the dine-in price on the channel.
atoms.lesson: Marketplace commissions run fifteen to thirty percent before payment processing, so a sixteen dollar dine-in entree nets around eleven to thirteen on the channel while carrying the same food and labor cost. Most operators price channel items fifteen to twenty percent above dine-in, which guests broadly accept, and remove low-margin or fragile items entirely. Remember the channel also loses the beverage attach and the alcohol margin that make a dine-in check profitable.

atoms.obligation: Give delivery its own prep and packing station with a separate ticket time target and one named packer.
atoms.lesson: The usual failure is sequencing rather than cooking: delivery tickets fire on the same rail as dine-in and then sit under a lamp while the driver is still ten minutes away. Fire against driver arrival time, not order receipt, and put one expeditor on bagging, checking against the ticket, and sealing. Platforms penalize long driver waits and inaccurate quotes with lower placement, so aim to have the bag ready within five minutes of the driver.

atoms.obligation: Match packaging to each item so the food survives twenty minutes closed inside a bag.
atoms.lesson: Steam is what ruins delivery. Use vented containers for anything fried, keep sauces and dressings separate, never lay fries against a burger, line pizza boxes to absorb moisture, and bag cold items away from hot. Seal with tamper-evident tape and label each container. Some dishes simply should not travel: souffles, seared rare fish, crisp salads dressed with hot protein, and anything whose texture is the entire point, so remove them from the channel rather than apologizing weekly.

atoms.obligation: Extend quoted times or pause the channel when the kitchen is past capacity instead of accepting every order.
atoms.lesson: Accepting orders you cannot cook produces refunds, one star ratings and driver cancellations that damage placement far more than a temporary pause does. Set a trigger the expeditor can act on, such as more than a set number of open tickets or a dine-in wait beyond a threshold, and give shift managers explicit authority to extend prep times or pause without calling anyone. Reopen deliberately, and record every pause so the pattern shows up in next week's schedule.

name: new-server-training
description: Plans and runs the onboarding of a new front of house hire from paperwork through certification to their first solo section. Use it when a new server or busser starts, when someone asks how many trailing shifts are needed, when a trainee is not retaining the steps of service, or when deciding whether a new hire is ready to take tables alone. Covers trainer pairing, menu testing, timed service standards and required certifications.
expansions: new server starts monday
how many training shifts
menu test for the new hire
trailing shift schedule
trainee forgetting steps of service
certify a server to take tables
training a busser to run food
onboarding paperwork first day

atoms.obligation: Give the new hire a written progression of trailing shifts by station, each with a named and paid trainer.
atoms.lesson: A typical full-service progression is four to six shifts: two shadowing across different dayparts, one running food and working expo to learn the kitchen and the plates, one trailing a closer, then one or two reverse trails where the trainee works the section and the trainer follows. Pay a trainer rate, use the same two or three trainers rather than whoever is on, and never teach closing procedures to someone who has only worked lunch.

atoms.obligation: Test menu, allergen and beverage knowledge in writing and on the floor before the trainee takes a table alone.
atoms.lesson: Test what a guest actually asks: ingredients and cooking method for every dish, which items contain the nine major allergens, what can be modified and what cannot, the wines by the glass with a one-line description, and the cocktail specs. Run a table-side role play, including a guest declaring a shellfish allergy and a guest sending back a steak. A trainee who cannot pass on the second attempt needs another shift, not a promotion to a section.

atoms.obligation: Teach the sequence of service as timed, measurable steps rather than as attitude or general hospitality language.
atoms.lesson: Give the trainee numbers they can hit: greet within sixty to ninety seconds, drinks down in three to five minutes, quote the appetizer time, check back two bites into each course, pre-bus before dessert, drop the check on request and return within ninety seconds of a card being placed. Teach ticket entry as part of service, since course, seat position, modifier order and the allergy field are what turn into a kitchen problem three stations away.

atoms.obligation: Complete required certifications, tax and eligibility paperwork and food handler cards before the first paid shift.
atoms.lesson: Depending on the jurisdiction that means a food handler card, an alcohol server certification before pouring a single drink, employment eligibility verification within three days of hire, tax withholding forms, direct deposit, the tip reporting acknowledgement and a signed handbook including the harassment and employee illness policies. Record expiry dates for the certifications on the same sheet, because an expired alcohol card discovered during a compliance check is a fine and an insurance problem.

name: tip-pool-compliance
description: Designs and audits how tips, tip-outs and service charges are distributed, and keeps that structure legal. Use it when the kitchen asks for a share of tips, when tip-out percentages are being changed, when a shift lead's role blurs into management, when banquet service charges are being paid out, or when a new hire asks how tips work. Covers who may be in a pool, the tip credit, service charge treatment and written disclosure.
expansions: kitchen wants a share of tips
tip out percentages for bussers
manager taking part of the pool
service charge versus gratuity payout
tip credit and side work rules
changing our tip out structure
credit card fee deducted from tips
new hire asking how tips work

atoms.obligation: Keep owners, managers and supervisors out of every tip pool regardless of how the wage is structured.
atoms.lesson: Under federal wage law an employer, manager or supervisor may never keep employees' tips, whether or not a tip credit is taken; a manager may retain only tips from guests they personally and solely served. The remedy is repayment of the tips plus an equal amount in liquidated damages and civil penalties. The exposure usually comes from a shift lead who also bartends, so apply the duties test to the actual work rather than to the job title on the schedule.

atoms.obligation: Decide who may be in the pool based on whether the operation takes a tip credit against the minimum wage.
atoms.lesson: If you take a tip credit, paying a cash wage as low as two dollars thirteen cents federally against a seven twenty-five minimum, the pool is limited to customarily and regularly tipped employees such as servers, bartenders, bussers, runners and in some readings hosts. If you pay the full minimum wage with no credit, back of house cooks and dishwashers may lawfully be included. Several states including California, Washington, Oregon, Nevada, Minnesota and Alaska prohibit the tip credit outright.

atoms.obligation: Treat mandatory service charges as wages rather than tips, including in overtime and tax calculations.
atoms.lesson: A mandatory charge on a banquet or a large party is house revenue, not a gratuity, so any portion distributed to staff is a commission that must be included in the regular rate when calculating overtime, and the charge itself is usually subject to sales tax. Calling it gratuity on the guest check while treating it as a service charge internally is a common source of litigation. State the distinction plainly on menus, contracts and checks.

atoms.obligation: Publish the tip-out percentages in writing and run the distribution identically every shift, with records kept.
atoms.lesson: Write the structure down, for example a percentage of tips or of sales to bar, runners and bussers, when it is calculated, how a split shift or a cut server is handled, and what happens on a walked check or a chargeback. Keep the daily tip declaration, the pool calculation and the payout for at least three years. Note also that some states prohibit deducting credit card processing fees from tips, and none allow deducting more than the actual fee.

name: alcohol-service-compliance
description: Keeps alcohol service inside the law: age verification, refusal of service to intoxicated guests, documentation and staff certification. Use it when a guest appears underage or presents a questionable identification, when a guest needs to be cut off, when a server certification lapses, when a liquor inspector visits, or when the operation's dram shop exposure is being reviewed. Covers what to check, what to observe, what to say and what to record.
expansions: guest looks underage
cutting off a drunk guest
fake id at the door
server certification expired
last call procedures
dram shop liability exposure
double pours to one guest
liquor inspector visit today

atoms.obligation: Physically inspect identification for anyone who could plausibly be under age, checking expiry, date, photo and security features.
atoms.lesson: Most houses card anyone who looks under thirty-five or forty. Take the card in hand: check the expiration date first, then the birth date arithmetic, then the photo and the physical description against the person, then feel the edges and laminate and tilt for the tactile and holographic features. A vertically oriented license signals it was issued to someone under twenty-one. Accept only unexpired government-issued photo identification with a birth date, never a photocopy or a phone image.

atoms.obligation: Refuse further service on observable signs of intoxication and record the refusal at the time it happens.
atoms.lesson: Train the visible cues rather than a drink count: slurred or noticeably louder speech, glassy or unfocused eyes, fumbling money or a card, repeating themselves, unsteadiness, and abrupt shifts to argumentative or overly familiar behavior. Cut off quietly, away from the party, offer food, water and a ride home, and never accuse or diagnose. Log the time, who made the decision, what was observed, what was offered and how the guest left the property; that log is the defense.

atoms.obligation: Never serve alcohol to a minor in any circumstance unless a state exception expressly and clearly permits it.
atoms.lesson: The pressure point is the family table where a parent orders a glass for a seventeen year old, or the large party where drinks are passed down. A small number of states permit parental service in a licensed premises and most do not, so know your own statute and put the answer in writing so no server has to improvise. Watch for adults ordering extra drinks that migrate, and treat furnishing to a minor as grounds for refusal to the whole table.

atoms.obligation: Keep every server and bartender certification current on file and track the expiry dates actively.
atoms.lesson: Dram shop statutes in most states make the establishment liable for injury caused by a guest who was served while visibly intoxicated or underage, and awards routinely exceed liquor liability policy limits. Certification is legally required in some states and a meaningful insurance discount in most others, and it typically runs two to three years. Keep certificates, the refusal log and the training records together, because that package is what an insurer and a licensing board ask for after an incident.

name: guest-incident-report
description: Documents a guest injury, illness claim or property incident so the record is accurate, factual and defensible. Use it when a guest slips, when broken glass causes an injury, when someone claims they became ill after eating, when a child is burned, or when the insurer asks what happened. Covers immediate care, what to write and what never to write, preserving evidence and footage, and the notification window.
expansions: guest slipped near the host stand
chipped glass cut a guest's lip
someone claims they got sick
child burned on a hot plate
guest fell in the parking lot
do we call an ambulance
what goes in the incident report
insurer asking for details

atoms.obligation: Offer medical assistance first and call emergency services whenever severity is uncertain or the guest may minimize it.
atoms.lesson: Head injuries, burns, chest symptoms, suspected fractures and allergic reactions all get an emergency call regardless of what the guest says, because adrenaline and embarrassment lead people to refuse help they need. Clear the area, keep the guest still rather than helping them up, and apply first aid only within your training. Assign one manager to the guest and another to the operation, so the dining room is not being run by the same person managing the injury.

atoms.obligation: Write the report during the same shift, recording only observed facts, times, names, conditions and direct quotations.
atoms.lesson: Capture the exact date and time, the precise location, what the guest and each witness said in their own quoted words, contact details for the guest and independent witnesses, which staff were present, the floor and lighting condition, footwear, and whether the guest accepted or declined help. Do not record an opinion about cause, never write that the floor was wet because we were behind, and never promise to cover medical bills, since that decision belongs to the insurer.

atoms.obligation: Preserve the physical evidence and the surrounding operational record before it is cleaned away or overwritten.
atoms.lesson: Bag and label the broken glass, foreign object or suspect food with the date and the ticket number; keep the check, payment record and server assignment; photograph the location before it is cleaned, including whatever was on the floor and any signage. Export and store the camera footage covering at least thirty minutes either side within the retention window, since many systems overwrite in seven to thirty days. For an illness claim also keep prep, cooling and holding logs and the delivery invoice for the lot.

atoms.obligation: Notify management and the insurance carrier within the required window and route all further contact through one person.
