atoms.lesson: Most liability policies require prompt notice, commonly measured in days, and late notice can jeopardize coverage. Send the report, the photographs and the footage together rather than in pieces. Give the guest a single named contact and tell colleagues not to discuss the incident with the guest, their family, a lawyer, an insurer or on social media. If the claim involves alleged illness, notify the health department where the local code requires it and expect an inspection.

name: housekeeping-room-turnover
description: Plans and runs guest room turnover: how boards are built, the cleaning sequence, inspection and maintenance handoff. Use it when checkout rooms are not ready by the posted time, when deciding credits per attendant, when an early arrival needs a room rushed, when an inspector keeps finding the same faults, or when linen par is short. Covers weighting departures against stayovers and tracking failures by item rather than by person.
expansions: checkout rooms not ready by three
credits per attendant per shift
rush a room for an early arrival
linen par is short
inspector found hair in the tub
stayover versus departure clean
lost and found in a checkout
deep clean rotation schedule

atoms.obligation: Build attendant boards in credits weighted by room type and clean type, not in flat room counts.
atoms.lesson: A common baseline is thirty minutes for a departure clean and fifteen to twenty for a stayover in a full-service hotel, so a fifteen credit board at half an hour each is roughly a seven and a half hour day including breaks. Suites, connecting rooms, rooms with rollaways and checkout-to-arrival rushes carry extra credits. Sequence each board against the arrivals list: early arrivals and VIP rooms first, then remaining departures, then stayovers.

atoms.obligation: Clean every room in the same fixed sequence so nothing is skipped when the shift is running late.
atoms.lesson: The standard order is strip and remove trash, make the bed, then the bathroom top down from mirror and vanity to tub and shower with the toilet last, then dust high to low, restock linen and amenities, and vacuum backwards out the door. Cleaning the toilet last and using colour-coded cloths prevents cross contamination. Bathrooms and high-touch points, the remote, switches, handles and phone, are what guests and inspectors judge first.

atoms.obligation: Inspect a defined proportion of rooms against a checklist and track failures by item as well as by attendant.
atoms.lesson: Full-service properties inspect every departure and spot-check stayovers; select-service typically inspects ten to twenty-five percent plus every VIP room and every room from a new attendant for their first month. Score against specific line items, hair in the tub drain, dust under the bed, missing do not disturb card, so the coaching is concrete. When the same item fails across several attendants the sequence, the chemical or the tool is wrong, not the people.

atoms.obligation: Report every maintenance fault from inside the room immediately, and place the room out of order when required.
atoms.lesson: An attendant is the only person who sees every room daily, so the burnt bulb, dripping tap, loose toilet seat, stained ceiling and failed lock all get reported from the room rather than at the end of the shift. Anything affecting safety, water or the guest's ability to use the room means out of order until cleared, communicated to the front desk before it can be sold. Log lost and found the same way, tagged with room and date and secured.

name: front-desk-oversell-walk
description: Manages an oversold night: how far to oversell, who gets walked, where they go and what the property pays. Use it when the house is oversold, when group pickup exceeds the block, when a guaranteed reservation arrives with no room available, or when the team needs a walk policy written before the night rather than argued at the desk. Covers the oversell calculation, the walk order, securing the alternate room and the guest conversation.
expansions: we are oversold by six tonight
who do we walk
no rooms and a guaranteed reservation
find a comparable hotel nearby
guest arriving at midnight with no room
walk letter and compensation
group pickup higher than blocked
how far can we safely oversell

atoms.obligation: Set the oversell figure from measured no-show, cancellation and early departure history for that specific day pattern.
atoms.lesson: Oversell equals expected no-shows plus same-day cancellations plus early departures, minus expected walk-ins, calculated by day of week and season. Non-guaranteed bookings, prepaid online travel agency reservations and group attendees each behave differently and must be modeled separately, since group blocks wash at their own rate. A property running four percent no-shows on a Tuesday can safely sell three or four over on a hundred rooms, while the same number on a citywide sellout is reckless because there is nowhere to walk anyone.

atoms.obligation: Decide the walk order by written policy before the night begins, never at the desk in front of a queue.
atoms.lesson: The convention is to walk whoever is least contractually protected and least costly to lose: one night stays, lowest rate, non-loyalty, non-guaranteed, not part of a group contract, arriving latest, with no special occasion noted. Never walk a top tier loyalty member, a guaranteed multi-night stay, a group attendee whose contract commits rooms, a guest with an accessibility requirement you have confirmed, or anyone travelling with young children where alternatives are poor.

atoms.obligation: Secure and pay for the alternate room at a comparable property in the guest's name before they arrive.
atoms.lesson: The accepted standard is the first night's room and tax at the receiving hotel paid by you, transport both ways, a call home, and rebooking into your hotel at the original rate for the remainder of the stay, usually with an upgrade and loyalty points or a future stay credit. Call the receiving hotel, confirm a comparable room type and amenities, and hold it under the guest's name. Handing a guest a list of hotels to try is the failure everyone remembers.

atoms.obligation: Tell the guest personally and early, with the solution already arranged and confirmed to them in writing.
atoms.lesson: Call ahead where the arrival time allows rather than letting them travel to a desk that has nothing. A manager, not the newest agent, delivers it: apologize without excuses, state plainly what has been arranged, hand over a walk letter naming the hotel, the confirmation, the transport and the compensation, and give a direct number. Then follow up the next morning to confirm the return booking. Record every walk with the reason, so the oversell model is corrected by real outcomes.

name: crop-rotation-planning
description: Builds a multi-year, field-by-field rotation that balances agronomy, market return and machinery capacity. Use it when a grower is deciding what goes where next season, when continuous corn or a tight cereal sequence is eroding yields, when new rented ground enters the operation, or when herbicide carryover and disease history restrict what can legally or safely follow.
expansions: what should follow corn on field seven
planning next season crop mix
too much wheat in the rotation
disease pressure from continuous soybeans
new rented ground needs a plan
want to add a break crop
herbicide carryover limits next crop
rotation for a newly converted block

atoms.obligation: Check every field previous herbicide applications before assigning next season crop and respect the label rotational intervals.
atoms.lesson: Residual chemistries carry over according to soil pH, rainfall and half-life. Imazethapyr and other ALS residues persist in dry high-pH soils and injure sugar beet, canola or sunflower eighteen months later; clopyralid restricts legumes and potatoes; atrazine limits soybeans at twelve months in low-rainfall years. Label rotational intervals assume a minimum accumulated rainfall, so a drought season effectively doubles the risk. Field records of rate, date and season rainfall decide whether the interval is genuinely satisfied.

atoms.obligation: Space host crops of the same soil-borne pathogen at least two non-host seasons apart on each field.
atoms.lesson: Sclerotinia sclerotiorum sclerotia survive four to five years and infect canola, soybean, sunflower and dry bean, so those four count as one crop for rotation purposes. Cyst nematode populations fall roughly half per non-host year but rebuild in a single susceptible season. Take-all in wheat peaks in the third consecutive cereal then declines, and one non-cereal break resets it. Cereal, legume and oilseed sequences with two-year gaps handle most of these together.

atoms.obligation: Balance the rotation so no single crop exceeds the acreage the planting and harvest windows can physically cover.
atoms.lesson: A rotation is limited by machine capacity, not only by agronomy. One combine covering 120 acres a day gives about 2,400 harvestable acres in a twenty-day fit window, so putting sixty per cent of the farm into one crop means half of it is cut past optimal moisture with dockage and shatter loss. Splitting between early and late maturities, or spring and winter crops, spreads the peak and lets the same machinery cover more ground.

atoms.obligation: Cost each candidate sequence across the full rotation cycle rather than comparing single-year gross margins.
atoms.lesson: Break crops usually lose the single-year comparison and win the rotation. A legume break typically leaves thirty to fifty pounds of nitrogen credit for the following cereal, lifts that cereal ten to fifteen per cent through the disease break, and cuts herbicide spend by allowing a different mode of action. Those credits land in the next year budget, so a one-year margin table always flatters the dominant cash crop. Compare average annual margin across the whole cycle.

name: soil-test-interpretation
description: Reads a soil laboratory report and turns it into lime, phosphate and potash decisions by field or management zone. Use it when annual sampling results come back, when a report shows base saturation or buffer numbers a grower does not recognise, when comparing two labs that use different extractants, or when deciding whether a field should be building, maintaining or drawing down fertility.
expansions: soil results came back from the lab
what does base saturation mean here
do these fields need lime
phosphorus index dropped since last sampling
comparing two labs different numbers
how much potash to apply
sampling depth looks wrong
zone results vary across the field

atoms.obligation: Confirm the extraction method and sampling depth before comparing any result to a critical value or a previous test.
atoms.lesson: Phosphorus numbers are method specific. Bray P1 under-reads on calcareous soils above pH 7.4 where the acid extractant is neutralised, Olsen is the correct test there, and Mehlich-3 typically runs 1.2 to 1.5 times Bray on acid soils. Critical values belong to the method, not to the nutrient. Depth matters as much: a nought to six inch core in a no-till field shows stratified surface phosphorus and potassium far above a nought to eight inch core.

atoms.obligation: Set lime rates from buffer pH and the target crop rather than from water pH alone.
atoms.lesson: Water pH says how acid the soil is now; buffer pH says how much reserve acidity sits on the exchange and therefore how much lime moves it. A sandy soil at pH 5.6 may need one ton per acre while a heavy clay at the same pH needs three or four. Target pH is crop driven: 6.5 for alfalfa and legumes, 6.0 to 6.2 for corn and soybean, lower where potato scab suppression matters. Adjust for neutralising value.

atoms.obligation: Decide build, maintain or draw-down for each nutrient by comparing the test level against the crop critical level.
atoms.lesson: Below roughly seventy-five per cent of the critical level a yield response to applied phosphate or potash is likely and build rates above removal are justified. Between critical and about 150 per cent, apply crop removal only, roughly 0.37 pounds of phosphate and 0.27 of potash per bushel of corn, and 0.8 and 1.4 per bushel of soybean. Above that, draw down and keep the cash, since extra phosphorus adds runoff risk without yield.

atoms.obligation: Flag the sulphur, chloride and micronutrient values the report prints but the summary recommendation usually ignores.
atoms.lesson: Sulphur mineralisation no longer covers demand where atmospheric deposition has fallen, and canola and alfalfa show striping on sandy low organic matter ground, responding to fifteen to twenty-five pounds of sulphate sulphur. Zinc below 0.8 parts per million on a DTPA test hits corn on cut high-pH knolls. Chloride below thirty pounds in the top two feet gives a wheat response independent of potassium. These columns sit in the report but fall out of the recommendation.

name: manure-nutrient-plan
description: Produces a compliant nutrient management plan for manure and slurry: how much, on which fields, in which window, with the setbacks and records attached. Use it when a livestock unit needs a plan for a permit or inspection, when storage is filling and land has to be found, when a manure analysis arrives, or when fields sit near watercourses or inside a vulnerable zone.
expansions: slurry store is nearly full
need a nutrient plan for the permit
manure analysis results just arrived
can we spread before the closed period
field borders a stream setback
how many acres for this herd
inspector asked for spreading records
calibrating the spreader application rate

atoms.obligation: Base application rates on a current manure analysis and the crop requirement, never on book values or load counts.
atoms.lesson: Nutrient content swings widely. Dairy slurry runs twenty to thirty pounds of total nitrogen, ten to fifteen of phosphate and twenty to thirty of potash per thousand gallons, but dry matter varies from two to ten per cent with parlour water and rainfall, and a sample taken after agitation differs from one drawn off the crust. Around half the organic nitrogen mineralises in year one, and surface ammonium can lose a quarter to half by volatilisation within a day.

atoms.obligation: Identify the limiting nutrient for each field and switch to a phosphorus-based rate where the soil index is high.
atoms.lesson: Manure carries a nitrogen to phosphate ratio near two to one while crops remove closer to four to one, so meeting nitrogen from manure alone over-applies phosphorus year after year. Once soil test phosphorus passes the agronomic threshold or the phosphorus index scores high, the plan must move to a phosphorus-based rate, which cuts the application to roughly a third and triples the land area needed. Nitrogen is then topped up with mineral fertiliser.

atoms.obligation: Respect closed periods, setbacks and ground conditions before every application and record why the day was suitable.
atoms.lesson: Typical rules block application on frozen, snow-covered or waterlogged ground and ahead of forecast heavy rain, and set closed periods over autumn and winter for high nitrogen materials. Setbacks commonly run ten metres from surface water and fifty from a spring or borehole, with wider distances on slopes. The defensible record names date, field, rate, weather, soil condition and the analysis used, held for the retention period, usually five years.

atoms.obligation: Check storage capacity against the length of the closed period before agreeing any spreading plan.
atoms.lesson: A plan that cannot be executed fails in the wettest week. Capacity requirements typically run five to six months for slurry in temperate regions, and the calculation must include parlour washings, undiverted yard and roof runoff, and freeboard. A herd of 150 cows producing twelve to fifteen gallons a day needs roughly 350,000 gallons for five months. Where capacity falls short the plan needs roof water diversion, extra storage or a written export agreement.

name: seed-variety-selection
description: Chooses hybrids and varieties field by field using trial data, maturity, disease package and end market. Use it when seed orders are due, when a grower is weighing an unproven hybrid against a known one, when multi-site trial results look contradictory, or when lodging, standability or a specific disease caused trouble at the last harvest.
expansions: seed order due next month
picking hybrids for each field
which variety for late planting
trial data across sites looks confusing
lodging problems at last harvest
need a resistant variety for rust
maturity spread across the farm
new variety worth trying or not

atoms.obligation: Rank varieties on multi-site and multi-year trial averages rather than on the best single-site result.
atoms.lesson: Variety by environment interaction is large: a hybrid can top one strip trial by twelve bushels and finish mid-pack across twenty sites. Two years of data from at least eight locations in the same maturity zone gives a usable ranking, and single-year data should never move more than a fifth of the acres. Weight sites by similarity to the target field, since drainage class, soil texture and typical rainfall matter far more than distance in miles.

atoms.obligation: Spread maturity so the whole farm does not reach harvest moisture in the same week.
atoms.lesson: Spreading relative maturity by eight to twelve days across the acreage staggers pollination and harvest, hedging a heat event at flowering and letting one combine cover more ground at optimal moisture. The latest maturity must still reach physiological maturity roughly ten days before the average first frost. Every extra day of maturity buys yield potential that the drying bill takes back at three to five points of additional grain moisture.

atoms.obligation: Read the disease and standability ratings against each field history rather than against a farm average.
atoms.lesson: Ratings are relative within a supplier scale, so a four for grey leaf spot from one company is not a four from another; independent trial disease scores are more comparable. Match trait to field: a continuous corn no-till field needs strong grey leaf spot and northern leaf blight scores, a field with phytophthora history needs both a resistance gene and high field tolerance, and headland compaction with high populations puts weight on root and stalk strength.

atoms.obligation: Confirm end market and trait requirements before ordering, including refuge obligations and identity preservation terms.
atoms.lesson: Contracts constrain genetics. Food grade, non-GM, high oleic and waxy contracts specify approved variety lists and usually demand isolation distances and cleaned equipment, and the premium vanishes on a failed test. Insect trait packages carry structured refuge obligations, commonly five per cent in blends or twenty per cent as a block in cotton regions. Export approvals also lag, so a variety cleared domestically can be unmarketable to a specific buyer.

name: pest-scouting-thresholds
description: Turns field scouting counts into a spray or no-spray decision using economic thresholds. Use it when a walker reports insect numbers or feeding damage, when someone asks whether an aphid or beetle population justifies an insecticide, when setting the scouting route and frequency for a crop, or when the damage looks alarming but the count may not have crossed threshold.
expansions: aphid counts came back high
do we spray or wait
beetle damage on field edges
setting up a scouting route
how many plants to sample
threshold for this growth stage
beneficials present in the counts
damage looks bad but count low

atoms.obligation: Sample enough plants at enough separated stops to represent the whole field rather than the worst patch.
atoms.lesson: Standard practice is five stops of twenty plants, or twenty sweeps per stop, at least thirty paces in from the margin, on a pattern crossing the soil types. Edge effects mislead badly, because cereal leaf beetle, stink bug and mite pressure concentrate in the first few passes and an edge-only count can be five times the field mean. Where infestation genuinely stops at the margin the answer is a border treatment, not a whole-field spray.

atoms.obligation: Compare the count against a threshold that accounts for crop value, control cost and current growth stage.
atoms.lesson: Economic thresholds are not fixed numbers; they sit below the injury level so the spray happens before loss occurs. Soybean aphid uses 250 per plant on eighty per cent of plants and rising before R5, which works because the injury level near 670 leaves a week of lead time. After R6 the crop no longer responds. High commodity prices or cheap control lower the threshold, but never below the level distinguishable from sampling noise.

atoms.obligation: Count natural enemies and parasitised individuals before treating a population that may already be collapsing.
atoms.lesson: A field at threshold with a high predator ratio often needs no spray. Roughly one lady beetle or lacewing larva per fifty to a hundred aphids, or twenty per cent parasitised mummies, signals a population that will crash within a week. Broad spectrum pyrethroids remove those predators and routinely flare spider mites in dry seasons, since mites are largely predator regulated and pyrethroids are only weakly miticidal. Record beneficials so the decision stays auditable.

atoms.obligation: Identify the species and life stage before choosing a product, because timing and label both depend on it.
atoms.lesson: Look-alikes drive wasted sprays. True armyworm and fall armyworm need different timings, and both are only reliably controlled at early instars under half an inch while larvae still feed exposed. Corn rootworm decisions come from adult beetle counts the previous August, not from root damage in June, because larvae cannot be reached once feeding. Sucking pests need a systemic; exposed larvae need a contact product with high water volume for coverage.

name: weed-resistance-program
description: Designs a herbicide programme that controls the weed spectrum while slowing resistance. Use it when a grower reports escapes after a spray that used to work, when planning pre-emergence and post-emergence applications for the season, when a resistant population has been confirmed, or when a field has run the same mode of action for several years running.
expansions: escapes after the post spray
same weed surviving every year
planning pre and post programme
confirmed resistance in that field
need a different mode of action
ryegrass no longer dying
overlapping residual timing question
tank mix partners for waterhemp

atoms.obligation: Diagnose whether escapes are resistance or application failure before changing the herbicide programme.
atoms.lesson: The pattern tells the story. Resistance appears as healthy plants of one species standing among dead plants of the same species and size, in patches that grow year on year. Application failure appears as strips, boom-width misses, uniformly stunted survivors, or escapes only where weeds were oversized, drought stressed or under the canopy. Check the spray record for rate, water volume, adjuvant, nozzle and weed height first; most claimed resistance is a six-inch window sprayed at twelve.

atoms.obligation: Build every application around at least two modes of action that are genuinely effective on the target weed.
atoms.lesson: Mixing modes of action within an application beats rotating them between years, because mixing multiplies survival probability while rotation only alternates selection. The partner must control that weed alone at the rate used, or it is a passenger. For amaranth species that usually means a group fifteen residual plus a group fourteen or group four contact, and never a solo group nine or group two applied post. Resistant populations may already carry cross-resistance across an entire group.

atoms.obligation: Layer residual chemistry so the soil surface never goes bare through the weed emergence window.
atoms.lesson: Small-seeded summer annuals emerge over eight to ten weeks, so a single pre-emergence application runs out mid-flush. Overlapping residuals means applying the second residual before the first breaks, typically twenty-one to twenty-eight days after planting or at the third to fourth leaf, rather than waiting for escapes. Residual longevity depends on rainfall for activation, within seven to ten days for most chloroacetamides, and on organic matter, which binds product and raises the rate needed.

atoms.obligation: Stop seed return from survivors during the same season in which the escapes were found.
atoms.lesson: One female amaranth plant produces 250,000 to a million seeds, so a thin scatter of survivors reseeds the field completely. The seedbank declines only about half per year without new input, meaning several clean years to make progress and one dirty year to undo them. Practical measures are hand roguing patches before seed set, mowing or spot spraying escapes, harvesting infested fields last, and blowing the combine down between fields.

name: fungicide-timing-decisions
description: Decides whether and when a fungicide application is justified using growth stage, weather and disease risk. Use it when a grower asks if a flag leaf or flowering spray pays this year, when lesions appear low in the canopy, when a wet forecast raises head blight risk, or when planning a one-spray versus two-spray programme.
expansions: is a fungicide worth it
lesions moving up the canopy
wet forecast at flowering
flag leaf spray timing
head blight risk this week
two spray programme worth it
rust found in neighbouring field
pre harvest interval question

atoms.obligation: Tie the application to the growth stage that protects the yield-forming leaves or the actual infection court.
atoms.lesson: In wheat the top two leaves supply most of grain fill, so the flag leaf timing at growth stage 39 protects yield and a spray after symptoms reach the flag is largely rescue. Fusarium head blight differs because the infection court is the anther, so the window is early flowering plus a few days, and a triazole then gives fifty to sixty per cent suppression at best. In corn most documented response sits between tasselling and brown silk.

atoms.obligation: Weigh the expected response against this season disease risk instead of spraying on the calendar.
atoms.lesson: Fungicide response tracks pressure and susceptibility. On a susceptible hybrid in a wet season following continuous corn residue the response commonly runs eight to fifteen bushels; on a resistant hybrid in a dry season after a break crop it is under three and does not pay. Practical triggers are lesions on the leaf below the ear at tasselling, a susceptible rating, high yield potential, and several consecutive humid nights with leaf wetness beyond eight hours.

atoms.obligation: Alternate fungicide groups and avoid applying single-site chemistry alone at reduced rates.
atoms.lesson: Strobilurins are single-site and lost efficacy against several pathogens through one target-site mutation, while sensitivity to the triazoles has shifted gradually. A durable programme mixes a single-site partner with a multi-site or a second group, uses full label rates instead of cut rates that select for partial resistance, and limits each group to two applications a season. Rate cutting on a curative timing is the fastest route to losing a chemistry.

atoms.obligation: Check pre-harvest intervals and buyer residue rules before the final application of the season.
atoms.lesson: Late applications are where residue problems arise. Pre-harvest intervals commonly range from fourteen to thirty days, and grazing or forage harvest restrictions are separate and often longer than the grain interval. Malting barley, seed crops and export contracts can carry buyer approved lists narrower than the label, and a maximum residue limit in the destination market may be lower than the domestic one. Confirm the buyer specification before spraying, not after rejection.

name: spray-record-compliance
description: Keeps pesticide application records and operator compliance in an inspection-ready state. Use it when preparing for an audit or farm assurance inspection, when records are missing detail after a busy spray week, when an operator certificate or sprayer test is close to expiry, or after a neighbour raises a drift complaint.
expansions: inspector visit next week
spray records missing details
operator certificate expiring soon
sprayer test due date
neighbour complained about drift
what has to be recorded legally
chemical store audit checklist
buffer zone documentation needed

atoms.obligation: Record every application with the full legal detail set at the time of spraying, not afterwards from memory.
atoms.lesson: The standard record set is product and registration number, active ingredient, rate per unit area, total quantity, crop and growth stage, field identifier and treated area, date with start and finish times, operator name and certificate number, weather including wind speed and direction and temperature, and the target pest. Retention is commonly three years, sometimes five. Records written days later fail on wind and timing, which is where inspections usually unravel.

atoms.obligation: Verify operator certification, equipment test status and store compliance ahead of the season rather than during it.
atoms.lesson: Three documents are checked at almost every inspection: a valid operator certificate, a current sprayer test which is annual or three yearly depending on scheme and machine age, and a pesticide store that is fire resistant, bunded to between 110 and 185 per cent of the largest container, lockable, signed and inventoried. Calibration is separate from the statutory test and should be repeated whenever nozzles, forward speed or product change.

atoms.obligation: Apply and document buffer zones, drift mitigation and no-spray areas for each product on each field.
atoms.lesson: Aquatic buffers attach to the product, commonly five metres from the top of the bank, extendable, and reducible only where low-drift nozzles from an approved list are used and that reduction is recorded. Other constraints stack: distances from dwellings and public rights of way, protected habitat exclusions, and windows around bee foraging. The record should name the nozzle and pressure that justified any buffer reduction, otherwise the reduction is indefensible.

atoms.obligation: Handle a drift or exposure complaint by preserving the records and physical evidence the same day.
atoms.lesson: Response quality decides the outcome. Within the same day secure the application record, product label and batch numbers, tank mix sheet, nozzle and pressure settings, and the on-farm weather log; photograph the affected boundary and symptom pattern with timestamps; and note wind direction and any inversion, since early morning inversions carry fine droplets much further than a moderate breeze. Notify the insurer, and the regulator where required, before making any admission.

name: irrigation-scheduling
description: Sets irrigation timing and depth from soil moisture, crop stage and evaporative demand. Use it when deciding whether to run a pivot this week, when moisture probes disagree with how the crop looks, when an allocation or licence is running short, or when a crop has reached a stage where water stress cannot be recovered later.
expansions: do we run the pivot
probe readings look dry
allocation is running short
crop at tasselling needs water
how much to apply per pass
refill point on the profile
rain forecast worth waiting for
pump capacity limits the schedule

atoms.obligation: Trigger irrigation from depletion of plant available water in the active root zone, not from a fixed interval.
atoms.lesson: Available water holding capacity runs roughly 0.6 to 0.8 inches per foot on sand, 1.5 to 2.0 on silt loam and 1.8 to 2.2 on clay loam, held between field capacity and wilting point. Most crops are irrigated at forty to fifty per cent depletion, tightened to thirty during the critical stage. Rooting depth grows with the crop, so early readings come from the top foot and mid-season from three or four feet; averaging all sensors hides a drying front.

atoms.obligation: Protect the moisture-critical growth stage first whenever the water supply is limited.
atoms.lesson: Stress is not equally costly across the season. In corn the fortnight around silking can cost three to eight per cent of yield per day of visible stress; in soybean it is pod fill; in potatoes it is tuber initiation and bulking, where stress also causes second growth and misshapen tubers; in cereals it is booting through grain fill. With a short allocation the correct plan often irrigates fewer acres fully rather than every acre partially.

atoms.obligation: Match application depth to infiltration rate and system capacity so the water actually enters the profile.
atoms.lesson: Applying faster than the soil accepts sends water to the tail drain or the wheel track. Infiltration falls with time under the nozzle and with slope, so a silt loam on a five per cent slope may take only 0.4 inches an hour while a pivot end tower applies far faster than the inner spans. Applying beyond the deficit also pushes nitrate below the root zone. Five to seven gallons per minute per acre supplies roughly a quarter inch daily.

atoms.obligation: Reconcile the schedule with the abstraction licence, the seasonal allocation and the pumping cost of each pass.
atoms.lesson: Water is a budgeted input. Abstraction licences carry annual and daily volume limits, hands-off flow conditions that stop pumping when a river gauge falls, and metering and return obligations. Costing a pass makes the trade-off explicit, since an inch over an acre is about 27,000 gallons and pumping cost depends on lift, pressure and fuel price. Comparing that cost against the expected yield response at that stage decides the marginal pass.

name: harvest-logistics-coordination
description: Plans the harvest campaign: field order, machine and cart pairing, trucking and where each load goes. Use it when the combine is about to roll and fields ripen at different times, when trucks queue or the combine sits waiting, when weather is closing a window, or when deciding which loads go to store and which go straight to a contract.
expansions: combine waiting on trucks
which field to cut first
rain coming in two days
grain cart cannot keep up
elevator queue is long
splitting loads between bins and delivery
harvest crew shift plan
moisture varies field to field

atoms.obligation: Order the fields by risk of standing loss rather than by convenience or proximity to the yard.
atoms.lesson: Standing crop deteriorates unevenly. Take first the fields with lodging, hail damage, stalk rot, shatter-prone varieties or early maturity that has already dried past target, and leave tough, late or well-standing fields until last. Sequence also serves sanitation: harvest fields with resistant weed patches or a seed-borne disease at the end so the combine does not distribute them across clean ground, and blow the machine down between problem fields.

atoms.obligation: Size the cart and truck fleet to combine throughput so the harvesting machine never stops moving.
atoms.lesson: The combine is the constraint and everything downstream is a buffer. A machine unloading three hundred bushels in about ninety seconds while cutting needs a cart that holds at least two hopperfuls and returns before the combine refills. Cycle time to the yard sets truck numbers: a twenty-five minute round trip with a thousand bushel truck supports roughly 2,400 bushels an hour, so a faster combine needs a spare truck or a field-side buffer.

atoms.obligation: Route each load by moisture, quality and contract obligation before it leaves the field.
atoms.lesson: The load decision is financial. Grain above safe storage moisture goes to the dryer or straight to delivery, while grain at or below target goes to the bin. Contracted bushels with delivery windows and quality specifications should be filled from loads that meet the specification, keeping off-spec grain for feed or blending. Test weight, damage and foreign material drive discounts at the scale, and knowing them before dispatch avoids a rejected load travelling twice.

atoms.obligation: Run combine loss checks repeatedly as crop conditions change through the harvesting day.
atoms.lesson: Settings drift with crop moisture through the day. A drop pan or counted-seed check over a known area gives a real figure, since about twenty soybean seeds per square foot equals one bushel per acre and four corn kernels per square foot is roughly one bushel. Total loss under two or three per cent is a normal target. Separate header loss, usually the majority and fixed by reel, cutterbar and ground speed, from rotor, concave and fan losses.

name: grain-storage-management
description: Keeps stored grain sound through the storage season using drying targets, aeration and monitoring. Use it when grain is going into the bin, when a hot spot or surface crust appears, when insects turn up in a sample, or when planning cooling and drying ahead of a long hold or a summer delivery slot.
expansions: grain going in the bin
hot spot in the middle bin
crusting on the grain surface
insects found in the sample
how long can we hold this
aeration fan run hours
drying down before storage
musty smell when opening bin

atoms.obligation: Dry to a moisture content matched to the crop and the intended holding period before closing the bin.
atoms.lesson: Safe storage moisture falls as the hold lengthens. Corn at fifteen per cent holds through winter but needs thirteen to thirteen and a half for carryover into summer; soybean stores at thirteen, wheat at thirteen and a half, canola at eight or nine because of its oil content. Mould growth is governed by equilibrium relative humidity in the interstitial air, and holding that below about sixty-five per cent blocks storage fungi. Warm grain at borderline moisture spoils within weeks.

atoms.obligation: Cool the bulk in stages with aeration and track each cooling front fully through the grain.
atoms.lesson: Aeration moves a cooling front at roughly 0.1 to 0.2 cubic feet per minute per bushel, needing a hundred to a hundred and fifty hours of fan run to push one front through the bulk. Cool in ten to fifteen degree steps as ambient allows, targeting under forty Fahrenheit for winter holding, and always finish a front rather than stopping halfway, which leaves a warm moist band that becomes the spoilage layer. Run fans on cool dry nights.

atoms.obligation: Inspect stored grain on a fixed schedule using temperature, smell and a probed sample from several depths.
atoms.lesson: Check weekly in warm weather and fortnightly when cold. A five degree rise on one cable or in one zone between checks means biological activity and needs action now, not at the next visit. Surface crusting indicates condensation where a warm core meets a cold roof, which happens when cooling was incomplete. Coring the bin, drawing the centre column of fines and light grain out after filling, removes the peak where fines, moisture and insects concentrate.

atoms.obligation: Control storage insects through sanitation and monitoring, treating only with what the intended market permits.
atoms.lesson: Most infestations originate in residues left in the empty bin, the auger and spilled grain around the base, so cleaning the structure before filling matters more than treating afterwards. Probe traps or sieved samples give counts per unit weight, and tolerance is near zero for milling and malting buyers. Fumigation is a licensed operation with sealing, monitoring and re-entry rules, and organic and some export contracts prohibit it entirely, leaving cooling and turning as the only tools.

name: machinery-maintenance-planning
description: Schedules servicing, wear-part replacement and pre-season checks across the equipment fleet. Use it when building the winter workshop list, when a machine approaches a service interval, when in-season downtime is costing money, or when deciding whether to repair, trade or hire a machine for the coming season.
expansions: winter workshop job list
tractor due for service hours
breakdown in the middle of drilling
wear parts to order early
repair or trade this combine
pre season checks before harvest
oil sample results came back
tyre pressures for field work

atoms.obligation: Plan servicing around the operational calendar so each critical machine is ready before its own season.
atoms.lesson: Every machine has a window it cannot miss: the drill before spring, the sprayer before the first pass, the combine and grain handling before harvest, the forage kit before first cut. Work backwards at least six weeks from each window to allow parts lead times, which run from days to months on driveline and electronic components. In-season failure costs far more than the repair, since one lost day at planting can cost yield across hundreds of acres.

atoms.obligation: Track hours and condition per machine and replace wear parts on measured evidence rather than after failure.
atoms.lesson: Service intervals are hour based, typically five hundred hours for engine oil on modern tractors and one to one and a half thousand for hydraulic and transmission oil, but heavy draft work shortens them. Wear parts have measurable limits: concaves and rasp bars, chopper knives, drill coulters and points, and sprayer nozzles replaced once output exceeds nominal by ten per cent. Oil analysis for iron, silicon and water warns of failure weeks before any noise appears.

atoms.obligation: Compare repair, trade and hire on total cost per hour or per acre rather than on the invoice alone.
atoms.lesson: Ownership cost is depreciation, interest, insurance and housing plus repairs and fuel. Repair spend rises nonlinearly after warranty and typically overtakes the depreciation saving somewhere past four to six thousand tractor hours or twenty-five hundred combine separator hours. For a machine used under about two hundred hours a year, hiring or using a contractor is usually cheaper once depreciation is charged honestly, and it moves downtime risk onto someone else.

atoms.obligation: Record every repair, part number and fault against the individual machine so patterns and resale value stay visible.
atoms.lesson: A per-machine log turns anecdote into evidence. Repeat failures on the same circuit, bearing or sensor usually point at a root cause such as misalignment, a chafed harness or contaminated oil, and only the log reveals the repetition. It also supports warranty claims, which frequently require proof that scheduled servicing was done with specified fluids, and it lifts trade value, because a documented service history is worth real money at valuation.

name: grain-marketing-hedging
description: Builds a marketing plan for the crop using cash sales, forward contracts, basis and futures or options. Use it when deciding how much of the crop to price and when, when a buyer puts a contract in front of the grower, when basis moves or a target price is hit, or when the risk of a particular contract type needs explaining before anyone signs.
expansions: how much should we price now
forward contract offer from the buyer
basis widened this week
target price hit today
hedge before harvest or after
risk of a hedge to arrive
storing versus selling at harvest
margin call on the futures position

atoms.obligation: Price the crop in increments against a written plan of targets and dates rather than in one decision.
atoms.lesson: Scale-up selling avoids the all-or-nothing outcome. A common frame prices twenty to twenty-five per cent by the previous winter, adds an increment on a pre-planting rally, more during weather risk at pollination or grain fill, and clears the rest after harvest. The ceiling on pre-harvest pricing is production risk: pricing beyond the insurance-guaranteed bushels means buying grain to fill contracts in a short year. Written dates beat waiting for the top.

atoms.obligation: Separate the futures decision from the basis decision and know which one each contract actually locks.
atoms.lesson: Cash price equals futures plus basis and the two move independently. A hedge to arrive locks futures and leaves basis open, a basis contract locks basis and leaves futures open, and a cash forward locks both. Harvest basis is typically at its weakest and narrows through the storage season, so selling cash at harvest gives that carry away. Several years of local basis history for the delivery point tells you whether today bid is strong or weak.

atoms.obligation: Cost the full carry before choosing to store grain instead of selling it now.
atoms.lesson: Storing pays only when the market pays you to store. Add interest on the grain value, drying and shrink, storage or bin ownership cost, insurance and quality risk, commonly three to five cents a bushel per month on corn. Compare that against the futures spread between nearby and deferred contracts plus expected basis improvement. An inverted market pays nothing to store and argues for selling now, while a full carry rewards a hedged storage position.

atoms.obligation: Understand delivery obligation, margin requirements and counterparty risk before signing any pricing contract.
atoms.lesson: A forward contract is an obligation to deliver quantity and quality on a date, and failure means buying out at market, which is ruinous in a drought when yield and price move against you together. Futures hedges require margin, and a rising market generates calls on the short position months before the cash sale funds them, so credit must be arranged first. Deferred payment and delayed pricing contracts leave you an unsecured creditor of the buyer.

name: enterprise-budget-cashflow
description: Builds field and enterprise budgets and the seasonal cash flow that sits around them. Use it when planning next year cost of production, when a lender asks for projections, when comparing whether an enterprise genuinely pays its way, or when cash is tight between buying inputs and receiving harvest income.
expansions: cost of production per acre
lender wants cash flow projections
does this enterprise actually pay
cash tight before harvest
input prices up this year
breakeven yield calculation needed
rent and machinery cost allocation
comparing two crops on margin

atoms.obligation: Separate variable, operating and fixed costs so break-even figures and enterprise comparisons stay honest.
atoms.lesson: Variable costs are seed, fertiliser, chemicals, fuel, drying and crop insurance; operating overheads are labour, repairs, insurance and interest; fixed costs are machinery depreciation, the land charge and unpaid family labour. Break-even over variable cost decides whether to plant this season, while break-even over total cost decides whether the business survives. Comparing enterprises on gross margin alone flatters whichever one consumes the most machinery hours, because those costs sit outside the line.

atoms.obligation: Build the cash flow month by month against the real timing of payments rather than an annual total.
atoms.lesson: Farm cash flow is deeply seasonal: fertiliser and seed leave in autumn and spring, rent often falls in one or two lumps, and income arrives in a few weeks after harvest or monthly from livestock. Peak borrowing usually occurs shortly before harvest, so the operating line must be sized to that peak, not the year-end position. Insurance indemnities and support payments arrive months after the triggering event and cannot cover an in-season gap.

atoms.obligation: Test the budget across realistic yield and price ranges instead of a single expected case.
atoms.lesson: Yield and price both vary twenty to thirty per cent and are usually negatively correlated locally but not globally, so a drought that halves your yield may not lift price if the drought is only yours. A useful frame runs three cases, low yield with low price, expected, and high, then reports the working capital required at the worst plausible case. Break-even yield at the current forward price is the number a lender wants most.

atoms.obligation: Charge owned land and owner labour at market rates even where no cash actually changes hands.
atoms.lesson: Owned land and unpaid family labour hide losses. Charging owned ground at local cash rent and family labour at a hired replacement wage shows whether the farming operation earns anything beyond the return on the land asset itself. Many operations that appear profitable are simply earning the land rent and nothing more, which changes decisions about expansion, taking on custom work, and whether renting the ground out beats farming it.

name: crop-insurance-claim
description: Handles a crop loss claim from notification through adjuster visit to settlement. Use it when hail, drought, flood or frost damages a crop, when deciding whether to destroy and replant, when an adjuster is due on the farm, or when a settlement offer looks wrong against the approved yield and production history.
expansions: hail went through last night
adjuster coming this week
replant or keep the stand
drought loss on dryland acres
settlement offer looks low
documenting the damaged field
deadline to report the loss
production history for the claim

atoms.obligation: Notify the insurer within the policy deadline and before disturbing, destroying or harvesting the damaged crop.
atoms.lesson: Most policies require notice of loss within seventy-two hours of discovery and always before destroying, replanting, grazing or harvesting affected acres. Working the ground before inspection can void the claim outright, because the damage can no longer be measured. Where a replant decision is genuinely urgent, the correct step is recorded consent from the adjuster plus representative untouched strips left across the field so the original condition can still be assessed.

atoms.obligation: Document the damage immediately with dated evidence tied to specific fields and measured areas.
atoms.lesson: Useful evidence is timestamped photographs with field identifiers, plant stand counts along measured lengths of row, bruise counts on stems, defoliation estimates against growth stage, and the local weather record including hail reports and rainfall totals. Keep input records showing the crop was managed to a normal standard, since a claim can be reduced for poor husbandry. Evidence gathered a week later is systematically weaker than evidence gathered the same day.

atoms.obligation: Make the replant decision on remaining yield potential net of costs rather than on how bad the field looks.
atoms.lesson: A thin damaged stand often out-yields a late replant. Corn at eighteen thousand evenly spaced plants per acre still carries roughly eighty-five to ninety per cent of yield potential, and defoliation before the sixth leaf has little effect because the growing point remains below ground. Against that, a replant costs seed and fuel and shifts into a later maturity with lower potential. Count the stand across several representative row lengths before deciding.

atoms.obligation: Reconcile the settlement against the guarantee, the approved yield and the price election written in the policy.
atoms.lesson: The payout is the guarantee minus production to count, valued at the policy price, so three numbers drive it: approved yield from the production history, coverage level, and the price election or harvest price. Check that appraised production on unharvested acres is realistic, that quality adjustments and unit structure were applied correctly, and that yields from other units were not blended in a way that erases the loss. Disputes usually turn on the appraisal, which is reviewable.

name: land-lease-negotiation
description: Negotiates and documents farmland tenancies: cash rent, crop share, flexible terms and the conditions attached. Use it when a lease comes up for renewal, when a landlord asks for an increase, when comparing cash rent against a share arrangement, or when writing terms about improvements, soil condition, compensation and notice.
expansions: landlord wants a rent increase
lease renewal coming up
cash rent versus crop share
flexible rent formula ideas
who pays for lime and drainage
notice period to end tenancy
new ground came available nearby
rent looks above what it pays

atoms.obligation: Set your own rent ceiling from what each field can pay at conservative yield and price before negotiating.
atoms.lesson: Rent is a residual, not a market quote. Take realistic yield for that soil, a conservative forward price, subtract variable costs, machinery and labour per acre, and a return to management and risk; what remains is the maximum rent. Fields differ twenty to forty per cent in productivity within a single farm, so one blanket rent overpays for the weakest ground. Walking away from an overpriced block usually costs less than farming it at a loss.

atoms.obligation: Match the lease structure to whichever party is best placed to carry price and yield risk.
atoms.lesson: Fixed cash rent gives the landlord certainty and hands the tenant all risk and all upside. Crop share, historically a third to a half depending on who supplies inputs, splits both and keeps the landlord engaged but needs shared decisions and transparent settlement. Flexible rents set a base with a bonus formula on actual yield times actual price above a trigger, which caps tenant downside; the formula must name the price source, yield measurement and a ceiling.

atoms.obligation: Write down the terms that outlast one season: improvements, soil condition and end-of-tenancy compensation.
atoms.lesson: Disputes are about durable items. Specify who funds and who owns lime, phosphate and potash build-up, drainage and fencing, and how unexhausted value is compensated if the tenancy ends soon after the investment. Include entry soil test results as the baseline, agree residue and cover crop practice, and record which party carries conservation compliance and any environmental scheme agreements that bind the land beyond the lease term.

atoms.obligation: Confirm notice periods, renewal dates and the tenancy type before assuming the arrangement continues another year.
atoms.lesson: Statutory notice rules control tenure and vary sharply by jurisdiction and lease type, with termination deadlines often several months before the lease year ends and automatic renewal once the date passes. A handshake arrangement can create an implied tenancy carrying more security than either party intended, or none at all. Put term, notice date, rent review mechanism and payment dates in writing, and diarise the notice deadline a month ahead.

name: seasonal-labour-scheduling
description: Plans and manages seasonal and permanent farm labour: crew size, rotas, pay rules and accommodation. Use it when building a harvest or picking crew, when a peak week needs more hands than the payroll carries, when checking hours, rest and piece rate rules, or when onboarding workers arriving under a seasonal scheme.
expansions: picking crew for next month
rota for harvest weeks
short handed at peak
overtime and rest break rules
accommodation deductions question
onboarding seasonal workers arriving
piece rate versus hourly pay
right to work checks

atoms.obligation: Build the crew requirement from measured work rates and the crop window rather than last year headcount.
atoms.lesson: Size the crew from output. If a picker averages twelve to fifteen kilos an hour on a good block and that block yields twenty tonnes over ten days, the arithmetic gives crew days directly, then add fifteen to twenty per cent for weather days, absence and the learning curve, since a new starter first week rate is often half the experienced rate. Ripening is temperature driven, so a warm spell compresses the window and the peak.

atoms.obligation: Apply working time, rest and record-keeping rules to every worker regardless of how they are paid.
atoms.lesson: Hours, breaks and days off are regulated even where piece rates apply, and the record of actual hours worked is the employer defence in a dispute. Common requirements include a daily rest period, a break within shifts over six hours, weekly rest, and tighter restrictions for under-eighteens. Piece rates must still deliver at least the applicable minimum wage for hours worked, which requires a fair rate calculation based on average output, retested when conditions change.

atoms.obligation: Verify right to work and scheme conditions before any worker starts, and retain the evidence.
atoms.lesson: Checks are pre-employment, not retrospective. Seasonal worker schemes attach conditions to both sponsor and worker, covering permitted work types, maximum stay, transfer rules between holdings, and reporting duties if a worker fails to arrive or leaves early. Penalties fall on the employer and licence loss during a harvest is existential. Recruiting through licensed labour providers shifts some risk but never removes the duty to check and document.

atoms.obligation: Set accommodation, transport and deduction terms in writing before workers arrive on the holding.
atoms.lesson: Where accommodation is provided, deductions are capped and must be disclosed, and the housing is subject to inspection standards covering occupancy, sanitation, cooking facilities and fire safety. Transport arrangements bring driver hours and vehicle insurance obligations. Charging above the permitted accommodation offset, or deducting for tools and protective equipment, is a common and expensive breach, and a written statement of terms is due on or before the first day.

name: pasture-grazing-rotation
description: Plans rotational grazing: paddock moves, residency, rest periods and matching stock demand to grass growth. Use it when grass is getting ahead of or behind the herd, when building a grazing wedge or a season plan, when deciding which paddocks to close for silage, or when drought or a wet spell forces the rotation to change.
expansions: grass getting ahead of cows
how long to rest this paddock
covers dropping across the platform
close paddocks for silage
drought plan for the grazing
residuals too high after grazing
stocking rate on the platform
setting up the spring rotation

atoms.obligation: Move stock on entry and residual covers rather than on a fixed number of days per paddock.
atoms.lesson: The working rule in ryegrass is to enter at the three-leaf stage, roughly 2,800 to 3,200 kilos of dry matter per hectare or ten to twelve centimetres, and to leave at a residual near 1,500 to 1,600 kilos or four to five centimetres. Grazing below that strips the leaf area driving regrowth and lengthens the next rest, while leaving above it lets stem and dead material accumulate, cutting intake and quality within a rotation or two.

atoms.obligation: Adjust the rest period to actual growth rate so rotation length matches regrowth through the season.
atoms.lesson: Rest is a consequence of growth, not a calendar entry. At spring peak growth the rotation can tighten to eighteen or twenty-one days, while in the summer slump or dry conditions it must stretch to thirty or forty days or the plant is grazed again before reserves recover. A weekly measured walk gives growth in kilos per hectare per day and average farm cover, and comparing growth against demand signals a surplus to cut or a deficit to fill.

atoms.obligation: Remove surplus paddocks as conserved forage as soon as the wedge shows the surplus.
atoms.lesson: A grazing wedge plots each paddock cover against a target line, and paddocks above the line are the surplus. Cutting them early preserves quality across the rest of the platform, because grass left to bulk passes its optimum and drags intake down for the whole rotation. Cut paddocks need a longer rest before returning and usually a nutrient application to replace offtake, roughly twenty-five kilos of potash per tonne of dry matter removed.

atoms.obligation: Write a feed deficit plan with numeric trigger points before covers actually run out.
atoms.lesson: Response options ranked by cost are extending the rotation, cutting demand by weaning early or culling empty and passenger stock, feeding conserved forage, then buying feed in. Waiting until covers hit the floor removes every cheap option and leaves bought feed at peak price, when everyone in the region is buying. Triggers should be numbers, such as average farm cover below a set figure for the stocking rate, or growth under demand for two consecutive weeks.

name: herd-health-protocol
description: Sets and runs herd health programmes: vaccination, parasite control, medicine recording and withdrawal periods. Use it when building the annual health plan with the vet, when an animal needs treating and the record and withdrawal must be correct, when a wormer appears to have stopped working, or when a screen or bulk test comes back positive.
expansions: annual herd health plan
withdrawal period for this treatment
wormer no longer working
vaccination timing before calving
medicine book missing entries
bulk screen came back positive
antibiotic usage review due
quarantine for bought in stock

atoms.obligation: Record every medicine given with the legally required detail and diarise the withdrawal date for that animal.
atoms.lesson: The record set is animal or group identity, date, product and batch, dose, route, person administering, reason for treatment, and the withdrawal for meat and for milk, retained typically five years. Withdrawal is product and route specific, and off-label use extends it under cascade rules, commonly to at least seven days for milk and twenty-eight for meat. Control it physically with leg bands and a diarised date, because a breach condemns a whole tank or carcass.

atoms.obligation: Time vaccinations so immunity is established before the exposure period, allowing for the primary course.
atoms.lesson: A primary course usually needs two doses three to six weeks apart with protection appearing two to three weeks after the second, so a pneumonia vaccine begun at housing is already late. Scour vaccines are given to the dam three to twelve weeks before calving so antibody reaches colostrum, which only helps if the calf receives enough good colostrum quickly. Fertility vaccines must finish before bulling, and any cold chain failure silently voids the programme.

atoms.obligation: Base parasite control on diagnostics and treat selectively rather than dosing whole groups by calendar.
atoms.lesson: Faecal egg counts, fluke tests and growth rates show whether treatment is actually needed. Anthelmintic resistance is now common to benzimidazoles and levamisole in sheep, so a drench check, an egg count seven to fourteen days after treatment, is how failure gets detected. Leaving the fittest animals untreated preserves a refugia population of susceptible parasites. Dose to the heaviest in the group by weighing rather than by eye, and calibrate the gun, since underdosing selects hard for resistance.

atoms.obligation: Quarantine and test incoming stock before they have any contact with the resident herd.
atoms.lesson: Bought-in animals are the main route for disease entry. A standard quarantine runs three to four weeks in separate airspace with separate drainage, including parasite treatment and a housed period so resistant worm eggs are shed off pasture, plus testing appropriate to herd status for diseases such as BVD, Johnes and IBR, and in sheep for footrot and scab. Buying from herds with a declared health status and demanding the certification is far cheaper than remediation.

name: calving-season-management
description: Runs the calving block: preparation, monitoring, intervention decisions and newborn care. Use it when a block is about to start, when deciding whether and when to assist a cow in labour, when calf scours or losses appear in the pens, or when reviewing why a season produced more dead calves and sick cows than it should have.
expansions: calving starts in three weeks
when to intervene with this cow
calf scours in the pens
colostrum protocol for the staff
twins and malpresentation handling
pens and hygiene setup
retained cleansing after calving
reviewing last season calf losses

atoms.obligation: Decide intervention from the stage of labour and elapsed time using a written rule the whole team follows.
atoms.lesson: Second stage labour, from the water bag or feet showing, should progress visibly. A mature cow should calve within about seventy minutes and a heifer within two hours, with progress every twenty to thirty minutes. No progress, or a malpresentation such as head back, leg back, backwards or breech, means examine now. Prolonged second stage sharply raises stillbirth, retained membranes and metritis, and delays return to cycling, so early help is cheap.

atoms.obligation: Get an adequate volume of good quality colostrum into every newborn calf within the first hours.
atoms.lesson: The gut absorbs immunoglobulin for a short window and efficiency falls steeply after six hours, closing near twenty-four. The practical rule is ten per cent of bodyweight in the first feed, roughly three to four litres for a dairy calf, within two to four hours, taken from a first milking of good quality above fifty grams per litre of IgG, about twenty-two per cent on a Brix refractometer. Failed passive transfer predicts pneumonia and scour.

atoms.obligation: Manage hygiene and pen flow so the calving area does not itself become the source of infection.
atoms.lesson: Pathogen load builds through the block, which is why late-born calves get sick more often than early ones. Keep calving pens separate from sick pens, allow roughly one pen per twenty-five to thirty cows in the block, bed deeply and clean between cows where possible, and move pairs out promptly instead of mixing ages. Where all-in all-out flow is impossible, moving cows onto fresh ground on a rotation breaks the rotavirus and cryptosporidium build-up.

atoms.obligation: Manage body condition and transition nutrition before the block so outcomes are set in advance.
atoms.lesson: Target condition at calving is roughly three to three and a quarter on the five point dairy scale and two and a half to three for suckler cows. Over-fat cows have harder calvings and more metabolic disease, while thin cows produce poor colostrum and cycle late. The final three weeks manage calcium and energy through low potassium forage or anionic salts to cut milk fever, plus adequate selenium and iodine, whose deficiency shows as weak calves and retained membranes.

name: feed-ration-formulation
description: Formulates and checks livestock rations against requirements, forage analysis and feed cost. Use it when a forage analysis arrives, when milk yield or growth rate slips, when feed prices force an ingredient substitution, or when a group shows loose dung, poor cudding or another sign that the rumen is not coping with the current diet.
expansions: silage analysis just came back
milk yield dropped this week
cheaper protein source swap
loose dung in fresh group
growth rates behind target
mineral specification for the ration
transition cow diet check
feed cost per litre rising

atoms.obligation: Formulate from an actual forage analysis, since forage makes up most of the diet and varies every year.
atoms.lesson: Grass silage ranges from nine to twelve megajoules of metabolisable energy per kilo of dry matter and ten to eighteen per cent crude protein, while maize silage swings on starch from twenty-five to thirty-five per cent. Feeding to book values misses by more than any concentrate adjustment can correct. Sample by coring several points of the clamp face, and retest when the face moves into a different cut or layer, because dry matter alone shifts intakes by kilos.

atoms.obligation: Balance for dry matter intake, energy, protein fractions and effective fibre rather than crude protein alone.
atoms.lesson: Rumen microbes need fermentable energy and degradable protein together; excess degradable protein leaves as urea, costs energy to excrete and shows as milk urea above roughly thirty milligrams per decilitre. Physically effective fibre maintains the rumen mat and chewing, generally twenty-eight to thirty-two per cent neutral detergent fibre with adequate particle length, while starch above about twenty-eight per cent risks subacute acidosis. Intake is the binding constraint, since a fresh cow eats far below her requirement.

atoms.obligation: Introduce ration changes gradually and judge them on animal response rather than on the formulation sheet.
atoms.lesson: Rumen microbial populations adapt over ten to fourteen days, so step ingredient changes in across that period, particularly when adding starch or switching forage source. Monitoring signals are dung consistency and undigested grain, cud chewing in at least sixty per cent of resting cows, a milk fat to protein ratio below 1.02 suggesting acidosis, body condition trend, and feed refusals. A ration that balances on paper but fails in the trough is usually an intake or sorting problem.

atoms.obligation: Compare feed ingredients on cost per unit of the limiting nutrient rather than on price per tonne.
atoms.lesson: Substitution decisions turn on relative value: price per megajoule of energy and per kilo of protein, corrected for dry matter and for handling, storage and shrink losses. Wet by-products look cheap per tonne but carry water and spoil quickly, while a dear high protein meal can still be the cheapest protein source. Check the constraints a swap breaks, such as total dietary fat above six or seven per cent depressing fibre digestion, or an inclusion ceiling on a by-product.

name: milk-quality-troubleshooting
description: Investigates milk quality problems: somatic cell count, bacterial counts, antibiotic failures and taints. Use it when the bulk tank result jumps, when a penalty notice arrives from the processor, when individual cow records point at a problem group, or when a plant wash fault, cooling failure or inhibitor positive needs tracing to its cause.
expansions: bulk tank cell count jumped
bactoscan failed this month
penalty notice from the processor
which cows are driving the count
plant wash temperature check
teat end scores look poor
cooling not reaching temperature
inhibitor test came back positive

atoms.obligation: Split the problem into udder health, plant hygiene or cooling before changing anything on the farm.
atoms.lesson: The results point in different directions. A rising somatic cell count means udder infection and is diagnosed from individual cow records and a California mastitis test, while a rising total bacterial count means hygiene or cooling failure. Thermoduric counts implicate plant cleaning, especially deposits in rubberware and jetters; psychrotrophs implicate slow chilling; coliforms implicate dirty teats and bedding. Ask the laboratory for the differential counts instead of acting on the headline number.

atoms.obligation: Find and manage the specific cows driving the bulk tank rather than treating the whole herd.
atoms.lesson: A small number of chronic high cows can dominate the tank. Using individual recording, rank cows by cell count multiplied by yield to identify true contributors, then culture to establish whether the pathogen is contagious, such as Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus agalactiae, or environmental, such as E. coli or Streptococcus uberis. Contagious spread is handled by milking order, post-milking teat disinfection, gloves and culling chronics; environmental by bedding, dry cow therapy and cleanliness.

atoms.obligation: Verify the plant wash cycle by measurement of temperature, chemical concentration, water volume and contact time.
atoms.lesson: Cleaning fails quietly. A hot wash should reach the plant above seventy-five degrees Celsius and still be above forty-three to forty-five at the drain when the cycle ends, with correct detergent concentration and enough water for slug flow, roughly eight to ten litres per unit. Check for perished rubberware, cracked jetters, an undersized boiler, air injection settings and dead-leg pipework. Milk residue films are where thermoduric organisms live, and a plant can look clean while failing.

atoms.obligation: Trace every antibiotic failure to a specific handling breakdown and close that gap before the next milking.
atoms.lesson: A positive inhibitor test costs the tank plus the collection and often a penalty period. Usual causes are a treated cow milked into the tank by a relief milker, a dry cow calving early while product is still active, milk from a treated quarter entering through a shared cluster, or a mis-set diverter line. Controls must be physical and redundant: leg bands and spray marks, a treatment board at the parlour entrance, a written list checked every milking, and testing suspect milk.

name: organic-certification-audit
description: Prepares a holding for organic inspection and keeps the standard-facing records straight. Use it when an annual inspection is scheduled, when a new field or enterprise is entering conversion, when checking whether an input, seed source or treatment is permitted, or when a drift, buffer or parallel production question threatens the certified status.
expansions: inspection booked for next month
converting a new block
is this input permitted
non organic seed derogation needed
spray drift from the neighbour
audit trail from field to sale
parallel production question arose
livestock feed percentage rules

atoms.obligation: Keep an unbroken audit trail from field records to sale with quantities reconciled at every step.
atoms.lesson: The inspection is essentially a mass balance exercise. An inspector should be able to take a sales invoice for a lot and trace it back through the store, the harvest date, the field and the input records for that crop, with quantities that add up across seed purchased, area sown, yield harvested, stock held and quantity sold. Unexplained volumes are the classic finding. Livestock need the same chain from feed purchase through movement records to the abattoir consignment.

atoms.obligation: Confirm every input against the permitted list and with the certifier before it is bought or used.
atoms.lesson: Permission is specific and frequently conditional. Many materials are allowed only where documented need exists, such as a soil analysis justifying a mineral or a veterinary diagnosis behind a treatment. Non-organic seed requires a derogation applied for before sowing with evidence that no organic equivalent variety was available. Cleaning products, post-harvest treatments, seed coatings, feed additives and mineral licks all sit inside the standard, and retrospective approval is rarely granted.

atoms.obligation: Manage conversion periods, split holdings and buffer strips so the certified status stays defensible.
atoms.lesson: Conversion typically runs twenty-four months before harvest for arable and pasture, with livestock carrying their own conversion periods by species. Where organic and non-organic run side by side, the standard demands visually distinguishable crops or complete separation, with equipment cleaning records and separate documentation. Buffer strips against sprayed neighbours must be defined and their produce sold as non-organic, and the neighbour spray notification arrangement should be agreed in writing.

atoms.obligation: Prepare for inspection by walking the standard yourself and closing non-conformances beforehand.
atoms.lesson: Most findings are documentary rather than agronomic: a missing input approval, a gap in the field record, an unreconciled sale, an unlabelled store, or an organic management plan that no longer describes the actual rotation and enterprises. Review the previous inspection report and hold evidence that each point was actioned, because a repeated non-conformance escalates from minor to major and can suspend certification for a batch or the whole holding at the worst possible moment.

name: protocol-amendment-drafting
description: Drafts protocol amendments and works out what each change ripples into across the study. Use it when the sponsor wants to widen eligibility, add a dose cohort, change the schedule of assessments, or respond to an emerging safety signal, and someone has to decide whether the change is substantial and what has to be re-approved. It produces the amendment rationale, the change table, and the downstream impact list.
expansions: sponsor wants to widen the eligibility criteria
adding a new dose cohort mid-study
is this a substantial amendment or not
protocol change after a safety signal
sites say the visit schedule is unworkable
country-specific addendum for the german sites
which consent version applies after amendment 3
need a rationale section for the amendment

atoms.obligation: Classify every proposed change as substantial or non-substantial before drafting, because that decides the approval route and the timeline.
atoms.lesson: A change is substantial when it affects participant safety or physical integrity, the scientific value of the trial, or the reliability of the data: new dose levels, a changed primary endpoint, loosened exclusion criteria, a removed safety assessment. Administrative changes such as a new sponsor contact, a corrected typo, or a site address update are non-substantial and only need notification and filing. Misclassifying a substantial change as administrative is one of the most common inspection findings.

atoms.obligation: Trace each change through the consent document, assessment schedule, case report forms, pharmacy manual and monitoring plan before release.
atoms.lesson: Amendments fail in the field when the downstream documents lag. Adding a pharmacokinetic sample means new lab kits, a new collection window in the assessment table, new form fields, and courier instructions. Loosening a laboratory cut-off means the screening checklist and the eligibility form both change. Build a change-control table listing every dependent document, its owner, and its target version so nothing is approved with a stale cross-reference.

atoms.obligation: State the effective date and version, and stop screening under the superseded version once approval is granted at each site.
atoms.lesson: Approval dates differ by country and by ethics committee, so a global amendment goes live in waves. Each site works under its own last-approved version until its own approval letter and any local consent translation are in hand. Screening a participant against amended criteria before local approval creates an eligibility deviation that usually cannot be corrected retrospectively. Keep a per-site matrix of version, approval date, and implementation date.

atoms.obligation: Explain the scientific rationale and the effect on the primary endpoint and the statistical assumptions inside the amendment summary.
atoms.lesson: Reviewers judge an amendment on whether the trial can still answer its question. If eligibility is widened, say how the expected event rate or effect size changes and whether the sample size still holds. If a visit is dropped, say how the endpoint window is preserved.
