Record the noise floor and revisit at the actual shoot hour, because a quiet Sunday recce lies about a Tuesday.

atoms.obligation: Document access, loading distance, lift dimensions, parking and any load-in restrictions the kit truck will face.
atoms.lesson: Measure the walk from the nearest vehicle bay to the room in metres and note stairs, thresholds and door widths, since a lighting flight case will not fit a passenger lift with the diagonal wrong. Check permitted loading hours, congestion or clean-air charges, height barriers on the car park, and whether the venue insists on a goods entrance. This determines crew numbers and whether you need runners for a carry.

atoms.obligation: Confirm in writing who grants permission, what hours are permitted, and what insurance evidence the venue requires.
atoms.lesson: Get the name, mobile and out-of-hours contact of the person who actually holds authority, not the receptionist who said it was probably fine. Most venues want a public liability certificate, commonly five or ten million, before they issue a permit, and councils often need lead time for a street filming notice or a parking suspension. Note curfews, whether the space is shared with the public, and what the venue wants credited.

name: shoot-risk-assessment
description: Produces and reviews the risk assessment a shoot cannot legally or contractually go ahead without. Use when a broadcaster, insurer or venue asks for the paperwork, when the shoot involves height, water, vehicles or vulnerable contributors, or when the plan changes on the day and the assessment needs revisiting.
expansions: risk assessment before we can film
filming beside a live road
working at height for the rig
lone working on a night shoot
insurers want the paperwork
contributor is a vulnerable person
shooting inside a working factory
cable run across a public walkway

atoms.obligation: List each hazard with who could be harmed, the control measures applied, and the risk rating that remains afterwards.
atoms.lesson: The assessment is judged on the control column, not the hazard column. Trailing cable becomes a hazard to public and crew, controlled by matting, taping and a runner on the door, leaving a low residual. Name the person responsible for each control. Generic assessments copied from the last job get rejected by broadcaster safety teams because they do not mention the actual staircase, the actual river or the actual crowd.

atoms.obligation: Escalate high-risk activities to a specialist assessment and competent supervision before anyone commits them to the schedule.
atoms.lesson: Work at height, filming on or near water, moving vehicles, firearms, pyrotechnics, animals and hostile environments all need a named competent person and usually a separate assessment: a rigger with an inspection certificate, a safety boat and rescue swimmer, a stunt coordinator, an armourer. Broadcasters have a mandatory referral list and will pull the shoot if it was not declared at commissioning, so this happens in prep, never on the morning.

atoms.obligation: Brief the whole crew on the assessment at the start of the day and record who attended the briefing.
atoms.lesson: A document nobody read protects nobody. Run a two-minute safety briefing at crew call covering the day's specific hazards, the emergency stop word, the fire assembly point, the first aider and the nearest hospital, then pass round a sheet for signatures. Repeat it for anyone joining late and for each new location. Where contributors are on set, the briefing includes them in plain language.

atoms.obligation: Reassess and reissue whenever the plan changes on the day, before the new activity begins rather than afterwards.
atoms.lesson: The dangerous moment on a shoot is the improvised shot: rain forces the scene into a stairwell, or the director wants the camera on the tailgate of a moving van. Stop, talk it through with the assistant director and the relevant head of department, write the change on the assessment, and get sign-off. Anyone on the crew can halt an unsafe setup, and the paperwork should say so explicitly.

name: camera-kit-spec
description: Specifies the camera package for a shoot: bodies, recording format, lenses, filtration, media and power, sized against the delivery requirement and the shooting day. Use when a rental house needs a kit list, when matching a second camera to the main body, or when working out how many cards and batteries a long day will actually consume.
expansions: what camera package for this job
kit list for the rental house
match a b-camera to the main body
which codec and frame rate
lens set for a tight interior
do we need nd and a matte box
batteries for a twelve hour day
shooting for high dynamic range delivery

atoms.obligation: Choose recording format, resolution and frame rate from the delivery requirement and the grading intent, not from habit.
atoms.lesson: A broadcaster wanting a fifty-frame interlaced or progressive high-definition master in a documentary strand does not need eight-K raw, but a log-encoded ten-bit four-two-two acquisition gives the colourist real latitude in skin tones and windows. Shoot at the delivery frame rate unless the sequence is deliberate slow motion, because mixed rates cause judder through a conversion. Confirm the broadcaster accepts the codec as an acquisition format before the truck leaves.

atoms.obligation: Calculate media and battery capacity against the actual shooting hours and specify spares beyond the calculated figure.
atoms.lesson: Work in gigabytes per minute for the chosen codec, multiply by expected runtime plus a third, and split across enough cards that one is always offloading while another rolls. Large-sensor bodies with an electronic viewfinder, monitor and wireless video draw far more than the body alone, so count the whole rig; plan roughly one high-capacity brick per two hours per camera plus a charger pair on set.

atoms.obligation: Match a second camera to the main body on sensor, colour science and settings and record the matched configuration.
atoms.lesson: Mismatched bodies cost hours in the grade and can never be fully reconciled when the noise structure and highlight rolloff differ. Where budget forces a different model, keep the manufacturer consistent, put both on the same colour space, gamma, white balance and shutter angle, and shoot a colour chart and grey card on both at every lighting change. Log the settings on the camera report so the colourist is not guessing.

atoms.obligation: Include filtration, support, monitoring and consumables in the list instead of only bodies and lenses.
atoms.lesson: The items that stop a shoot are small: variable or graduated neutral density to hold an exterior at a wide aperture, a matte box and flags for lens flare, a follow focus, spare card readers, gaffer and camera tape, lens tissue, rain covers, and a calibrated monitor with the viewing look loaded. Also list the head and legs rated for the built-up weight of the camera, because a light head with a heavy rig is unusable.

name: lighting-plan-design
description: Designs and documents a lighting setup for interviews, studio sets or drama, including instrument positions, ratios, colour temperature and control of the background. Use when planning a rig, when the background is blowing out or skin tones look wrong, when practicals are flickering, or when a look has to be matched to a previous shoot day.
expansions: lighting plan for a two camera interview
background is blowing out
need a soft key for the presenter
practical lamps flickering on camera
mixed daylight and tungsten in the room
studio rig plot for the set
glasses reflecting the key light
match the lighting from yesterday

atoms.obligation: Build the setup as key, fill and separation with stated ratios and a consistent colour temperature across all sources.
atoms.lesson: A conventional interview key sits around forty-five degrees off the lens axis and slightly above eye line, softened through a large source so the shadow edge is gentle. A two-to-one key to fill ratio reads as natural on broadcast, four-to-one as dramatic. Backlight or a hair light lifts the subject off the background at roughly half key. Mixing three-thousand and fifty-six-hundred kelvin sources on one face gives a split colour cast no grade fixes cleanly.

atoms.obligation: Light the background separately from the subject and set its level as a deliberate stop relative to the face.
atoms.lesson: Background exposure is the difference between a flat corporate look and depth. One to two stops under the key reads as moody, half a stop under as clean and modern. Use a separate source with a gobo, or a splash of colour, rather than letting spill from the key do it. Where a window sits behind the subject, either neutral density gel the glass or accept and control the clip, because a blown window pulls the eye.

atoms.obligation: Check every light source and practical for flicker against the camera shutter and frame rate before rolling.
atoms.lesson: Cheap dimmable light-emitting diode fixtures and fluorescent tubes pulse at the mains or driver frequency, so on a fifty-hertz supply a one-fiftieth or one-hundredth shutter is safe while an off-speed shutter or high-speed shooting bands the frame. Older discharge heads need flicker-free ballasts. Test by rolling ten seconds at the intended shutter, scrubbing at full resolution, and if a practical bands, swap the bulb rather than fixing it in post.

atoms.obligation: Record the plot with positions, heights, distances, gel, diffusion and dimmer levels so the setup can be rebuilt exactly.
atoms.lesson: Continuity across days depends on numbers, not memory. Sketch a top-down plot with the subject and camera marked, then list each fixture with its distance and height, the modifier, gel and grid, the output percentage and the colour temperature, plus the exposure reading at the face. Photograph the setup from the camera position. Anyone reshooting a pickup three weeks later can then match a two-shot without re-lighting from scratch.

name: production-sound-plan
description: Plans field and studio sound capture: microphone choice, radio frequency coordination, track layout, levels and timecode. Use when a panel or multi-contributor shoot needs miking, when radio mics are dropping out in a venue, when hum or air conditioning is spoiling recordings, or when sound has to sync with several cameras.
expansions: sound plan for a six person panel
radio mics dropping out in the venue
which frequencies are legal here
boom or lavs for this interview
aircon hum on the recording
timecode across two cameras
backup recorder for the keynote
grab room tone and wild track

atoms.obligation: Scan the venue for interference, coordinate spacing between wireless channels, and log every assigned frequency before the shoot.
atoms.lesson: Run a scan on site at the shoot hour, since a hall is clean in the morning and full of comms and audience phones by transmission. Keep channels off local television transmitter blocks and space them to avoid third-order intermodulation products, which is why coordination software beats guessing. In the United Kingdom the shared channel thirty-eight band needs no licence but is crowded, while cleared channels need a site licence. Carry a wired fallback for the key contributor.

atoms.obligation: Record each contributor on an isolated track alongside a mixed track rather than committing to a mix at source.
atoms.lesson: Isolated tracks let the dubbing mixer fix an overlap, mute a cough or rebalance a quiet speaker weeks later, which a baked mix forbids. On a six-way panel that means six lavalier tracks plus the boom, plus a stereo mix as a safety and a guide for the editor. Name the tracks in the recorder metadata by contributor, not by channel number, because in post nobody knows who was on four.

atoms.obligation: Capture room tone at every location and jam timecode across cameras and recorders at the start of each session.
atoms.lesson: Sixty seconds of room tone with everyone still gives the mixer the glue to cover edits and to sit added lines in the same space; without it, every cut in the dialogue breathes. Jam timecode from a single master at crew call and re-jam every few hours because free-running clocks drift; note the frame rate and whether the cameras are set to record run or free run, and slate the take for a visual fallback.

atoms.obligation: Monitor with headphones throughout and set levels to leave headroom rather than chasing the loudest possible recording.
atoms.lesson: Aim for dialogue averaging around minus twenty decibels full scale with peaks kept below minus six, so a sudden laugh or shout does not clip; digital clipping is unrecoverable, whereas a quiet track lifts cleanly. Listen on closed-back headphones for handling noise, clothing rustle on a lavalier, radio hits and mains hum, and stop the take when you hear it, because the sound department is the only person who will.

name: contributor-release-clearance
description: Manages consent and release paperwork for everyone appearing on camera, including children, vulnerable contributors and members of the public. Use when checking whether a contributor signed, when filming in a sensitive setting such as a hospital or school, when someone asks to withdraw, or when post needs to know which rushes are cleared.
expansions: did that contributor sign a release
child appearing in the film
filming on a hospital ward
public in the background of the shot
contributor wants to withdraw consent
release form for a paid actor
consent for a sensitive interview
rights for online in perpetuity

atoms.obligation: Obtain a signed release before or at recording that names the media, territories and term of the intended use.
atoms.lesson: A release signed after transmission is worth little, and a release covering only broadcast blocks the online catch-up, the promo trail and the international sale. Standard wording grants all media, all territories, in perpetuity, including excerpts and promotion. Where a contributor negotiates a limit, record it precisely and pass it to compliance and the archive, because five years later somebody will license the clip and nobody will remember the carve-out.

atoms.obligation: Secure consent from a parent or guardian for anyone under eighteen and arrange required supervision on the day.
atoms.lesson: Under-eighteens need a signed guardian consent, and in the United Kingdom performance work usually needs a local authority child licence plus a registered chaperone, with strict limits on hours on set and schooling. Filming in a school also needs the head teacher's authority. Never rely on a teacher or coach to consent on a parent's behalf, and check whether any child in the group is subject to a court order or in care, which normally bars identification.

atoms.obligation: Take informed consent for sensitive contributions and agree in advance how a withdrawal request will be handled.
atoms.lesson: Informed means the contributor understood the programme's subject, angle and likely audience, and where the material concerns health, crime, bereavement or abuse that is best evidenced by a note of the conversation as well as the form. Consent can be withdrawn before transmission and broadcasters generally honour it for vulnerable contributors even where the release does not require it. Duty of care includes offering aftercare contacts and warning before transmission.

atoms.obligation: Log every signed form against the rushes and timecodes so the edit can check clearance without re-contacting people.
atoms.lesson: Keep a contributor spreadsheet listing name, shoot date, camera roll, any restrictions, and whether the form is on file, then flag uncleared faces in the offline. Crowd scenes are handled with prominent filming notices at the entrances plus a photograph of the notice in place, which covers incidental members of the public. Anyone who becomes a focus of a shot rather than background needs an individual release.

name: live-show-rundown
description: Builds and retimes the running order for a live or as-live show, with item durations, sources and back timing to the hard out. Use when a rundown is needed for tonight, when the show is running heavy or light, when an item is dropped or a live cross is added, or when the presenter needs an authoritative running order.
expansions: build the rundown for tonight
show is running two minutes heavy
item durations and back timing
add a live cross at the top
what time is the hard out
break pattern for the hour
drop an item and retime
presenter needs the running order

atoms.obligation: Give every item a duration and back-time the whole running order to the hard out from the last item upwards.
atoms.lesson: Forward timing tells you where you should be; back timing tells the director how much trouble they are in. Each item carries an estimated duration, and the rundown shows the clock time it must start to make the hard out, which for a networked programme is a fixed junction that will be taken from you regardless. Live interviews should carry a target and a minimum, so the presenter can wrap in fifteen seconds when the floor manager cues.

atoms.obligation: Mark each item as fixed or droppable and rank the droppable ones in the order they will be sacrificed.
atoms.lesson: Live shows never run to time, so the rundown must already contain the decision. Fixed items are the ones with a contractual or editorial reason to exist: the lead story, a live guest booked to the minute, the sponsor bumper. Droppables are typically a soft feature, a second look at the weather or a discussion segment that can lose ninety seconds. Agree the order in the production meeting, not through the talkback at nineteen fifty-eight.

atoms.obligation: Name the source, format and transition for every item so the gallery and operators can pre-set ahead of the cut.
atoms.lesson: Each row should say where the pictures and sound come from: studio camera, a server clip with its identifier and duration, a remote line with the contributor's location, graphics with the template name and text status, and whether the item ends on a countdown or runs out to black. The director builds the switcher memories from that. An item marked simply as VT with no identifier is how the wrong clip goes to air.

atoms.obligation: Maintain a single authoritative version of the rundown and communicate every change to every position that acts on it.
atoms.lesson: The rundown is read by the director, vision mixer, sound supervisor, autocue operator, floor manager, graphics and the presenter, and a change to item order silently breaks all of them. Number versions, timestamp them, and announce changes verbally as well as on screen. In the last thirty minutes before air, changes should be made by one named person only, with the others reading back the amendment.

name: gallery-comms-plan
description: Plans talkback, in-ear feeds, tally and return video for a studio or gallery operation. Use when setting up comms for a new show, when a presenter cannot hear the director, when camera operators are on the wrong ring, when tally lights are not following the cut, or when a remote guest needs a clean feed.
expansions: talkback setup for the studio
presenter cannot hear the director
who needs an earpiece
tally not following the cut
camera ops on the wrong ring
in ear feed for the remote guest
clean feed for the guest
comms plan for two galleries

atoms.obligation: Assign every role to a named talkback ring and state who can talk to whom and who is switched-talk only.
atoms.lesson: Camera operators normally sit on a director ring with open listen and switched talk, so the director's instructions are constant but a chatty operator does not fill the channel. Sound, vision engineering and graphics each carry their own partyline plus the director. The floor manager is the only person who should hear both the director and the studio floor. Write the matrix down; a comms plan discovered during rehearsal costs the first hour.

atoms.obligation: Feed talent an in-ear mix that carries programme sound minus their own voice plus director cue.
atoms.lesson: A presenter hearing their own voice delayed by the processing chain cannot speak fluently, so the earpiece takes a mix-minus: programme audio with that presenter's microphone removed, with talkback ducked over it. Remote contributors on a delayed line need the same treatment or they will talk over the studio. Check the mix-minus by asking each contributor to count aloud and confirming they hear nothing of themselves before the show opens.

atoms.obligation: Verify that tally and return video map correctly to the switcher inputs before rehearsal rather than during it.
atoms.lesson: Tally tells the operator they are live and the presenter which lens to address, and a crossed mapping puts a red light on camera two while camera three is on air, which sends the presenter's eyeline to the wrong place on transmission. Cut to every source in turn and have each position confirm out loud. Check return video too, since operators framing off a stale return will not see their own shot being tightened.

atoms.obligation: Run a full comms check with every position before rehearsal and agree the fallback if a channel fails on air.
atoms.lesson: Go around the horn: each camera, sound, lighting, graphics, autocue, floor manager, presenter, and any remote site, in order, confirming both directions. Note who has a spare earpiece and pack a wired fallback. Agree the hand signals the floor manager will use if talkback dies entirely, typically wind up, stretch, cut, and a countdown on fingers, because that is the only channel that survives a comms failure mid-show.

name: outside-broadcast-signal-path
description: Designs and documents the signal path for a remote or outside broadcast, from camera positions through the truck to the contribution link back to base. Use when planning a remote site, when working out how the feed gets home and what the backup is, when cameras will not genlock, or when latency between site and studio is causing problems.
expansions: signal path for the remote site
cable run from pitch to truck
how are we getting the feed back
backup route if the link drops
power supply for the truck
cameras will not genlock
latency between site and studio
audio embedded or on separate pairs

atoms.obligation: Document the path end to end, naming format, connector and level at every hop from source to output.
atoms.lesson: Write it as a chain: camera head, fibre or triax to base station, serial digital output at three gigabits for high frame rate, into the router input, out to the switcher, embedded audio on pairs one and two with commentary on three and four. The value of the diagram appears at two in the morning when a picture is missing and someone has to work out which of eleven boxes is not passing it.

atoms.obligation: Provide a physically separate backup contribution route home and rehearse the switchover before the event starts.
atoms.lesson: A single fibre circuit fails when a contractor puts a digger through the duct, so the standard is a primary fibre with a bonded cellular or microwave secondary on a different physical path and, where possible, a different carrier. Test both under load, not idle, because a cellular bond that looks fine on a deserted pitch collapses when forty thousand people fill the stands. Agree with base who calls the switch and on which telephone number.

atoms.obligation: Lock all video sources to a common reference and check timing so switching between them does not disturb the picture.
atoms.lesson: Cameras, servers, graphics and remote feeds must be genlocked to a shared reference or the switcher will glitch on the cut. Sources arriving from elsewhere are usually frame synchronised on the way in, which costs a frame or two of delay and pushes lip sync out; measure it and compensate the audio rather than trusting the label. Check the reference distribution has a backup generator, since losing it takes every source at once.

atoms.obligation: Label both ends of every cable and record the patch so a fault can be traced without following the run by hand.
atoms.lesson: On a stadium rig with three hundred metres of cable in the stands, an unlabelled tail is an hour lost. Number each drum and camera position, label at the plug and at the panel, and keep a patch sheet showing every router input and output with its source. Test each run with a signal before the crew disperses. Record where cables cross public routes so the matting and the safety documentation match reality.

name: sports-replay-workflow
description: Sets up replay and highlights operation for a live sporting event: angle assignment, isolated recording, clip logging and delivery of packages during the event. Use when planning replay positions for a match, when deciding who owns which angle, when officials need a review feed, or when a highlights package is due at the interval.
expansions: replay setup for the match
operator on the reverse angle
clipping highlights during play
super slow motion camera assignment
feed for the referee review
how many angles into the server
highlights package at half time
log the goals as they happen

atoms.obligation: Assign each replay operator specific camera angles and record every camera in isolation for the full event.
atoms.lesson: A typical football rig gives one operator the high wide and halfway tight, another the two eighteen-yard cameras, and a third the super slow motion behind the goal. Each operator cues from their own angles so nobody is hunting the same record train. Isolated recording of every camera for the whole match, not just around incidents, is what allows a foul three minutes earlier to be found when the referee stops play.

atoms.obligation: Log clips as events happen using a consistent naming convention with player, action and match clock.
atoms.lesson: Logging in play is what makes a half-time package possible in six minutes. Use a fixed pattern such as minute, team, player surname, action, so a search for a name pulls every touch. Mark goals, cards, saves, near misses and injuries as they occur, with the best angle noted, because scrubbing back through ninety minutes of isolated feeds during the interval never works. The logger sits beside the producer cutting the package.

atoms.obligation: Agree who calls a replay to air and what the cue protocol is so replays never collide with live action.
atoms.lesson: The director owns air, but the replay producer offers, typically over talkback with the angle and the length: reverse angle, four seconds, ready. Replays go only in dead time such as after a stoppage, and the standing rule is to bail out the moment play restarts, since missing a live goal for a replay of a throw-in is the classic sin. Officials' review feeds go out on a dedicated path with no graphics.

atoms.obligation: Protect and export match highlights while recording continues rather than waiting until the event finishes.
atoms.lesson: Servers on a long event can wrap and overwrite, so clips destined for highlights, news access and rights holders must be protected as they are cut and pushed to shared storage. Rights deals usually oblige delivery of near-live clips within a stated window, often ninety seconds for a goal. Keep a running edit assembled through the match so the post-match package needs only a top and tail rather than a build from nothing.

name: media-offload-ingest
description: Handles the transfer of camera and sound media from cards into a verified, organised media store, with reports and proxies for the edit. Use when cards come back from a shoot, when a card is reporting errors, when the offline needs proxies, or when somebody asks how much footage the day actually produced.
expansions: cards from the shoot need offloading
verified copies to two drives
media report for the shoot day
proxies for the offline edit
card is showing read errors
naming convention for the rushes
sound files alongside camera clips
how much did we shoot today

atoms.obligation: Copy every card to at least two separate destinations with checksum verification before anyone touches the original media.
atoms.lesson: A straight drag and drop can silently drop or corrupt files, so use a copy tool that reads back and compares a checksum for every file, and keep the verification report. Two destinations means two physically separate drives, ideally with one leaving the location that night or going to cloud, because a single case containing both copies is one taxi away from a total loss. Report a mismatch immediately, while the scene can still be reshot.

atoms.obligation: Never reformat a card until the verified copies exist and the shoot has confirmed the material is safe.
atoms.lesson: The card is the third copy and the only one that still holds the original bits. Keep cards full until the media is on two verified drives and, on a longer shoot, until it has been checked in the edit. Format in camera rather than on a computer so the file system matches the body, label full cards clearly with tape, and keep them physically separated from blank ones to stop an assistant grabbing the wrong one.

atoms.obligation: Apply one folder and file naming convention across camera, sound and every shoot day of the production.
atoms.lesson: A workable pattern is production, shoot day, unit, camera letter and roll number, so a clip is traceable from an edit bin back to the physical card. Keep sound rolls parallel to camera rolls and stored alongside, never buried inside a camera folder. Preserve the camera's own folder structure intact, since sidecar metadata, look-up tables and clip spanning break when someone rearranges the contents by hand.

atoms.obligation: Generate edit proxies and a written report listing clip counts, total duration and any errors or unusable takes.
atoms.lesson: Proxies at a light codec let the editor start on a laptop while the originals stay on the shared store. The daily report is what the producer reads: cards offloaded, total runtime and file size, frame rate and codec confirmed, plus flagged problems such as a dropped frame, a focus miss the operator called, or a clip that failed verification. Attach the camera and sound reports and the circled takes from the day.

name: edit-assembly-notes
description: Structures viewing notes on a rough cut or assembly and turns them into a workable revision list for the editor. Use after a screening with an executive or client, when the cut is over duration, when the opening is not holding attention, or when notes from several people contradict each other.
expansions: notes on the rough cut
film is four minutes over
the opening does not grab
viewing session with the exec
which sequence to lose for time
two people gave contradictory notes
the interview keeps repeating itself
structure sags in the middle

atoms.obligation: Anchor every note to a timecode and state the problem and intent rather than dictating the fix.
atoms.lesson: A note reading at four minutes twelve the reason she left is still unclear tells the editor what to solve; a note reading cut to the wide there removes their judgement and often creates two new problems. Watch the whole cut once without stopping before writing anything, then a second pass making notes, because notes taken cold in the first five minutes usually describe a setup that pays off later.

atoms.obligation: Separate structural notes from polish notes and resolve the structure before anyone works on frame-level detail.
atoms.lesson: Structural notes move, cut or reorder whole sequences and invalidate any fine cutting inside them, so asking for a music change or a trim on a specific cut during an assembly viewing wastes the work. Order the pass as: does the story hold, is the running order right, is each sequence earning its place, then only afterwards pacing, sound and picture detail. Say explicitly which stage the cut is at when circulating it.

atoms.obligation: Reconcile contradictory notes into one prioritised list with a named decision-maker before sending anything to the editor.
atoms.lesson: An editor given the executive's note to lose the archive and the producer's note to expand it will either stall or pick a side and be wrong. Collate notes into a single document, mark conflicts explicitly, and get a decision from whoever holds editorial authority, usually the commissioning editor or series producer. Group by sequence rather than by who said it, so the editor works through the film once instead of jumping about.

atoms.obligation: State the target duration and identify specifically where the time will be recovered from.
atoms.lesson: Broadcast slots are unforgiving: a fifty-eight minute forty second programme cannot deliver at sixty-one and be trimmed at transmission. Time comes out of whole sequences far more cleanly than from thirty frames a cut, so identify the two weakest sequences and the repeated point that appears in both act two and act three. A rough guide is that trimming alone recovers perhaps five percent, while removing a strand recovers real minutes.

name: online-conform-turnover
description: Prepares a locked offline for online conform, grade, visual effects and the audio mix, so the finishing suite can relink to camera originals without surprises. Use when picture is locked, when a conform comes up with missing clips, when effects shots need pulling with handles, or when a change comes in after turnover.
expansions: turn over the offline for online
relinking back to camera originals
conform has missing clips
list of effects shots with handles
sending the sequence to the mix
speed ramps not translating
titles and graphics for the online
picture changed after we locked

atoms.obligation: Lock picture formally and issue a written change list for any alteration made after the lock.
atoms.lesson: Picture lock is a contract with the finishing departments: the colourist, mixer and effects artists all start work assuming frame counts are fixed. When a late change is unavoidable, publish a change note listing each affected sequence with old and new timecodes and durations, so the mixer can conform the audio session rather than reopening it blind. Silent recuts after lock are the single most common cause of a mix arriving out of sync.

atoms.obligation: Export a turnover that carries source clip identifiers, reel names and frame rates alongside the edit decisions.
atoms.lesson: Relinking depends on the metadata matching what is on the original media: reel or clip name, source timecode, and a consistent frame rate throughout. Mixed frame rates, renamed rushes and clips that were transcoded without carrying source timecode all break the conform. Send both an edit decision list and a richer sequence file, plus a reference movie with burned-in timecode and clip names so anything ambiguous can be resolved by eye.

atoms.obligation: Flag and document every effect, resize, retime or stabilisation that will not translate between systems.
atoms.lesson: Offline speed ramps, corner pins, warp stabilisation and third-party plug-in looks rarely survive the move to a finishing system and quietly reconform as straight cuts. List them by timecode with a description and a still, and where an effect is essential, render a self-contained clip from the offline as a reference. Supply visual effects pulls with handles, typically twelve to twenty-four frames each side, since a shot trimmed to the frame cannot be repositioned later.

atoms.obligation: Deliver the audio turnover with a guide mix and a matching reference picture carrying burned-in timecode.
atoms.lesson: The mixer needs the full audio session with every original track, not the offline's flattened stereo, plus the guide mix to hear the intended balance and any temp music. The reference movie must be the same length as the turnover, start at the same timecode, and carry a two-pop or leader so sync can be proved at frame one. Include a music and effects requirement note if the deal calls for a separate international track.

name: colour-grade-brief
description: Prepares the brief and the technical groundwork for a colour grade, covering matching, look references, legal broadcast levels and versioning for different display standards. Use when cameras do not match, when skin tones look wrong, when a broadcaster rejects levels, or when both a high dynamic range and a standard version are required.
expansions: grade brief for the documentary
two cameras do not match
skin tones look green
reference stills from the director
shot in log, need a viewing look
broadcaster rejected our levels
night scenes crushed to black
hdr and sdr versions needed

atoms.obligation: Balance and match every shot within a scene before applying any creative look to the sequence.
atoms.lesson: Grading runs in two passes. The first neutralises: set exposure and contrast from the waveform, correct white balance against a known reference such as a grey card or a white shirt, and match the second camera and any reverse to the master shot. Only then does the look go on top, usually as a grade applied across the scene. Applying the look first hides mismatch that reappears the moment anyone adjusts the shot.

atoms.obligation: Check the graded picture on scopes against the delivery standard's legal range rather than judging by eye alone.
atoms.lesson: Broadcasters reject masters for illegal levels, typically luminance outside the range the standard permits or chroma excursions from saturated reds and blues in graphics and clothing. Read the waveform and vectorscope continuously, watch for super-white peaks in specular highlights and blown windows, and keep an eye on the gamut display. Grade on a calibrated reference monitor in a controlled viewing environment, since a bright room drags every scene darker than intended.

atoms.obligation: Agree a viewing look on the shoot and carry the same reference through dailies into the grade.
atoms.lesson: Log or raw acquisition looks flat and unappealing on set, so a viewing look-up table is loaded into the monitor and the same file travels to dailies and to the colourist as the starting point, together with the camera reports and any chart shots. This stops the director seeing a lively image on set, a grey one in the edit, and a third interpretation in the grade. Photograph reference frames and keep them with the brief.

atoms.obligation: Create each display-standard version by trimming from a single master grade rather than regrading from scratch.
atoms.lesson: Where a high dynamic range and a standard dynamic range deliverable are both required, the usual workflow grades the wide dynamic range master, then performs a trim pass for the standard version, adjusting highlight rolloff and mid-tone placement so faces sit at a comfortable level. Two independent grades drift apart under notes and double the change work. Confirm which is the contractual master and which is derived before starting, because the broadcaster's spec dictates it.

name: broadcast-loudness-mix
description: Gets a programme mix to meet the broadcaster's loudness and peak requirements while keeping dialogue intelligible. Use when a master is rejected for loudness, when dialogue is buried under music, when true peak is over the ceiling, or when stereo and surround versions plus stems are needed for delivery.
expansions: mix rejected for loudness
dialogue buried under the music
true peak over the limit
what loudness target for this channel
stereo and surround versions
the ad break is louder than the show
measure the whole programme
stems needed for the delivery

atoms.obligation: Mix to the specified integrated loudness target measured across the whole programme, not to a peak meter.
atoms.lesson: European delivery generally means minus twenty-three loudness units full scale integrated with a true-peak ceiling of minus one decibel, while North American practice is minus twenty-four with a two-decibel ceiling. Integrated measurement is gated and covers the entire programme, so a quiet twenty minutes lets a loud finale sit higher. Check the loudness range too, since a compliant average with an extreme range fails on a domestic set and prompts viewer complaints.

atoms.obligation: Protect dialogue intelligibility by shaping music and effects around speech instead of compressing the whole mix.
atoms.lesson: Dialogue is the load-bearing element, so ride music down under speech, carve a small dip around the two to four kilohertz region where consonants live, and keep reverb and low-frequency rumble from masking it. Heavy full-mix compression to hit a number flattens dynamics and makes speech less clear, not more. Audiences complain about mumbling far more than about quiet music, and older viewers and small television speakers make the problem worse.

atoms.obligation: Deliver stems and a music and effects version alongside the full mix so the programme can be revoiced.
atoms.lesson: International sales and audio description both depend on separate elements: dialogue, music and effects as discrete stems at matching lengths and start timecodes, plus a full music and effects mix with no dialogue. Any narration or on-screen text that carries story information must exist in the effects or as a separate element so a foreign version can replace it. Building stems is cheap during the mix and expensive to reconstruct afterwards.

atoms.obligation: Audition the finished mix on small and limited playback systems before signing it off for delivery.
atoms.lesson: The mix is judged in a treated room on full-range monitors, but it is heard on a flat-panel television, a laptop and a phone. Check on a single small speaker and at low level: bass-heavy music disappears, sibilance sharpens and quiet dialogue vanishes entirely. Check the mono fold-down too, since phase problems in a stereo music bed can hollow it out. Fix by rebalancing rather than by pushing the overall level up.

name: subtitle-caption-qc
description: Checks and corrects subtitle and caption files against broadcast access requirements: timing, reading speed, line layout, speaker identification and file format. Use when captions drift out of sync, when a subtitle file fails technical checks, when text collides with on-screen graphics, or when subtitles are being prepared for another market.
expansions: captions out of sync with speech
subtitle file failed qc
reading speed is too fast
speaker labels are missing
burned in versus sidecar file
captioning a live programme
subtitles covering the graphic
translate subtitles for another market

atoms.obligation: Time each caption to the speech it covers and align its in and out points to shot changes where possible.
atoms.lesson: A caption should appear as the speaker starts, within a few frames, and clear when they stop, holding a minimum of about one second even for a single word. Captions that cross a cut make the viewer re-read, so snap the boundary to the shot change or hold through it deliberately. On pre-recorded programmes the tolerance is tight; on live output a delay of several seconds is accepted but must not run into the next item.

atoms.obligation: Enforce reading speed, line length and lines per caption so viewers can finish reading before the text clears.
atoms.lesson: Common broadcast guidance caps reading speed near one hundred and sixty to one hundred and eighty words per minute for adult programming and lower for children's, with a maximum of two lines, around thirty-seven characters each. Break lines at natural syntactic points, keeping an article with its noun and a verb with its object, rather than filling to the character limit. Where speech is too fast, edit the text for sense rather than dropping the caption.

atoms.obligation: Identify who is speaking and describe sound that carries meaning for viewers who cannot hear it.
atoms.lesson: Off-screen or ambiguous speakers need a label or a colour convention, commonly white, yellow, cyan and green assigned to the main voices and held consistently through the programme. Non-speech information matters: a doorbell, a gunshot off screen, music with lyrics that comment on the action, a sarcastic tone. Write these in brackets and only where they affect understanding, since captioning every ambient noise clutters the screen and slows reading.

atoms.obligation: Position captions to avoid burned-in text and validate the file against the delivery specification before sending.
atoms.lesson: Captions default to the lower centre, but must move to the top when they would cover a name strap, subtitles already burned in, scoreboard or credits. Check the file type the broadcaster demands, whether a timed-text file or embedded data, along with the frame rate and whether the timecode starts at ten hours to match the master. A file that reads correctly in one player and not another usually has a frame rate mismatch.

name: audio-description-script
description: Writes and times audio description for blind and partially sighted viewers, fitting description into the gaps in dialogue and prioritising what the story depends on. Use when a series needs description delivered, when an opening sequence is dense with visual information, when on-screen text goes unspoken, or when the description mix is fighting the programme audio.
expansions: audio description for the series
gaps in dialogue for description
describe the on screen text
how much description in the opening
blind viewer cannot follow the plot
describing a character's appearance
description mix against programme audio
which visuals are essential to describe

atoms.obligation: Write description only into gaps where no dialogue or story-critical sound is playing, timed to the measured gap length.
atoms.lesson: Never speak over dialogue, a punchline, a scream or a musical cue that carries the moment. Measure each gap in seconds and write to it: roughly three words per second is comfortable, so a two-second gap holds about six words. Where the gap is a second or less, drop the description rather than rushing it. Long dialogue-free title sequences and landscapes are where the real information can be delivered unhurried.

atoms.obligation: Prioritise the visual information the plot depends on over decorative detail when description time is scarce.
atoms.lesson: With limited gaps, describe what changes the viewer's understanding: who entered the room, where the scene has moved to, that a character pockets the key, that someone is lying. Costume, decor and weather come only when time allows or when they carry meaning, such as a black armband. Introduce a character by name at the point the audience learns it, and use a consistent descriptor beforehand, for instance the man in the grey coat.

atoms.obligation: Read out on-screen text, captions, locations and credits that are never spoken in the programme audio.
atoms.lesson: Location supers, dates, name straps, text messages, signs the camera lingers on, and the closing credit block all carry information that is otherwise lost. Read them verbatim and at the moment they appear. Where a programme is heavily reliant on text, such as a documentary using archive documents, agree with the producer which items are essential, because reading everything leaves no room to describe the pictures around them.

atoms.obligation: Mix the description to sit clearly above the programme without masking dialogue or key effects underneath it.
atoms.lesson: The description track is usually recorded dry in a booth and mixed with the programme ducked a few decibels beneath it, enough for clarity without the audience losing the atmosphere. Delivery is either a separate description audio track or a pre-mixed version, depending on the broadcaster's specification, alongside the description script as a timed file. Voice choice matters: neutral, unhurried, and distinct from the programme's own narrator so the two never blur.

name: editorial-compliance-review
description: Reviews a programme against broadcast editorial rules before transmission: scheduling suitability, fairness, commercial references, harm and offence. Use when a cut needs compliance sign-off, when deciding whether material is acceptable before the watershed, when someone is criticised on air and needs a right of reply, or when a brand is unavoidably prominent.
expansions: compliance check before transmission
is this suitable pre watershed
we name a company in the film
right of reply for the accused
strong language in the interview
flashing images in the sequence
impartiality on a contested subject
product on screen looks like advertising

atoms.obligation: Assess the material against the intended transmission slot and flag anything needing a warning, a later slot or an edit.
atoms.lesson: In the United Kingdom the nine o'clock watershed governs the most obvious cases, but expectation of the audience matters as much as the clock: a daytime strand carries stricter limits than a post-watershed documentary. The strongest language, sexual content, drug use shown without context and detailed method in suicide or self-harm all need referral. Where material stays, an accurate pre-transmission warning that names the issue gives the viewer a real choice.

atoms.obligation: Offer a fair and timely opportunity to respond to anyone facing significant criticism, and record what was offered.
atoms.lesson: Fairness rules require that a person or organisation accused of wrongdoing hears the specific allegations, not a vague summary, with enough time to reply, commonly measured in days rather than hours for a complex claim. Keep the letter, the deadline given and any reply on file, and represent the response fairly in the cut. A no comment must be reported accurately. This is the most common ground on which broadcast complaints are upheld.

atoms.obligation: Check for undue prominence of products, brands and services and confirm any commercial arrangement is properly signalled.
atoms.lesson: Editorial content must not promote. A branded label filling frame, repeated verbal mentions, or a contributor's business plugged without editorial reason all count as undue prominence, and the usual fixes are reframing, blurring or a line of commentary that justifies the reference. Where there is a genuine commercial arrangement such as product placement or sponsorship, it must be declared, signalled on screen where required, and kept out of news and current affairs.

atoms.obligation: Test the picture for flashing and pattern risk and log every issue with its timecode and a proposed remedy.
atoms.lesson: Rapid flashing above roughly three flashes per second, or strong regular stripe and grid patterns, can trigger photosensitive seizures, and material is normally machine-tested before delivery with failures either graded down, slowed or replaced. Deliver the compliance review as a timecoded list, each row stating the issue, the rule engaged, the recommendation and who decides. A verbal note that the third act needs a look at does not survive to the transmission edit.

name: music-cue-clearance
description: Clears music for a production and documents every cue for the broadcaster. Use when deciding whether a commercial track is affordable, when music is playing behind an interview, when clearance must cover online as well as broadcast, or when a cue sheet is required at delivery.
expansions: can we use this track in the film
library music or commercial track
cue sheet for the broadcaster
music behind an interview
clearance for online as well as broadcast
cost to clear a famous song
brief a composer for original score
track cleared in one territory only

atoms.obligation: Clear the recording and the underlying composition separately, matching each licence to the media, territory and term needed.
atoms.lesson: Two rights sit in every commercial track: the master, controlled by the record label, and the publishing, controlled by the songwriter's publisher, and both must be licensed for the same scope or the track is unusable. A licence for United Kingdom broadcast does not cover the streaming catch-up, the international sale or the promo. Library music is simpler because one licence covers both, which is why most factual output leans on it.

atoms.obligation: Record every cue with its timecode, exact duration, usage type and rights holders as the edit proceeds.
atoms.lesson: The cue sheet is a delivery requirement and the mechanism by which composers and publishers are paid, so it lists each cue's title, composer, publisher, performing rights society, precise in and out timecodes to the second, duration, and whether the use is background, featured, theme or visual vocal. Build it in the edit rather than reconstructing it at the end, because a fifty-minute documentary can carry forty cues and the durations change with every recut.

atoms.obligation: Treat music heard incidentally in a recording as requiring clearance or removal, not as accidental and therefore free.
atoms.lesson: A radio in a kitchen, a shop playlist, a marching band, a ringtone or a wedding first dance all appear in the finished programme and all need licensing. Prevent it at source by asking for music to be turned off before rolling, which also protects continuity in the edit. Where it cannot be avoided, note it on the sound report and hand it to the edit as a flagged issue so it is either cleared, replaced or mixed out.

atoms.obligation: Establish the cost and lead time for any commercial track before it is cut into the film and keep an alternative ready.
atoms.lesson: A well-known song can cost tens of thousands per side and take weeks to clear, and either rights holder can simply refuse, particularly if the programme's subject matter is contentious. Get a quote against the actual usage before the editor builds a sequence to it, because a temp track becomes emotionally locked in the room. Always carry a second choice and, on a tight budget, brief a composer for an original cue instead.

name: archive-footage-licensing
description: Sources third-party footage and stills and manages the licences, credits and technical handling that come with them. Use when a documentary needs news archive or a film clip, when footage came from social media, when an archive owner requires specific credit wording, or when a licence term is about to expire.
expansions: news archive for the documentary
clip from a feature film
how many seconds are we licensing
footage taken from social media
credit wording for the archive owner
standard definition archive in an hd film
rights expire in five years
find a shot of the city in the seventies

atoms.obligation: Log each archive item with its owner, source reference, exact duration used and the terms actually granted.
atoms.lesson: Archive libraries price by the second and by the scope, so a log listing owner, library reference, in and out points, seconds used, media, territory and term is the only defence against a bill computed on the whole reel. Track stills separately, since photographic rights often sit with an agency and the photographer. Keep the licence document itself with the log, because the invoice is not the licence and does not record the restrictions.

atoms.obligation: Clear archive before picture lock and keep any unlicensed use inside a defensible fair dealing or fair use argument.
atoms.lesson: Clearing after the cut is built means paying whatever is asked or recutting under deadline. Limited unlicensed use is possible in some jurisdictions for criticism, review, quotation or news reporting, but it is narrow: the extract must be no longer than needed, genuinely commented on rather than used for illustration, and properly attributed. That judgement belongs to the broadcaster's lawyers before delivery, and errors and omissions insurance depends on it.

atoms.obligation: Obtain a broadcast-quality master of every clip rather than finishing with a watermarked viewing copy.
atoms.lesson: Libraries supply low-resolution screeners with burned-in identification for the offline and release the master only once the licence is signed and paid, so budget the time for that exchange before the online. Older material may arrive as standard definition or at a different frame rate, needing conversion, upscaling and often reframing from four by three, which the colourist should handle deliberately rather than the finishing system stretching it automatically.

atoms.obligation: Apply the required on-screen credit wording exactly and diarise the expiry date of every time-limited licence.
atoms.lesson: Contracts frequently specify the courtesy credit's wording, placement and minimum duration, and getting it wrong is a breach even when the fee is paid. Many archive licences run for a fixed term such as five or seven years, or for a limited number of transmissions, after which the programme cannot legally be shown or streamed until renewed. Hand the schedule of expiries to the broadcaster and the production company's rights records at delivery.

name: delivery-spec-qc
description: Prepares and checks the finished master against a broadcaster's delivery specification, covering programme structure, durations, audio layout, textless elements and technical quality control. Use when a master has been rejected, when building the delivery checklist, when the programme runs over slot duration, or before sending a file to a broadcaster.
expansions: broadcaster rejected the master
what is in the delivery spec
textless elements at the tail
audio track layout for delivery
bars and tone at the head
programme is over slot duration
check the file before we send
slate and part clock details

atoms.obligation: Read the delivery specification first and turn it into a checklist covering every technical and editorial deliverable.
atoms.lesson: Specifications run to dozens of pages and cover far more than the video file: the master itself, textless elements, music cue sheet, subtitle and description files, programme-as-completed form, compliance notes, credits list, stills and metadata. Build the checklist at the start of post, not the week of delivery, because items like the programme-as-completed form and the cue sheet need information gathered throughout production and cannot be reconstructed at the end.

atoms.obligation: Lay the master to the required leader, slate, part structure and durations, including any breaks between parts.
atoms.lesson: A typical broadcast master starts at ten hours less a minute of bars and tone, carries a slate identifying the programme, episode, duration, audio layout and aspect ratio, counts down to programme start at ten hours exactly, and holds specified black between parts for the commercial breaks. Slot duration is contractual to the second. Textless elements, meaning shots without straps or captions, sit at the tail after a stated gap for foreign versioning.

atoms.obligation: Map audio to the exact track layout the specification demands and confirm each track carries what its label claims.
atoms.lesson: A common layout puts the stereo full mix on tracks one and two, the music and effects on three and four, and where surround is required, six discrete channels in a stated order, with the description or a clean commentary elsewhere. Listen to every track individually before delivery: a music and effects track that still has dialogue, or a swapped left and right, is a rejection. Confirm the loudness of each deliverable mix independently.

atoms.obligation: Run an automated quality check and a full human viewing, then fix the faults rather than disputing the report.
atoms.lesson: Automated checks catch illegal levels, gamut errors, photosensitive flashing, black frames, freeze frames, loudness failures and file wrapper problems, but they cannot see a missing name strap, a spelling error in the credits, a dropped subtitle or a shot that never got its effect. Watch the finished master end to end in real time with someone who has not lived in the edit, and keep the quality report with the delivery record.

name: mic-placement-tracking
description: Chooses microphones and positions them for a source in the room you actually have, then diagnoses the tone or bleed problem you hear back. Use when someone is about to track drums, vocals, acoustic guitar, horns or a guitar cabinet and wants a starting placement. Also use when a recorded take sounds boxy, thin, phasey or full of headphone bleed.
expansions: drum kit sounds boxy in overheads
where to put the mic on a cab
acoustic guitar take sounds thin
vocal take is too sibilant
snare bleed all over the hat mic
setting up a room mic for drums
picking a mic for a baritone singer
two mics on one source phasing

atoms.obligation: Check every multi-microphone setup for phase agreement before recording, flipping polarity and moving mics until the combined tone is fullest.
atoms.lesson: Two mics on one source comb filter when their path lengths differ. The three to one rule keeps bleed down: the second mic sits at least three times the source distance away. On a snare, top and bottom mics are almost always opposite polarity because the bottom head moves away from the top, so flipping the bottom restores the low mids. On a cabinet, close and room mics often need a millisecond nudge to keep the 100 to 250 Hz region intact.

atoms.obligation: Move the microphone before reaching for equalization, treating position as the first tone control on any source.
atoms.lesson: A dynamic mic on a guitar speaker changes character across three inches: dead centre on the dust cap is bright and aggressive, halfway to the cone edge is rounder, at the edge it is dark. On acoustic guitar, aiming at the twelfth fret gives balanced string detail while pointing at the soundhole gives boomy low mids around 100 to 200 Hz. Distance controls proximity bass buildup on any cardioid mic.

atoms.obligation: Match the microphone pattern and type to the room and the source dynamics rather than to the price of the mic.
atoms.lesson: Condensers capture detail but overload on loud transients unless padded, typically by 10 or 20 dB. Ribbons roll off the high end naturally, which tames a harsh amp, but they need a preamp with high gain and high input impedance and they hate wind blasts from kick drums. Omnidirectional patterns have no proximity effect and sound natural up close, but they capture the whole room, so use them only where the room sounds good.

atoms.obligation: Set the singer up with a pop filter, a stable working distance and a headphone level that does not leak into the take.
atoms.lesson: Plosives hit the capsule as a burst of air rather than sound, and no equalizer removes them cleanly. A filter four to six inches from the grille plus a slightly off axis angle prevents most of them. Singers drift closer as they get quiet, so proximity effect lifts the low end exactly when the level drops. Closed back headphones at a moderate level stop click and mix bleed printing under sustained notes.

name: gain-staging-headroom
description: Sets recording and internal levels so nothing clips, converters and plugins sit in their useful range, and the mix keeps room to breathe. Use when takes are peaking red, when a mix is crushed before any processing is added, or when someone asks what level to print at. Also use when imported stems are so hot that the mix bus distorts.
expansions: takes are clipping the interface
what level should i record at
mix is peaking before mastering
imported stems are way too hot
preamp gain versus fader confusion
plugins sound harsh when driven hard
master bus is red every chorus
quiet take with loud noise floor

atoms.obligation: Record with peaks around minus twelve to minus six decibels full scale and leave the loudest transients well below zero.
atoms.lesson: Twenty four bit recording offers about 144 dB of theoretical dynamic range, so chasing the top of the meter buys nothing but risk. Peaks near minus 12 to minus 6 dBFS keep intersample overs away and land analogue modelled plugins near their calibration point, usually minus 18 dBFS equals zero VU. Drum transients read far higher than a slow peak meter shows, so leave at least 6 dB of margin for a hard hit.

atoms.obligation: Set the preamp for tone and the fader for balance, never using a fader to fix a distorted input.
atoms.lesson: Clipping at the input is baked into the file and nothing downstream undoes it. The preamp decides how hard the input stage runs, which is a tone choice on tube and transformer designs and a noise choice on clean ones. A ribbon or other passive source may need 55 to 65 dB of gain, while a hot keyboard output may need a pad. Faders after conversion only scale an already fixed digital signal.

atoms.obligation: Restore mix bus headroom by trimming every channel together rather than by pulling the master fader down.
atoms.lesson: Pulling the master fader down leaves every channel plugin still overdriven and the internal balance still wrong. Grouping all channels and trimming them as one preserves relative levels while recovering headroom. Floating point mix engines tolerate internal overs, but fixed point plugins, analogue emulations and the final print stage do not. Aim for a mix bus peak near minus 6 dBFS so the mastering stage still has somewhere to work.

atoms.obligation: Compare processed and unprocessed versions at matched loudness rather than by peak meter whenever judging a change.
atoms.lesson: Louder reads as better for about ten seconds, which is why almost every compressor and saturator sounds like an improvement until levels are matched. Match by short term loudness or by ear on a sustained section, then bypass. A limiter adding 3 dB of apparent loudness needs the same 3 dB removed for the comparison. Peak meters mislead here because dense material peaks lower than sparse material at equal loudness.

name: cue-mix-for-tracking
description: Builds and troubleshoots headphone mixes so performers can play in time and in tune. Use when a singer keeps drifting flat, when a drummer cannot hear the click, or when the band asks for more of themselves in the cans. Also use when setting up a tracking session with several headphone feeds and a talkback path.
expansions: singer keeps drifting flat in takes
drummer cannot hear the click
band wants more of themselves
setting up separate headphone feeds
talkback mic is feeding back
headphone latency throws the player off
reverb in the singer headphones
bass player says the cue is muddy

atoms.obligation: Give every performer a cue mix built for their part rather than a shrunken copy of the control room balance.
atoms.lesson: A singer needs pitch references loud: bass, plus a keyboard or guitar playing the changes, plus their own voice on top, with drums low enough not to mask them. A drummer needs the click, the bass and a rhythmic anchor, with the click bright enough to cut through cymbals, often a wood block around 1 to 3 kHz. Control room balances are built for judging tone, which rarely helps anyone keep time.

atoms.obligation: Add light reverb and gentle compression to the singer cue without printing either to the recorded track.
atoms.lesson: Vocalists push harder and sing sharp when they hear a dry, exposed voice. A short plate or hall at low level, roughly 1.2 to 1.8 seconds, plus a compressor doing 3 to 6 dB of gain reduction on the cue send alone, makes a singer relax and sing softer. Keeping the effect on the monitor path leaves the recorded file dry so the mix engineer retains every option later on.

atoms.obligation: Keep monitoring latency under about ten milliseconds by routing performer feeds around heavy processing.
atoms.lesson: Round trip latency above roughly 10 ms makes singers sit behind the beat and drummers rush to compensate. A 64 or 128 sample buffer at 48 kHz gives a few milliseconds each way, but delay compensation adds more: linear phase equalizers and lookahead limiters can each contribute 30 to 100 ms. Route the performer through low latency direct monitoring, or disable those plugins while tracking and restore them for mixing.

atoms.obligation: Confirm the talkback path dims the speakers, sits under the cue level, and mutes when the transport rolls.
atoms.lesson: An open talkback feeding the same headphones the control room monitors creates a feedback loop, which is why the standard fix is dimming the control room speakers whenever talkback is keyed. Performers also hate the level jump of a hot talkback between takes, so keep it a few decibels under the cue mix. Muting talkback while recording stops control room chatter printing onto open room mics.

name: vocal-comping-tuning
description: Assembles a lead vocal from multiple takes and corrects pitch and timing without turning the performance into plastic. Use when there are a dozen passes of a chorus to choose between, when a line goes flat only on the sustain, or when doubles do not line up with the lead. Also use when a client says the vocal sounds over processed.
expansions: twelve takes of the same chorus
vocal goes flat on long notes
double is not lining up with lead
tuning sounds robotic and gluey
picking the best take per line
breaths are too loud between phrases
consonant edits are clicking
harmony stack is out of tune

atoms.obligation: Comp by phrase and by emotion first, then fix pitch, keeping a complete playlist of every source take.
atoms.lesson: The best comp is usually the take with the right attitude on a phrase, not the most in tune one, because pitch is repairable and delivery is not. Work through the song line by line with the lyric written out, marking candidate takes as you go. Keep original playlists intact so any edit can be revisited later; a flattened comp with no surviving source takes is the most common reason a revision round stalls.

atoms.obligation: Place every crossfade on a breath or a consonant, never in the middle of a sustained vowel.
atoms.lesson: Vowels carry continuous pitch and formant information, so a splice inside one lurches audibly even under a long fade. Breaths, plosives and sibilants mask edits because they are noisy transients. A five to fifteen millisecond crossfade at a consonant onset is inaudible, while longer fades across a held note create phasing as two slightly different pitches overlap. Audition each edit soloed and then inside the full track.

atoms.obligation: Correct pitch centres and slow drift while leaving vibrato, scoops and note entries intact.
atoms.lesson: Automatic retune at a fast speed setting flattens the pitch envelope, removing the scoop into a note and the vibrato that make it sound human. Better practice moves the average pitch of a note to centre and leaves its internal modulation alone. Watch for a singer landing correctly then drifting flat across a two second sustain, since correcting only the drift usually fixes it. Formant shifts beyond about three semitones start sounding artificial.

atoms.obligation: Tune doubles and harmonies to the lead vocal rather than to absolute concert pitch.
atoms.lesson: A stack sounds tight when every layer agrees with the lead, including the small deviations the lead makes. Tuning each layer independently to perfect pitch leaves the lead sounding out against them. Align timing at consonant onsets and, more importantly, at the ends of words, because mismatched word endings are what listeners hear as sloppy. Leave a few cents of variation between layers or the stack collapses into one thin voice.

name: drum-editing-replacement
description: Tightens recorded drum performances and blends or replaces samples with an acoustic kit. Use when the kick is inconsistent from hit to hit, when the snare in one verse is a dud, or when someone asks to trigger samples under a live kit. Also use when quantized drums have lost their groove or edits are flamming against the overheads.
expansions: kick sounds different every hit
snare on verse three is a dud
trigger samples under the live kit
drums feel stiff after quantizing
hi hat bleed ruining the snare edit
tighten a sloppy drum take
flams between kick and snare edits
sample layer sounds like it flams

atoms.obligation: Align replacement samples to the original transient sample accurately and check polarity against the acoustic hit.
atoms.lesson: A sample landing even one or two milliseconds late doubles the attack and smears the transient, and a polarity mismatch cancels most of a kick drum low end. Trigger detection should read the close mic rather than the overheads, with a hold time long enough to reject the second stroke of a buzz roll. Blending usually works best with the sample supplying 60 to 150 Hz weight and the original supplying stick attack and room.

atoms.obligation: Edit the whole kit together against the overheads and room mics so bleed does not create flams or gaps.
atoms.lesson: Every close mic edit also moves the bleed inside it. Editing close mics independently makes a snare appear twice in the overheads, once from the moved close mic and once from the untouched overhead. Grouping the entire kit so all tracks cut at the same point keeps it coherent, and crossfades of five to twenty milliseconds across all tracks hide the joins. Fills need editing by hand because grid quantization ruins their feel.

atoms.obligation: Preserve groove by quantizing partially and by anchoring edits to the drummer own strong beats.
atoms.lesson: Full quantization to a hard grid strips the push and pull that makes a track breathe. A strength of 50 to 80 percent tightens without flattening. Many drummers place the kick slightly early and the snare a few milliseconds late, which reads as drive, so measuring that offset and building a groove template from their best bars preserves it. Snap only what is genuinely out, most often the entries after fills.

atoms.obligation: Rebuild a bad hit from a neighbouring bar of the same performance before reaching for an outside sample.
atoms.lesson: A hit taken from elsewhere in the same session already matches the kit, the tuning, the room and the mic balance, so it drops in invisibly. Copy it across every kit track at once so the bleed matches, and land it on the same beat position in the bar so the overhead tail sits correctly. Only when no usable hit exists anywhere in the session does an external sample become worth the blending work.

name: reamping-di-guitars
description: Captures direct instrument signals alongside amplifiers and re-records them through different rigs afterwards. Use when a guitar tone turns out wrong once the arrangement changes, when the band wants to try another amp after tracking, or when a direct signal is buzzing or hitting the amp input too hot. Also use when someone asks how to wire a reamp chain.
expansions: guitar tone was wrong in hindsight
want to try a different amp now
di sounds thin and buzzy
reamp box levels are too hot
hum when the reamp box is connected
kept the di but not the amp
bass di needs a cabinet later
matching reamp to the original take

atoms.obligation: Print a clean direct signal on every electric guitar and bass pass, even when the amplifier tone already sounds right.
atoms.lesson: The direct signal costs one track and one input and it is the only insurance against a tone that stops working once the arrangement fills out. Take it from a passive splitter or an instrument level output ahead of any amp distortion, keeping input impedance high, around one megohm, so the pickups do not lose top end. Label it with guitar, pickup position and tuning, since none of that is recoverable from the file later.

atoms.obligation: Convert line level back to instrument level and impedance before feeding any amplifier input.
atoms.lesson: An interface output is line level and low impedance while an amp front end expects an unbalanced high impedance signal around minus 20 dBu. Feeding line level straight in overdrives the input stage in a fizzy rather than musical way, and the impedance mismatch changes the frequency response. A transformer based reamp box handles both and gives ground isolation. Set its level so the amp reacts the way it did during tracking.

atoms.obligation: Break ground loops at one end of the reamp path and move cables away from power supplies when hum appears.
atoms.lesson: A reamp path creates a loop between the control room and the amp room, and mains hum at 50 or 60 Hz with its harmonics is the result. A transformer isolated box with a ground lift breaks it. Single coil pickups and unshielded cables also collect buzz from dimmers, screens and power conditioners, so rotate the guitar or the amp and listen for the null before blaming the wiring.

atoms.obligation: Match the reamped performance to the original in arrival time and loudness before judging which tone is better.
atoms.lesson: The reamped signal returns later by the round trip latency of the interface plus the acoustic distance from speaker to microphone, roughly one millisecond per foot. If loop back compensation is not exact the new take sits behind the band and every comparison is unfair. Nudge it until the transient lines up with the original amp track, then match loudness before deciding which amplifier actually sounds better.

name: midi-groove-programming
description: Programs drum, bass and keyboard parts that feel played rather than typed. Use when a programmed beat sounds mechanical, when every note carries the same velocity, or when hi hats need swing that matches a sampled loop. Also use when a virtual instrument gives machine gun repeats or jumps timbre between velocity layers.
expansions: programmed beat sounds mechanical
every note has the same velocity
hats need swing to match the loop
machine gun repeated snare hits
bass line does not lock with kick
piano part sounds typed not played
need a shuffle feel on the grid
velocity layers jump in tone

atoms.obligation: Vary velocity and micro timing note by note instead of applying one blanket randomizing pass across a part.
atoms.lesson: Real players vary loudness in patterns rather than randomly: backbeats are strongest, ghost notes sit 20 to 40 velocity units below, and hi hats accent downbeats. A blanket randomize spreads variation everywhere and reads as sloppy rather than human. Timing offsets of five to twenty milliseconds are the useful range, since beyond about thirty milliseconds a note simply sounds late. Draw the accent pattern first, then add small deviations within it.

atoms.obligation: Match the swing of programmed parts to the swing already present in any sampled loop in the track.
atoms.lesson: Swing is the delay of the offbeat subdivision, running from straight at 50 percent to a full triplet near 66 percent. Two elements at different swing values fight and produce a flamming feel. Extract the groove from the loop rather than guessing, then apply that timing template to the programmed hats and bass. A shuffled blues sits nearer 60 percent while many hip hop grooves land between 54 and 58 percent.

atoms.obligation: Respect the sampled instrument velocity layers and round robin behaviour when choosing note strengths.
atoms.lesson: A multisampled kit switches sample and timbre at layer boundaries, so notes clustered around a boundary flip tone unpredictably. Sitting a few velocity units clear of the boundary keeps the sound stable. Repeated identical hits retrigger the same sample once round robins run out, producing the machine gun effect, so varying velocity or nudging timing forces different samples. Fast rolls usually need a dedicated roll articulation instead of repeated single hits.
