atoms.obligation: Include a calibrated colour and resolution target in the capture setup and image it with each batch or session.
atoms.lesson: A greyscale and colour target with a resolution element in the frame is what makes the file measurable rather than merely attractive: it records tone reproduction, white balance, sharpening and geometric accuracy at the moment of capture. Photograph it at the start of each session and after any lighting or lens change, keep the target frames with the batch, and re-profile when performance drifts. Without a target, a claim about colour accuracy in a specification is unenforceable at delivery.

atoms.obligation: Produce an unedited preservation master plus defined derivatives, and keep all editing out of the master file.
atoms.lesson: The master is an uncompressed or losslessly compressed file with an embedded colour profile, holding the whole object including its edges and any mount or margin, with no cropping, rotation beyond orientation, sharpening or tonal manipulation. Access derivatives are generated from it, sized and compressed for delivery, and can be regenerated when standards change. Recording the capture device, operator, date and settings alongside the master lets a later curator judge the file without re-examining the original.

atoms.obligation: Specify handling and cradle requirements for bound and fragile originals, and set a condition threshold that stops capture.
atoms.lesson: Tight bindings must not be forced flat: a book cradle with an adjustable opening angle, often limited to around one hundred and twenty degrees, plus a glass platen or overhead capture, protects the spine. Brittle paper, flaking emulsion, mould, cellulose acetate with vinegar syndrome and rolled items needing humidification stop the workflow and go to conservation first. The specification should say who decides, and that a digitised page is never worth a broken text block.

name: digital-preservation-ingest
description: Takes digital content into managed preservation storage with fixity, multiple copies, format policy and recorded preservation events. Use when a batch is ready for ingest, when a checksum no longer matches, when deciding how many copies to keep and where, when a format is heading for obsolescence, or when a storage audit is overdue.
expansions: checksum mismatch on a folder
ingest a batch into preservation storage
how many copies and where
format at risk of obsolescence
record the preservation events
verify fixity on the archive store
restore a file from a backup copy
the storage audit is overdue

atoms.obligation: Generate a fixity value for every file at the point of receipt and store it with the content and its inventory.
atoms.lesson: A cryptographic digest computed before the material moves is the baseline against which all later verification is judged; a checksum generated after files have already sat on a staging drive certifies whatever damage happened before. Package the files with a manifest listing each path and its digest so the package is self-describing and can be validated anywhere. Verify the manifest immediately after any transfer, because silent truncation during copying is common and invisible.

atoms.obligation: Keep multiple independent copies in separate locations with different failure modes, and confirm each copy is readable.
atoms.lesson: Established practice is at least three copies, on at least two kinds of storage, with at least one geographically distant and one offline or otherwise insulated from a mistaken deletion propagating everywhere. Copies inside one building, one account or one synchronising folder are one copy wearing disguises. Test restoration on a sample each year: a copy nobody has ever read back is an assumption, not a backup, and tape or cloud retrieval terms often surprise on first real use.

atoms.obligation: Run scheduled fixity checks across the holdings and treat any mismatch as an incident with a repair from a good copy.
atoms.lesson: Audit frequency is a trade-off between assurance and read cost; annual verification of everything with more frequent sampling of recent or high-value content is typical. A mismatch means either bit rot, a failed transfer or an unauthorised change, and the response is to identify which copies still validate, restore the file from one of them, re-verify, and record what happened. Repeated failures in the same storage location are a signal to migrate off it.

atoms.obligation: Record preservation events with their date, agent and outcome so the chain of custody of each file is reconstructable.
atoms.lesson: Ingest, virus scan, fixity check, format identification, normalisation, migration and any repair are each events tied to the object they acted on, with who or what performed them and whether they succeeded. This history is what lets a future archivist trust that the file they open is the file that was received, and is the digital equivalent of provenance and custody documentation. Also record the format identification and the significant characteristics that any future migration must preserve.

name: born-digital-media-capture
description: Recovers content from donated physical media and personal devices without altering the original, and documents what was captured. Use when an accession contains floppies, optical discs or drives, when a retiring staff member hands over a laptop, when a donor has obsolete cartridges nobody can read, or when a carrier is degrading and needs capturing now.
expansions: box of floppy disks in the accession
laptop from a retiring professor
capture a hard drive without altering it
zip disks nobody can read
donor emailed a folder of files
image a disc before it fails
virus scan a donor drive
obsolete media in a manuscript collection

atoms.obligation: Connect original media only through a device that prevents writing, and never mount a donor disk directly for browsing.
atoms.lesson: Attaching media to an ordinary workstation modifies it: the operating system updates access times, writes recovery and index files, and can trigger automatic synchronisation. A hardware write blocker or a verified software equivalent sits between the carrier and the workstation so the evidence stays as received. Photograph each carrier and its labels before capture, since handwritten labels are often the only provenance information and the only clue to dates, authorship and content.

atoms.obligation: Capture a complete image of each carrier rather than copying visible files, and record the capture outcome per item.
atoms.lesson: A disk image preserves deleted-but-recoverable content, file system metadata, timestamps and slack space, and lets the carrier be set aside afterwards. File-level copying loses all of that and silently drops anything the current operating system cannot see. Record the media identifier, the capture device, whether the read succeeded fully or with errors, the number of bad sectors, and the fixity value of the image. Failed reads may be retried later with a different drive rather than declared lost.

atoms.obligation: Scan captured content for malware and quarantine infected material before anyone opens it for appraisal.
atoms.lesson: Media from the 1990s carry boot sector and macro viruses that modern staff machines will happily execute, and drives from an office may carry recent malware. Scan the image on an isolated machine with current definitions, log what was found, and quarantine rather than clean where cleaning would alter the archival object. Appraisal should then happen on a copy in a controlled environment, never on the original carrier and never on a networked administrative workstation.

atoms.obligation: Triage carriers by degradation risk and capture the most endangered formats before the stable ones.
atoms.lesson: Optical discs, particularly recordable ones, suffer dye and reflective-layer failure within a decade or two; magnetic floppies lose signal and shed oxide; hard drives seize after long storage; flash media lose charge unpowered. Cartridge and proprietary formats are limited by the shrinking supply of working drives more than by the media. So capture recordable discs, five and a quarter inch floppies and exotic cartridges first, and treat a working legacy drive as a scarce shared asset to be booked and maintained.

name: rights-and-reuse-assessment
description: Determines the copyright status of material and what the institution and its users may lawfully do with it, ending in a public rights statement. Use when deciding whether a collection can go online, when a creator death date is known but publication is not, when a publisher requests permission to reproduce, or when a rights holder cannot be found.
expansions: can we put this collection online
the photographer died in 1968
unpublished letters from 1930
rights statement for the digital collection
publisher asks permission to reproduce
orphan work with no findable heir
student wants to use an image
is this pamphlet public domain

atoms.obligation: Establish publication status, date, author death date and jurisdiction before applying any term of protection.
atoms.lesson: The four facts drive everything and are gathered from the item and its file: was it published or does it survive only as unpublished correspondence, drafts or photographs; when was it created and when if ever issued to the public; who created it and when did they die; and under which country law was it first published. Corporate and anonymous works run on a different clock. Record the evidence for each fact, since the assessment must be defensible years later.

atoms.obligation: Treat unpublished works under the rules for unpublished material rather than assuming age alone puts them in the public domain.
atoms.lesson: Unpublished letters, diaries, manuscripts and photographs are typically protected for the life of the creator plus seventy years, so a 1930 letter by someone who died in 1975 remains in copyright well past the point when a published 1930 book has expired. Anonymous and corporate unpublished works run on a term from creation. This is why archival digitisation programmes usually mix genuinely expired material, protected material used under an exception, and material shown with a rights statement rather than a licence.

atoms.obligation: Document a reasonably diligent search for the rights holder and record the risk assessment when none is found.
atoms.lesson: A diligent search checks copyright registration and renewal records, obituaries and probate, publisher and estate contacts, professional associations, genealogy sources and prior published uses. When it fails, the work is effectively orphaned, and most repositories proceed on a documented risk assessment weighing the commercial value, the sensitivity of the content and the likelihood of a claim, publishing with a clear takedown notice and a contact route for anyone who comes forward.

atoms.obligation: Publish a standardised rights statement with each digitised item and keep the licence separate from the physical fee.
atoms.lesson: Users need to know status and permitted use at the point of viewing, using a standardised statement such as no known copyright, in copyright with educational use permitted, or copyright undetermined, rather than a blanket assertion of institutional ownership over public domain scans. A reproduction fee pays for staff time and imaging; it is not a copyright licence and cannot create rights in an expired work, so keep the two clauses distinct in the order form.

name: restricted-access-screening
description: Screens collections for personal, medical, educational and confidential content, and sets closure periods, redaction or mediated access accordingly. Use when identifiers turn up in the files, when a researcher requests restricted boxes, when a donor imposed a closure, or when a series must be reviewed before it opens or is scanned.
expansions: social security numbers in the files
student grades in a faculty collection
set a closure period for personnel files
researcher requests restricted boxes
redact before scanning
medical records in family papers
donor imposed a twenty five year restriction
screen a series before it opens

atoms.obligation: Screen at the series level for the record types that reliably carry sensitive content rather than reading every page.
atoms.lesson: Whole-collection page review is unaffordable, so target the categories that predictably contain protected information: personnel and search committee files, student records including grades and disciplinary matters, patient and clinical material, adoption and social service case files, legal files under privilege, financial account records and anything with government identification numbers. Sample within those series to confirm, and describe the restriction at series level so a reader learns the boundary from the finding aid rather than at the desk.

atoms.obligation: Set a defined closure period tied to the record date or the individual, and record when the restriction lapses.
atoms.lesson: Common practice closes personnel files for a term measured from the end of employment, student records for a long fixed term, and clinical material for decades from the date of the record or a period after death. The closure must carry an expiry the repository actually tracks; otherwise the default becomes permanent. Store the review date with the series so that boxes reopen on schedule, and note in the finding aid the year in which each restricted series becomes available.

atoms.obligation: Redact only surrogates and never mark, cut or obscure the original archival document.
atoms.lesson: Redaction happens on a copy: a photocopy or a digital surrogate is masked and served, while the original stays intact in the box for the day the restriction lapses. Redact by covering, not by relying on a layer that can be lifted, and verify the delivered copy carries no recoverable text. Record which items were redacted and why, because a researcher who finds blanked passages needs to know the basis, and a later reviewer needs to know what was withheld.

atoms.obligation: Offer mediated access with a use agreement where the risk is to identifiable individuals rather than closing outright.
atoms.lesson: Between fully open and fully closed sits supervised access: the researcher signs an agreement not to publish identifying details, works in the reading room without personal cameras, and submits notes or a draft for review where the donor agreement requires it. This suits health, social work and personnel material where the research value is high and the harm is to named people. Apply the same terms to every requester and keep a record, so the arrangement is equitable rather than ad hoc.

name: preservation-condition-survey
description: Assesses the physical condition of collections and their storage environment, and turns the findings into a prioritised treatment and rehousing plan. Use when the stacks smell musty, when temperature or humidity swing, when insects appear in the cases, when leather or paper is deteriorating, or when a survey is needed to justify enclosures or a conservation budget.
expansions: musty smell in the stacks
temperature swings in the reading room
silverfish in the map cases
brittle paper crumbling at the edges
survey the condition of a collection
which items need new enclosures
red rot on the leather bindings
climate control shut down over the weekend

atoms.obligation: Monitor temperature and humidity continuously in each storage area and act on the fluctuation as well as the average.
atoms.lesson: General collections storage typically targets a stable temperature in the region of eighteen to twenty degrees Celsius with relative humidity between thirty and fifty percent, colder for photographic and film material. Stability matters as much as the set point, since repeated swings drive expansion and contraction that cracks emulsions and cockles paper. Place loggers at shelf height in several spots, including outside walls and floor level, and review the plotted curves rather than a single spot reading.

atoms.obligation: Run a monitoring programme for pests with placed traps, scheduled inspection and a no-food rule in collection areas.
atoms.lesson: Blunder traps placed along walls, under shelving and near doors, checked and dated on a schedule, show which species are present and where they enter. Silverfish and booklice indicate damp; carpet and drugstore beetles attack adhesives, leather and specimens; rodents build nests from paper. Response is environmental first, drying and sealing entry points, with freezing at around minus twenty for a sustained period used to treat infested items rather than routine chemical spraying in the stacks.

atoms.obligation: Isolate any suspected mould immediately, correct the moisture source, and do not disturb the growth in an open stack.
atoms.lesson: Mould germinates when relative humidity at the surface sustains above about sixty five to seventy percent, and disturbing bloom releases spores through the whole room. Bag suspect items, move them out, dehumidify and increase air movement to bring the area down, and let material dry before any cleaning. Cleaning is done under a hood or outdoors with appropriate respiratory protection using gentle suction; dead mould still stains and still triggers allergic reactions, so handling controls remain in force.

atoms.obligation: Record condition findings in a consistent format and rank the resulting treatment work by risk and use.
atoms.lesson: Survey by sample rather than item where collections are large, scoring each unit for paper embrittlement, binding failure, media flaking, mould, pest damage and enclosure adequacy. Prioritisation weighs the severity of the deterioration, the rarity and value of the material and how heavily it is consulted, since a fragile item that circulates weekly is more at risk than one in cold storage. The ranked list becomes the supply order, the conservation queue and the grant application evidence.

name: disaster-salvage-triage
description: Directs the first response to water, fire or mould emergencies affecting collections, deciding what to stabilise, what to freeze and what to dry. Use when a pipe bursts over the stacks, when a sprinkler discharges, when boxes are found sitting in water, or when deciding between air drying, freezing and calling a recovery contractor.
expansions: pipe burst over the stacks
wet boxes on the floor
the sprinkler discharged last night
how to dry soaked photographs
freeze these books or air dry them
call a recovery vendor tonight
salvage priorities for the collection
document the damage for insurance

atoms.obligation: Make the area safe and stop the water before touching collections, and confirm power and structural safety first.
atoms.lesson: Nobody salvages anything in an unsafe room. Shut off the water source, have electrical circuits isolated where ceilings or fittings are wet, check for hazards such as unstable shelving and contaminated water from sewage or firefighting run-off, and issue gloves and protective equipment. Then reduce temperature and raise air movement in the affected space, because the objective in the first hours is to slow mould germination while triage decisions are being made.

atoms.obligation: Get wet material stabilised or frozen within roughly forty eight hours of getting wet before mould establishes.
atoms.lesson: At normal room temperature mould can germinate on damp paper within about two days, so the window governs every decision. Items that cannot be air dried within it go into a freezer, packed spine down in crates with a single layer, interleaved from other items rather than tightly packed, at around minus twenty. Freezing does not repair damage but stops the clock indefinitely and allows a considered choice between vacuum freeze drying and air drying later.

atoms.obligation: Salvage by priority list first, and separate the material types whose treatment differs before any drying begins.
atoms.lesson: Work from the pre-agreed priority list of irreplaceable and high-value holdings rather than starting at the nearest shelf. Then sort by material: coated paper must be kept wet and frozen because its pages block solid once dried; photographic prints and negatives are best kept wet in cool clean water and frozen or dried promptly; parchment, leather and audiovisual carriers each need distinct handling; and soluble media may run if blotted. Never open a wet volume more than gently.

atoms.obligation: Photograph and log the damage as it is found, with counts, locations and identifiers, before material is moved.
atoms.lesson: Insurance settlement, recovery contractor scoping and later reporting all depend on documentation made during the response, not reconstructed afterwards. Photograph the room, the shelf ranges, and representative damaged items, log the shelf marks or accession numbers and the number of containers affected, and note the water source and the elapsed time before response. Keep the log with the freezer manifest so that crates can be tracked back to their collection when they return.

name: records-retention-schedule
description: Appraises the records an institution creates and sets how long each series is kept, who keeps it and what happens at the end. Use when an office asks how long to keep files, when a department wants to purge, when drafting or revising a schedule, when a legal hold arrives, or when deciding which office records are archival.
expansions: how long do we keep these records
the office wants to purge old files
draft a retention schedule
records are under legal hold
which office records are archival
annual disposition certificate
shared drive full of old files
auditors are asking for a schedule

atoms.obligation: Build the schedule around record series defined by function, not around the office, the medium or the file name.
atoms.lesson: A series is a group of records created and used together for one function, such as grant financial reports, student admission files or governing board minutes, and it keeps its retention wherever it lives and whatever form it takes. Scheduling by department breaks the moment a reorganisation moves the function; scheduling by folder name breaks the moment somebody renames things. Interview the office about what they do, then name the series after the activity that produces them.

atoms.obligation: State the retention as a trigger event plus a period, and name the disposition that follows.
atoms.lesson: Retention such as seven years after the end of the contract, or three years after the student leaves, is enforceable, whereas simply seven years is not, because nobody knows from what. The trigger has to be an event the office can identify from the record itself. Disposition is then destroy, transfer to the archives for permanent retention, or review, and the schedule should say which, because a series with a period but no ending decision is still stored forever by default.

atoms.obligation: Appraise each series for enduring value and mark the small proportion that transfers permanently to the archives.
atoms.lesson: Typically well under a tenth of institutional records merit permanent retention. Look for evidence of policy and decision making such as board and senior committee minutes, founding and legal instruments, annual reports, budgets and audited statements, organisation charts, publications, photographs, and records documenting the institution effect on people and community. Routine transactional records, duplicates and reference copies of material held elsewhere are scheduled for destruction however voluminous, since keeping everything obscures the material that matters.

atoms.obligation: Suspend all destruction for records under legal hold and resume only on written release from counsel.
atoms.lesson: Once litigation, audit or investigation is reasonably anticipated, the routine schedule stops for the affected series regardless of how long they have sat past retention, and destroying under schedule at that point is still spoliation. Communicate the hold in writing to every custodian, including the holders of shared drives and mailboxes, list the series and date ranges affected, and track the hold to a written release. Document each authorised destruction with a certificate signed by the office and the records officer.
